You arrive while the sky is turning blue-grey, hear the first burst of music from the midway and realise the Canadian National Exhibition has opened for another season. The event began in 1879 as the Toronto Industrial Exhibition, designed to bring together farming, industry and new ideas from across Canada. More than a century later, that purpose still survives in the exhibits and demonstrations spread across the grounds.

A first-time visitor might start with the giant slide, then drift towards the soaring swings, game booths and live performances. The food is part of the tradition too, with poutine, corn dogs, butter tarts and ice cream drawing long queues alongside the CNE's famous over-the-top creations. Look up and you may also catch the Canadian International Air Show, scheduled for September 5-7 over Toronto's waterfront. By evening, thousands of lights flicker on, rides glow against the darkening sky and the whole place hums with late-summer excitement. So, what's your first stop at the CNE this year?

bing-57296.jpg.title: Winding road of Julier Pass, Switzerland
bing-57296.jpg.headline: The climb is calling. Winding road of Julier Pass, Switzerland
bing-57296.jpg.description:
Some mountain roads become destinations in their own right, and Julier Pass is one of them. This Swiss mountain pass rises to 7,493 feet and has linked Alpine valleys along a route used for nearly 2,000 years. Its story began long before modern traffic. No guardrails, no pavement—just a route used by Roman travelers, merchants, and messengers. Archaeological finds near the summit, including countless coins and two Roman soapstone columns, suggest there was once a sanctuary or stopping place for those tackling the climb.

The road seen in today's image was built between 1820 and 1828. From 1935 to 1940, the pass became the first Swiss alpine road to be paved with asphalt. Today, roughly 3,000 vehicles cross Julier Pass every day. In winter, drivers may need snow chains when conditions are severe. Every switchback comes with another spectacular view, making the drive as memorable as the destination. If you had the keys, would you take the scenic route?

bing-57301.jpg.title: Vista general del pelotón durante la 77ª Vuelta a España 2022, Etapa 20, Navacerrada, España
bing-57301.jpg.headline: Vuelta a casa sobre ruedas. La Vuelta a España
bing-57301.jpg.description:
En la imagen vemos cómo el pelotón de La Vuelta a España asciende el puerto de Navacerrada, uno de los escenarios más míticos de la carrera desde 1941, con sus rampas de hasta el 13% en plena Sierra de Guadarrama.

Hoy arranca la 81ª edición desde Mónaco, y lo hace con una novedad histórica: por primera vez, Granada acogerá la llegada final el 13 de septiembre, con la Alhambra como telón de fondo. La Vuelta, que nació en 1935 y forma parte de las tres Grandes Vueltas del ciclismo mundial junto al Tour de Francia y el Giro de Italia, recorrerá 3.275 kilómetros en 21 etapas bordeando el Mediterráneo hasta Andalucía. El maillot rojo del liderato ha pertenecido a leyendas como Bahamontes, Induráin y Contador. Una carrera que no solo atraviesa España, sino que escribe su historia kilómetro a kilómetro.

bing-57303.jpg.title: Torre Sant'Andrea, Salento, Puglia, Italia
bing-57303.jpg.headline: Il suono della Taranta
bing-57303.jpg.description:
Le acque turchesi di Torre Sant'Andrea, nel Salento pugliese, con i loro faraglioni di roccia bianca levigata dal mare, sono una delle coste più spettacolari d'Italia. Ed è proprio in questo lembo di Puglia che stasera si accende la 29ª edizione de La Notte della Taranta, il più grande festival di musica popolare d'Europa: nato a Melpignano nel 1998, ogni anno attraversa venti borghi del Salento prima del Concertone finale.

Al cuore del festival c'è la pizzica, danza ipnotica nata dai riti del tarantismo: un'antica pratica coreutica e musicale che si usava per esorcizzare dolori e traumi. Oggi la pizzica incontra le sonorità del mondo intero, mescolando tradizione e contaminazione sotto le stelle salentine. La 29ª edizione vede come maestro concertatore Ermal Meta, che guiderà l'Orchestra Popolare in una notte da ballare e ricordare. Il Salento chiama: il ritmo risponde.

bing-57306.jpg.title: Integrantes da Salgueiro na Marquês de Sapucaí em 2022, Rio de Janeiro
bing-57306.jpg.headline: A longa dança da história
bing-57306.jpg.description:
Algumas histórias vivem no papel. O Dia do Folclore celebra as que atravessam gerações cantadas, dançadas, bordadas e reinventadas. A palavra "folklore" nasceu na Inglaterra, em 1846, para definir os saberes de um povo, mas no Brasil ganhou ritmos, cores e vozes moldados por séculos de encontros entre indígenas, africanos e europeus. Por aqui, o Saci apronta, a Iara encanta rios, o Boto muda de forma e o Curupira insiste em despistar quem entra na mata. Bumba Meu Boi, frevo, maracatu, carimbó, fandango, cordel, capoeira, repentes, cantigas e receitas continuam circulando de voz em voz, de mãos em mãos e de festa em festa.

O Carnaval é um dos maiores palcos do folclore brasileiro. Na imagem, a escola de samba Acadêmicos do Salgueiro desfila pela Marquês de Sapucaí, no Rio de Janeiro, transformando lendas, personagens populares e tradições regionais em alegorias monumentais diante de milhões de pessoas. Nosso folclore não sobrevive porque resiste ao tempo. Sobrevive porque dança com ele.

bing-57308.jpg.title: Common blue butterfly, Devon, England
bing-57308.jpg.headline: Sky tinted wings. Common blue butterfly
bing-57308.jpg.description:
That quick glimpse of blue fluttering through a field has a story that begins much earlier, with a tiny caterpillar and a surprising survival trick. The common blue is found across Europe, North Africa, and parts of Asia, feeding on flower nectar as an adult. It starts life as a small egg, often placed by a female on a host plant such as bird's-foot trefoil. The real surprise comes during its caterpillar stage, when ants play an unexpected role in its survival. After hatching, the caterpillar feeds on leaves before entering the next stage of its transformation. Along the way, it produces a sugary substance called honeydew that ants feed on. As a way of saying thanks, the ants may protect the cocooned caterpillar from predators.

When the adult butterfly emerges, males reveal the blue wings that gave the species its name. Microscopic wing structures create the color by reflecting light. Females usually have brown wings with orange spots along their edges. The common blue butterfly's journey shows that nature's smallest creatures have surprisingly complex lives.

bing-57310.jpg.title: 夏の森を潤す清流, 静岡県
bing-57310.jpg.headline: 今日は処暑
bing-57310.jpg.description: 今日 8 月 23 日は二十四節気の一つ、「処暑」です。次の二十四節気である「白露」までの期間を指す言葉でもあり、厳しい夏の暑さが峠を越え、少しずつ秋の気配が感じられる頃とされています。そして、今日の画像は、静岡県内を流れる川の風景。自然豊かな川辺は真夏でも涼しさを感じることができ、夏の終わりにキャンプや散策を楽しむのにもぴったりの場所です。

bing-57311.jpg.title: 在处暑时节的村庄田野与寺庙佛塔，江阴市，江苏省，中国
bing-57311.jpg.headline: 暑气渐消，金秋已至
bing-57311.jpg.description: 处暑时节将至，航拍视角下的古塔迎着晨雾耸立于渐染秋色的林木之间，生动呈现了暑气消退、金秋将至的自然韵律，以及中国传统文化景观的悠久魅力 。这一时节的传统习俗包括放河灯、迎秋赏景以及饮用中草药煎剂（如凉茶/防暑汤），以调和四季交替时的身体平衡 。

bing-57320.jpg.title: Brown bear fishing in river, Katmai National Park, Alaska
bing-57320.jpg.headline: Meet Katmai's fishing giants. National Park Week
bing-57320.jpg.description:
At Katmai National Park, crowd-pleasers don't need a stage. Brown bears wait by the river, and when the salmon jump, the show begins. National Park Week—held in August this year—is the perfect time to celebrate these iconic bears and the wild home that helps them thrive.

Katmai National Park in Alaska is home to around 2,200 brown bears, one of the highest concentrations in the world. During the sockeye salmon run, as many as 40 bears can gather along the Brooks River to fish. Some catch salmon midair at Brooks Falls, while others dive beneath the surface in search of a meal. With so much food available, these usually solitary animals often fish side by side.

Many adult bears weigh 700 to 900 pounds by late summer, and the largest males may exceed 1,200 pounds before hibernation. Yet even these giants begin life as a 1-pound cub. It's no wonder the park's annual Fat Bear Week has become a favorite—these animals are simply un-bear-lievable.

bing-57332.jpg.title: Brooklyn Bridge, New York City
bing-57332.jpg.headline: Crossing into history. Brooklyn Bridge, New York City
bing-57332.jpg.description:
The Brooklyn Bridge doesn't just connect Manhattan and Brooklyn—it bridges history, engineering, and a few surprising stories too. Opened in 1883 after 14 years of construction, it became the world's first steel-wire suspension bridge, forever changing the way New Yorkers crossed the East River.

The project was a true family affair. After designer John A. Roebling died and his son Washington became too ill to oversee construction, Washington's wife, Emily, learned engineering and higher mathematics to supervise the project's completion.

Not everyone trusted the new structure. In 1884, showman P.T. Barnum marched 21 elephants and 17 camels across the bridge to prove it was strong enough. Hidden vaults inside the bridge later stored wine and champagne before serving as Cold War fallout shelters, where forgotten emergency supplies were rediscovered in 2006. Today, peregrine falcons nest atop its stone towers, proving this iconic landmark still has plenty of high-flying residents. Some bridges simply never go out of style.

bing-57338.jpg.title: Kitesurfer bei Sonnenuntergang in Deutschland
bing-57338.jpg.headline: Wellen, Wind, Weltklasse. Kite-Surf World Cup auf Sylt
bing-57338.jpg.description:
Im goldenen Licht der untergehenden Sonne gleiten Kitesurfer über das Wasser. Die Sportart verbindet Elemente des Surfens, Segelns und Wakeboardens: Ein großer Lenkdrachen sorgt für den Antrieb, während die Fahrer über die Wellen rasen und spektakuläre Sprünge und Tricks ausführen. Kitesurfen entstand in den 1990er-Jahren und hat sich seitdem zu einer beliebten Wassersportart entwickelt. Ob auf dem Meer, an Seen oder in Lagunen – entscheidend sind ausreichend Wind, Geschicklichkeit und ein gutes Gespür für die Bedingungen auf dem Wasser.

Vom 25. bis 30. August steht die Sportart beim Kite-Surf World Cup auf Sylt im Mittelpunkt. Auf Deutschlands größter Nordseeinsel treffen internationale Spitzenathleten zusammen, um sich in Disziplinen wie Wave Riding und Strapless Freestyle zu messen. Die Kombination aus Wind, Wellen und anspruchsvollen Bedingungen macht Sylt zu einem beliebten Austragungsort und den Wettbewerb zu einem festen Bestandteil des internationalen Kitesurf-Kalenders. Dabei erleben Besucher Spitzensport vor der Kulisse der Nordsee.

bing-57340.jpg.title: Plage de sable blanc sur l’archipel des Glénan, Bretagne
bing-57340.jpg.headline: Sable blanc et lagons bretons. Plage de sable blanc sur l’archipel des Glénan, Bretagne
bing-57340.jpg.description:
Au large de la côte sud du Finistère, l’archipel des Glénan déploie un chapelet d’îlots aux eaux turquoise, si limpides qu’elles évoquent parfois des lagons lointains. Pourtant, nous sommes bien en Bretagne. Façonnées par les vents, les marées et les tempêtes, ces terres de sable blanc et de granite abritent un patrimoine naturel exceptionnel.

Au printemps, les dunes se parent de la délicate narcisse des Glénan, une fleur rare présente presque exclusivement dans ces îles. Sous le soleil estival, les plages semblent suspendues entre ciel et mer. Les herbiers marins abritent une riche vie sous-marine, tandis que les sternes et autres oiseaux marins animent l’horizon de leurs cris. La lumière danse sur les lagons peu profonds et dévoile des paysages en perpétuel mouvement.

Longtemps refuge de pêcheurs et de navigateurs, l’archipel reste aujourd’hui un sanctuaire de calme. Entre lumière changeante, parfum iodé et murmure des vagues, les Glénan invitent à ralentir, contempler et apprécier la beauté fragile du littoral breton.

bing-57344.jpg.title: Sunrise in Redwood National and State Parks, California
bing-57344.jpg.headline: Protecting America's treasures. Anniversary of National Park Service
bing-57344.jpg.description:
For 110 years, America's greatest outdoor classroom has been open for exploration. On August 25, the National Park Service marks over a century of protecting the nation's natural and cultural treasures. Established in 1916 when President Woodrow Wilson signed the Organic Act into law, the agency now cares for hundreds of parks, monuments, seashores, and historic sites across the country. Ranger-led programs, family activities, and educational events invite visitors to connect with the landscapes and stories that define the national park system.

Today's image shows Redwood National and State Parks in northern California, where sunlight illuminates a trail winding among some of the tallest trees on Earth. Towering coast redwoods rise above a lush understory of ferns and mosses, creating a forest that feels both ancient and alive. Part of an ecosystem supporting diverse wildlife and centuries-old trees, these groves showcase the natural wonders the National Park Service has helped protect for generations, offering visitors the chance to walk beneath living giants and experience a landscape unlike any other.

bing-57349.jpg.title: Parroquia San Pedro Apóstol, Buñol, España
bing-57349.jpg.headline: ¡Huele a verano y gazpacho!. La Tomatina de Buñol, Valencia
bing-57349.jpg.description:
El último miércoles de agosto, Buñol, un municipio valenciano de menos de 10.000 habitantes situado entre montañas a 38 kilómetros de Valencia, recibe a más de 20.000 personas para la Tomatina: una hora en la que los participantes se lanzan unos 115.000 kilos de tomates por las calles del casco histórico.

Todo empezó de forma accidental en 1945: durante un desfile de gigantes y cabezudos, unos jóvenes provocaron un altercado junto a un puesto de verduras y los tomates acabaron volando. Lo que nació como una pelea espontánea se convirtió en tradición, sobrevivió a una prohibición en los años cincuenta —el pueblo organizó un simbólico «entierro del tomate» en protesta— y fue declarada Fiesta de Interés Turístico Internacional en 2002. Antes de la batalla, los participantes intentan superar el palo jabón: trepar un poste enjabonado para alcanzar un jamón en lo alto. Buñol prueba que las mejores tradiciones nacen sin querer.

bing-57356.jpg.title: Auroras over Kirkjufell, Iceland
bing-57356.jpg.headline: A sky alive with color. Auroras over Kirkjufell, Iceland
bing-57356.jpg.description:
As darker nights return to Iceland, visitors will soon look to the skies for a chance to see the aurora borealis. Better known as the northern lights, this luminous phenomenon occurs when particles from the sun interact with gases high in Earth's atmosphere, creating shimmering ribbons of green, pink, purple, and sometimes red light. Iceland's northern location and increasingly dark autumn and winter nights make it one of the world's premier destinations for aurora viewing.

Beneath this ever-changing display stands Kirkjufell, one of the country's most photographed mountains. Its name means 'Church Mountain' in Icelandic, inspired by its church-like shape. Rising above the Snæfellsnes Peninsula, its striking silhouette and the nearby Kirkjufellsfoss waterfall have made the area a favorite of photographers and aurora seekers alike. On clear nights, the mountain, waterfall, and sky align in a scene that seems almost unreal—a remarkable combination that has become one of Iceland's most iconic views.

bing-57368.jpg.title: Lesser flamingo flock at sunrise, Lake Magadi, Kenya
bing-57368.jpg.headline: Water, wildlife, and wonder. World Lake Day
bing-57368.jpg.description:
Imagine a world without the natural wonders that hold about 90% of Earth's surface freshwater. Lakes are among our planet's most valuable resources. They provide clean water, support wildlife, help regulate climate, and sustain communities around the globe. In recognition of their vital role, the United Nations designated August 27 as World Lake Day, first observed in 2025. The need for action is greater than ever. More than 117 million lakes cover nearly 4% of Earth's land surface, yet many face growing pressure from pollution, overuse, and climate change.

Pictured here is Lake Magadi, a shallow alkaline lake in Kenya's Great Rift Valley. Its mineral-rich waters support abundant algae, attracting vast flocks of lesser flamingos that gather there to feed. The birds' pink hues often transform the shoreline into a dazzling spectacle. On World Lake Day, scenes like this remind us that healthy lakes nurture extraordinary wildlife and help sustain life far beyond their shores.

bing-57380.jpg.title: Mont-Saint-Michel during high tide, Manche, Normandy, France
bing-57380.jpg.headline: Where tides shape a legend. Mont-Saint Michel during high tide, Normandy, France
bing-57380.jpg.description:
At sunset, Mont-Saint Michel rises from the waters of Normandy, France, like a fortress shaped by the sea. Perched on a rocky tidal island, the abbey and village stand at the center of one of Europe's most dramatic coastal settings. Twice a day, the sea retreats to reveal vast stretches of sand before surging back to reclaim the landscape. At high tide, the mount becomes an island once again. For centuries, travelers timed their journeys to this rhythm, crossing the flats when conditions allowed and watching the sea return hours later.

A legend traces the site's origins to the year 708, when the Archangel Michael appeared to a bishop and instructed him to build a sanctuary here. Over time, the site grew into one of Europe's most important pilgrimage destinations. Today, Mont-Saint Michel and its surrounding bay are recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, where centuries of history and the movement of the tides continue to shape every visit.

bing-57382.jpg.title: 全国花火競技大会, 秋田県, 大仙市
bing-57382.jpg.headline: 今日は大曲の花火の開催日
bing-57382.jpg.description: 今日 8 月 29 日は全国花火競技大会の開催日。秋田県大仙市で行われるこの大会は、「大曲の花火」とも呼ばれ、日本三大花火大会の一つとして知られており、全国から選抜された花火師が、「昼花火の部」と「夜花火の部」で技を競います。昼花火とは、光ではなく煙で美しさを表現する花火です。また、大曲の花火最大の特徴であり、大会を象徴する競技が、夜花火の部で行われる「創造花火」。既成概念に囚われず、形や色、大きさなど全てがオリジナルの花火を、音楽にあわせて披露する競技です。

bing-57389.jpg.title: Notting Hill Carnival, London
bing-57389.jpg.headline: A city painted in rhythm. Notting Hill Carnival
bing-57389.jpg.description:
Some weekends ask you to slow down. This one turns the volume up. Streets become dance floors, steel pans replace traffic noise, and the scent of Caribbean food follows every step. At Notting Hill Carnival, London's roads don't just close to traffic, they open to celebration.

Held every August Bank Holiday, Notting Hill Carnival welcomes more than two million visitors, making it Europe's largest street festival and the second largest in the world. Its story began in 1959 when activist Claudia Jones organised an indoor Caribbean carnival in response to racial tensions. The outdoor celebration followed in 1966, inspired by Trinidad's Canboulay traditions.

Today, around 40 sound systems keep west London moving with reggae, dub, soca and calypso, while masquerade bands, towering floats and dazzling costumes bring the parade to life. Monday starts with J'Ouvert, where paint, powder and even chocolate fly through the air. So, are you joining?

bing-57392.jpg.title: Aerial view of surfers, Santa Catarina, Brazil
bing-57392.jpg.headline: Reading between the waves. Aerial view of surfers, Santa Catarina, Brazil
bing-57392.jpg.description:
Off the coast of Santa Catarina, a state in southern Brazil, the image captures a familiar ritual: surfers waiting beyond the breaking waves, their boards rising and falling with the Atlantic. From above, almost nothing seems to happen. But that's when the real work begins.

Every wave carries energy generated by wind that may have blown hundreds or even thousands of miles away. The challenge is meeting that traveling pulse at just the right moment. Wind, tides, currents, and the shape of the seafloor determine how each swell will break, and a subtle shift can turn a perfect ride into tumbling whitewater.

Few coastlines showcase that variety better than Santa Catarina. With more than 200 beaches, it produces everything from gentle beginner breaks to world-class barrels. What looks like a sport is really learning a language spoken entirely in moving water. The best surfers aren't simply stronger or faster. They're the ones who know how to listen.

bing-57393.jpg.title: Camí de Ronda, Lloret de Mar, Catalonia, Spain
bing-57393.jpg.headline: Camí de Ronda, Lloret de Mar, Catalonia, Spain
bing-57393.jpg.description:
From the cliffs of Lloret de Mar in Girona, Catalonia, the Camí de Ronda winds along the Costa Brava, a coastline true to its name: wild, rugged and full of surprises. This historic route passes hidden coves, rocky outcrops battered by the Mediterranean and pine forests that reach almost to the sea. It was originally established so that customs officers could patrol the coastline and help prevent smuggling. Today, it is considered one of the most spectacular coastal walks in Spain.

Between Blanes and Portbou, the path alternates between wide-open horizon views and descents to beaches with waters so turquoise they seem almost dreamlike. In August, the evening light often turns the rocks a golden ochre, while gulls glide above a sea that shifts from deep blue to green depending on the depth of the water. Few Mediterranean routes combine history, nature and the simple pleasure of walking with no destination beyond the next headland so successfully.

bing-57404.jpg.title: Whale shark and golden trevally, Cenderawasih Bay, West Papua, Indonesia
bing-57404.jpg.headline: The fish that outgrew its name. International Whale Shark Day
bing-57404.jpg.description:
Today, International Whale Shark Day makes room for the world's largest fish. Despite their name, whale sharks are not whales but fish, reaching lengths of up to 60 feet and weighing around 20 tons. Found in warm tropical seas, they glide through the water with their mouths open, filtering plankton, fish eggs, and other tiny prey. This species' distinctive white-spot patterns are unique to each individual, much like human fingerprints.

The image captures one of these giants in Cenderawasih Bay, West Papua, Indonesia, accompanied by a school of golden trevally. These bright fish often swim alongside whale sharks, taking advantage of food scraps and the protection offered by their enormous companion.

International Whale Shark Day highlights the challenges this endangered species faces, including bycatch, vessel strikes, habitat degradation, and climate change. By raising awareness, the day encourages efforts to safeguard these peaceful ambassadors of the sea for generations to come.

bing-57416.jpg.title: Building detail of Registan Square, Samarkand, Uzbekistan
bing-57416.jpg.headline: A master class in pattern. Building detail of Registan Square, Samarkand, Uzbekistan
bing-57416.jpg.description:
Stand in Registan Square and it's easy to see why it is considered the architectural heart of Samarkand—one of Central Asia's oldest cities. This plaza in Uzbekistan is framed by three magnificent madrasas—Islamic centers of learning—whose soaring portals draw the eye upward. Yet some of the square's greatest treasures reveal themselves only when you look closer.

The detail in today's image offers a glimpse of the artistry that covers nearly every surface. Glazed tiles, geometric motifs, floral designs, and elegant calligraphy come together with remarkable precision, turning brick and plaster into a dazzling display of color and pattern. Shades of turquoise, cobalt, gold, and white shift with the changing light, giving the architecture a sense of movement throughout the day.

Built as centers of learning and religious scholarship, the madrasas surrounded a lively public square that was once a focal point of life along the Silk Road. Today, Registan remains just as captivating, inviting visitors to admire both its monumental scale and its extraordinary craftsmanship.

bing-57417.jpg.title: Sellin Pier, Rügen, Germany
bing-57417.jpg.headline: Sellin Pier, Rügen, Germany
bing-57417.jpg.description:
When the first rays of sunlight gild the horizon, Sellin Pier reveals its most striking side. Located on the eastern coast of the island of Rügen in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, this structure is one of the best-known landmarks on Germany's Baltic coast. Its history dates back to 1906, when the first pier was opened. Over the decades, the structure suffered repeated damage from storms and other factors and was eventually demolished.

The present-day Sellin Pier was rebuilt in 1998 based on the historic design and continues the tradition of classical spa architecture with its distinctive pier house. With its white wooden structure, pavilions, restaurant above the water and the characteristic diving gondola at the end of the pier, it still shapes the appearance of the coastline today. At sunrise, its elegant silhouette stands out beautifully against the sky and sea, capturing the timeless charm of this historic seaside resort, which has attracted and delighted visitors for generations.

bing-57420.jpg.title: The stranded wreck at Surathkal Beach, Karnataka
bing-57420.jpg.headline: The tide that carries tales. Surathkal Beach, Karnataka
bing-57420.jpg.description:
At Surathkal Beach, the waves aren't the only things making an impression. A lighthouse watches over the shore, a historic temple keeps centuries-old legends alive and, until recently, a stranded ship added an unexpected chapter to its story.

Located about 20 kilometres north of Mangaluru, Karnataka, this Arabian Sea beach lies beside the National Institute of Technology Karnataka campus. The red-and-white Surathkal Lighthouse, built in 1972 on a rocky hillock, rewards visitors with panoramic views of the coastline. Just below it stands the Sadashiva Temple, where local tradition says a fragment of a sacred shivalinga, linked to the legend of Ravana and Lord Ganesha, came to rest.

The beach was also home to the Bhagvati Prem, a 114-metre dredging vessel that was deliberately beached in 2019 after flooding. By June 2026, however, the vessel had been completely dismantled and removed due to environmental concerns. From mythology to maritime history, Surathkal Beach continues to offer far more than a walk along the sand.

bing-57423.jpg.title: Vista aerea del Fiordo di Furore, Costiera Amalfitana, Italia
bing-57423.jpg.headline: Buon Capodanno Bizantino!
bing-57423.jpg.description:
Il Fiordo di Furore è un'insenatura scavata dal torrente Schiato nella roccia calcarea della Costiera Amalfitana, in Campania: un anfiteatro naturale che si apre tra pareti verticali sul mare Tirreno, con una spiaggia di appena venticinque metri raggiungibile solo attraverso un percorso nella roccia. Il ponte che lo sovrasta, a oltre venticinque metri di altezza, è parte della Statale Amalfitana che unisce tutti i comuni di questa costa.

Proprio qui, oggi, si celebra il Capodanno Bizantino: nel calendario della Repubblica di Amalfi medievale, il primo settembre segnava l'inizio del nuovo anno. La rievocazione parte dalla chiesa di San Salvatore de Birecto ad Atrani — la cappella palatina dove veniva incoronato il Doge — con una sfilata in costume medievale che ricorda i secoli in cui Amalfi fu una delle Repubbliche Marinare più potenti del Mediterraneo. Una costa che non ha mai smesso di celebrare la propria storia.

bing-57428.jpg.title: Horsehair parachute fungus, Belarus
bing-57428.jpg.headline: A world beneath your feet. National Mushroom Month
bing-57428.jpg.description:
September's National Mushroom Month celebrates a world that often goes unnoticed. Beneath forest floors, lawns, and fallen leaves, fungal networks recycle nutrients, helping ecosystems thrive. The mushrooms we notice are only the fruiting bodies of these hidden organisms, emerging briefly to release spores before fading back from view. They are not plants; fungi form a kingdom of their own and play an essential role in nature's cycles.

Today's image captures horsehair parachute fungi, a species that rewards a closer look. Growing on fallen pine needles and woodland debris, these tiny mushrooms balance delicate caps on dark, wiry stems so fine they resemble strands of horsehair. Easy to miss at first glance, they reveal the surprising diversity hidden on the forest floor.

Look closely and National Mushroom Month becomes a reminder that some of nature's most important work happens out of sight. From sustaining woodland ecosystems to enriching our plates, fungi prove that even the smallest structures can have an outsized impact.

bing-57440.jpg.title: Traditional beach huts, Southwold, Suffolk Heritage Coast, England
bing-57440.jpg.headline: Painted along the shore. Beach huts, Southwold, Suffolk Heritage Coast, England
bing-57440.jpg.description:
Along England's east shore, the Suffolk Heritage Coast blends windswept heaths, marshes, shingle beaches, and expansive North Sea views. One of its best-known towns is Southwold, where water and history are inseparable. Almost encircled by the sea, the River Blyth, and surrounding wetlands, the town occupies a slender peninsula shaped by centuries of fishing, trade, and life at the edge of the water.

The colorful wooden beach huts are among Southwold's most recognizable landmarks. Originally built as simple bathing and fishing shelters, today hundreds line the shore, adding bright bands of color against the sand and sky. Some remain treasured family possessions, passed down through generations.

Beyond the huts, visitors find a working lighthouse, a pier stretching into the North Sea, and easy access to coastal paths that reveal some of England's most celebrated scenery. It's a shoreline that rewards wandering—one where every bend seems to open onto another story of the sea.

bing-57446.jpg.title: Römerberg, historischer Altstadtplatz in Frankfurt am Main
bing-57446.jpg.headline: Frankfurts historische Mitte. Römerberg, Frankfurt am Main
bing-57446.jpg.description:
Der Römerberg im Herzen von Frankfurt am Main zählt zu den bekanntesten Plätzen Deutschlands. Seit Jahrhunderten bildet er das historische Zentrum der Stadt und dient bis heute als Kulisse für Märkte, Feste und öffentliche Veranstaltungen. Trotz der modernen Skyline, für die Frankfurt heute berühmt ist, erinnert dieser Platz an eine Zeit, in der Handel, Handwerk und Bürgersinn das Leben prägten. Besonders die rekonstruierten Fachwerkhäuser entlang der Ostzeile verleihen dem Römerberg sein unverwechselbares Erscheinungsbild und schlagen eine Brücke zwischen Vergangenheit und Gegenwart.

Im Mittelpunkt steht das Rathaus „Römer“ mit seiner charakteristischen Treppengiebelfassade, die seit über 600 Jahren das Stadtbild prägt. Davor erhebt sich der Gerechtigkeitsbrunnen mit der Statue der Justitia, ein bekanntes Wahrzeichen der Altstadt. Der Römerberg ist bis heute ein beliebter Treffpunkt für Einheimische und Besucher. Nur wenige Schritte entfernt treffen mittelalterliche Gassen auf moderne Architektur und zeigen eine andere Seite der Finanzmetropole Frankfurt.

bing-57452.jpg.title: Coyote Buttes, Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, Arizona
bing-57452.jpg.headline: An act of wilderness. Coyote Buttes, Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, Arizona
bing-57452.jpg.description:
Waves usually belong to the ocean. In northern Arizona, they rise from the desert instead. The swirling sandstone formations of Coyote Buttes, part of Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, were shaped by ancient dunes and millions of years of erosion, creating a landscape that seems to ripple even while standing still.

Places like this are one reason the Wilderness Act of 1964 was signed into law on September 3, a milestone commemorated today. Concerned that an expanding nation could transform nearly every corner of the country, Congress established the National Wilderness Preservation System to protect lands that retain their natural character and offer opportunities for solitude, exploration, and discovery.

The act initially safeguarded 54 wilderness areas covering 9.1 million acres. More than six decades later, the system now encompasses over 110 million acres nationwide. From remote forests to sculpted desert rock, these protected landscapes invite visitors to experience a side of America shaped not by blueprints, but by time itself.

bing-57458.jpg.title: Horizontobservatorium, Halde Hoheward, Herten, Nordrhein-Westfalen
bing-57458.jpg.headline: Bögen zum Horizont. Horizontobservatorium, Halde Hoheward, Herten, Nordrhein-Westfalen
bing-57458.jpg.description:
Hoch über dem Ruhrgebiet erhebt sich auf der Halde Hoheward das Horizontobservatorium, eines der ungewöhnlichsten Wahrzeichen des Strukturwandels in Nordrhein-Westfalen. Die gewaltigen Stahlbögen, die das Gipfelplateau überspannen, wirken wie ein modernes Kunstwerk unter freiem Himmel. Tatsächlich dient die Anlage jedoch nicht nur als Blickfang: Sie wurde als astronomisches Bauwerk entworfen, das die Bewegungen der Sonne und die Wechsel der Jahreszeiten veranschaulicht und Besucher ins Staunen versetzt.

Die Halde Hoheward im Süden der Stadt Herten entstand aus Bergematerial des Steinkohlenbergbaus und zählt heute zu den bekanntesten Ausflugszielen im Ruhrgebiet. Vom Plateau aus eröffnet sich ein weiter Panoramablick über die Städte der Region. Das 2008 eröffnete Horizontobservatorium knüpft mit seiner Ausrichtung an uralte Methoden der Himmelsbeobachtung an und verbindet industrielle Vergangenheit mit moderner Architektur. An klaren Tagen reicht die Sicht weit über das Revier hinaus. So wurde aus einer ehemaligen Bergehalde ein Ort, an dem Landschaft, Wissenschaft und Kultur auf eindrucksvolle Weise zusammenfinden.

bing-57464.jpg.title: Westerheversand Lighthouse in Westerhever, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
bing-57464.jpg.headline: Red and white on the horizon. Westerheversand Lighthouse, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
bing-57464.jpg.description:
Rising above the salt marshes along Germany's North Sea coast, the Westerheversand Lighthouse is instantly recognizable thanks to its distinctive red-and-white stripes. Built between 1906 and 1908, the lighthouse has stood as an icon on the Eiderstedt Peninsula for more than a century, guiding ships through the waters of the North Sea. Today, it remains one of northern Germany's best-known coastal landmarks. Visitors who climb its 157 steps are rewarded with sweeping views of the surrounding scenery.

A narrow tidal channel meanders through the marshland, leading the eye toward the striped beacon in the distance. The surrounding landscape is part of the Schleswig-Holstein Wadden Sea National Park, within the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Wadden Sea. Shaped by the constant rhythm of tides, this remarkable coastal environment changes throughout the day as water levels rise and fall. Salt marshes and extensive tidal flats support a rich variety of wildlife, making the Wadden Sea one of the world's most important wetland ecosystems.

bing-57468.jpg.title: Khairul Manazil, New Delhi
bing-57468.jpg.headline: Where Mughal echoes linger. Khairul Manazil, New Delhi
bing-57468.jpg.description:
Delhi has no shortage of monuments built by emperors. But opposite Purana Qila stands one that tells a different story. Built in 1561–62, Khairul Manazil was commissioned by Maham Anga, Emperor Akbar's powerful foster mother and wet nurse. Its name, meaning 'the most auspicious of houses,' has a clever hidden detail. The Persian letters of Khairul Manazil form a chronogram corresponding to 969 AH, the Islamic calendar year of its completion.

This monument captures a shift in architectural styles. Its grand red sandstone gateway reflects emerging Mughal tastes, while the prayer hall and other elements retain influences from Delhi Sultanate architecture. The complex served both as a mosque and a madrasa (Islamic centre of learning). Historical accounts record that an assassination attempt was made on Akbar near the mosque in 1564, as he returned from Nizamuddin.

Today, it is a centrally protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India, quietly preserving the story of a woman who wielded power at the Mughal court.

bing-57472.jpg.title: La Grand’Place, Lille
bing-57472.jpg.headline: Le rendez-vous des chineurs. Braderie de Lille
bing-57472.jpg.description:
Chaque année, le premier week-end de septembre, Lille se transforme en un immense théâtre à ciel ouvert. Cette année, la célèbre Braderie a lieu les 5 et 6 septembre et invite les visiteurs, les chineurs et les curieux à parcourir une cinquantaine de kilomètres d’étals au cœur de la capitale des Flandres.

Dans les rues pavées, l’air se remplit des parfums de gaufres et des incontournables moules-frites. Sous les façades de briques rouges, héritage de l’histoire flamande de la ville, les trésors oubliés retrouvent une seconde vie : livres anciens, objets insolites, souvenirs d’un autre temps. Au fil de la journée, le tumulte joyeux des conversations se mêle aux sonorités des animations urbaines. La Deûle, qui traverse la métropole, rappelle que Lille s’est construite depuis des siècles au carrefour des échanges et du commerce.

La Braderie est bien plus qu’un marché : c’est une expérience vivante, chaleureuse et profondément humaine, où chaque trouvaille raconte une histoire et chaque rue réserve une surprise.

bing-57476.jpg.title: Green-crowned brilliant hummingbirds feeding on lobster-claw flowers, Costa Rica
bing-57476.jpg.headline: Small birds, big impact. National Hummingbird Day
bing-57476.jpg.description:
National Hummingbird Day celebrates some of nature's most extraordinary aerial specialists. Found only in the Americas, these tiny birds can hover in place, fly backward, and beat their wings dozens of times per second. As they visit flowers in search of nectar, they also serve as important pollinators, helping sustain ecosystems from alpine meadows to tropical rainforests. Their shimmering plumage, remarkable agility, and high-energy lifestyles make them some of the world's most fascinating birds.

Today's image shows green-crowned brilliant hummingbirds feeding on lobster-claw flowers in Costa Rica. Among Central America's larger hummingbird species, they are known for their iridescent emerald-green plumage and long, slightly curved bills, perfectly adapted for reaching deep into tubular blossoms. They inhabit humid forests from lowland regions to mountain slopes, where flowering plants provide a reliable source of nectar year-round. This feeding behavior highlights the close relationship between rainforest plants and their pollinators, offering a glimpse into the interconnected web of life in tropical rainforests.

bing-57483.jpg.title: Regata Storica di Venezia, Venezia, Italia
bing-57483.jpg.headline: Una regata attraverso la storia
bing-57483.jpg.description:
Oggi il Canal Grande di Venezia (Italia) si trasforma in una pista d'acqua: è la prima domenica di settembre e va in scena la Regata Storica, l'appuntamento più atteso della voga alla veneta.

Si apre con il corteo storico, una sfilata di imbarcazioni cinquecentesche con equipaggi in costume che rievoca l'accoglienza riservata nel 1489 a Caterina Cornaro, regina di Cipro. Seguono le gare, divise per età e tipo di barca: i giovani sui pupparini, le donne sulle mascarete, gli equipaggi sulle caorline a sei remi e, come gran finale, i campioni sui gondolini a due remi, la prova che in città chiamano la Formula 1 del remo.

L'arrivo è davanti a Ca' Foscari, sulla machina, il palco galleggiante da cui si consegnano le bandiere: rossa al primo, bianca al secondo, verde al terzo, azzurra al quarto. Le prime testimonianze risalgono al Duecento e il canale è ancora pieno.

bing-57488.jpg.title: Lake Fyans, Grampians National Park, Victoria, Australia
bing-57488.jpg.headline: A reservoir of reflections. Lake Fyans, Grampians National Park, Victoria, Australia
bing-57488.jpg.description:
At first glance, today's image looks more like a drowned woodland than a lake. Bare tree trunks emerge from the water, their reflections stretching across the surface as the Grampians glow in the distance. This is Lake Fyans, an artificial reservoir on the edge of the Grampians (Gariwerd) National Park in Victoria, Australia. Popular with boaters, anglers, sailors, and water-skiers, it offers a front-row seat to one of the country's most striking landscapes.

The mountains beyond the lake are part of the Grampians, a range shaped over hundreds of millions of years. Today, the region is known for its rugged sandstone peaks, dramatic lookouts, waterfalls, and rich Aboriginal cultural heritage. Trails crisscross the park, leading hikers to sweeping views and encounters with kangaroos, emus, and other native birds. Lake Fyans captures that wild spirit in a single scene: flooded trees, open skies, and an ever-changing backdrop of ancient mountains.

bing-57497.jpg.title: Old Town Hall, Bamberg, Germany
bing-57497.jpg.headline: Where history flows along the canal. Old Town Hall, Bamberg, Germany
bing-57497.jpg.description:
Perched above the Regnitz River, Bamberg's Old Town Hall is one of Germany's most distinctive landmarks. According to local legend, the town's bishop refused to give citizens land for their town hall, so they created their own artificial island in the river by driving wooden piles into the riverbed. The building that rose there became a symbol of civic independence and remains one of Bavaria's most photographed scenes.

The Old Town Hall blends Gothic and Baroque elements, but its colourful exterior holds an even bigger surprise. Elaborate trompe-l'œil frescoes create the illusion of columns, shadows and architectural details, while a mischievous cherub appears to poke a three-dimensional leg through the painted wall. The historic Upper Bridge also passes directly through the building, allowing pedestrians to walk through it as they cross the river.

Inside, the ornate Rococo Hall and the Ludwig Collection of European porcelain add another layer to the landmark's rich cultural story, making the Old Town Hall as fascinating up close as it is from the river.

bing-57498.jpg.title: Esquadrilha da Fumaça no desfile do Dia da Independência em Brasília, 2023
bing-57498.jpg.headline: Manobras de liberdade
bing-57498.jpg.description:
Dizem que Brasília foi planejada para ser vista do alto. Hoje, o Dia da Independência convida a fazer o contrário. Em 7 de setembro de 1822, depois de uma longa crise entre Brasil e Portugal, Dom Pedro proclamou nossa Independência. A cena virou pintura, monumento, feriado e desfile. E, em Brasília, ganhou uma atualização bastante brasileira: aviões fazendo piruetas no céu.

A imagem de hoje mostra o Esquadrão de Demonstração Aérea da Força Aérea Brasileira, que nasceu em 1952 quando instrutores da então Escola de Aeronáutica, no Rio de Janeiro, passaram a praticar acrobacias nas horas vagas. Um ano depois, a fumaça entrou em cena. O público aprovou. O apelido, Esquadrilha da Fumaça, não demorou a decolar.

O famoso grito de “independência ou morte” atribuído a Dom Pedro às margens do Ipiranga, há mais de dois séculos, não deixou registro sonoro. A fumaça também desaparece. Mas, a cada 7 de setembro, ela escreve no céu mais um capítulo de uma história que ainda estamos contando.

bing-57500.jpg.title: 'Industries of California' mural by Ralph Stackpole at Coit Tower, San Francisco, California
bing-57500.jpg.headline: Labor's legacy. Labor Day
bing-57500.jpg.description:
Labor Day honors the contributions of American workers and the history of labor in the United States. Established as a federal holiday in 1894, it emerged during a period of rapid industrial growth and social change. Today, Labor Day recognizes the people whose efforts have helped build communities, industries, and infrastructure across the nation. From farms and factories to railroads and construction sites, generations of workers have played a vital role in shaping the country's history.

That story comes to life in today's image, showing a section of 'Industries of California,' a mural by artist Ralph Stackpole at San Francisco's Coit Tower. Completed in 1934 as part of a New Deal public art program, the mural depicts agriculture, manufacturing, transportation, and daily life during the Great Depression. It celebrates the labor and ingenuity that powered California's economy, making it a fitting tribute on a day dedicated to the people whose work continues to move society forward.

bing-57505.jpg.title: Real Monasterio de Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe, Cáceres, Extremadura, España
bing-57505.jpg.headline: Una comunidad llena de riquezas. Día de Extremadura
bing-57505.jpg.description:
El Real Monasterio de Santa María de Guadalupe, en la provincia de Cáceres (España), es el corazón del Día de Extremadura, que se celebra cada 8 de septiembre desde 1985. La fecha coincide con la fiesta de la Virgen de Guadalupe, patrona de la región, y el edificio esconde un guiño extraordinario: su eje principal apunta al punto exacto por donde sale el sol precisamente ese día.

Levantado desde el siglo XIV con el impulso de Alfonso XI, el conjunto encadena gótico, mudéjar, renacimiento, barroco y neoclásico sin que nada chirríe, y es Patrimonio Mundial desde 1993. En su sacristía cuelgan ocho lienzos de Francisco de Zurbarán, el único grupo de obras del pintor extremeño que permanece en el lugar para el que fue pintado.

Alrededor se extienden las sierras del geoparque mundial de Villuercas-Ibores-Jara. Pocas fiestas regionales pueden presumir de semejante escenario.

bing-57512.jpg.title: Beech tree in a cereal field, East Meon, South Downs National Park, Hampshire, England
bing-57512.jpg.headline: Fields of gold. Beech tree in a cereal field, Hampshire, England
bing-57512.jpg.description:
A beech tree stands alone amid golden fields near East Meon in Hampshire, providing a striking focal point in the rolling landscape of England's South Downs National Park. Agriculture has shaped these chalk hills for centuries, and farming remains an important part of the region today. The area's free-draining chalk soils support extensive arable farming, with wheat and barley among the most common crops. Throughout the summer, these crops ripen in the fields before harvest transforms the countryside into a patchwork of gold and stubble.

Early September coincides with the main harvest season, when rural communities begin celebrating the year's bounty. In villages such as East Meon, harvest traditions remain an enduring part of local life, reflecting the deep connection between the land and the people who work it. Framed by open skies and sweeping farmland, this solitary tree stands as a symbol of the South Downs' long agricultural heritage.

bing-57514.jpg.title: 菊の花
bing-57514.jpg.headline: 今日は重陽の節句
bing-57514.jpg.description:
今日 9 月 9 日は「重陽の節句」です。七草の節句、桃の節句、端午の節句、笹の節句（七夕）と並ぶ五節句の一つで、その起源は古代中国に遡ります。中国の陰陽五行説では、奇数が重なる縁起のよい日とされ、厄除けや長寿を願う行事が行われます。これが日本に伝わり、旧暦の 9 月 9 日頃は菊の花が咲き誇る季節でもあったことから、日本では「菊の節句」とも呼ばれるようになりました。平安時代には、貴族たちが菊の宴を催しました。また、菊の花に宿った露を真綿に移した「菊の被綿（きせわた）」で体をぬぐい、無病息災や長寿を祈ったといわれています。

画像には、水滴をまとった淡いピンク色の菊の花が咲いています。この菊は、平安時代に貴族たちが無病息災や長寿を祈る「菊の被綿（きせわた）」に用いられた花といわれています。現代でも観賞用や菊酒、食用などで幅広く親しまれています。

bing-57524.jpg.title: Gabit Keni Beach near Ankola, Karnataka, India
bing-57524.jpg.headline: Life on India's west coast. Gabit Keni Beach near Ankola, Karnataka, India
bing-57524.jpg.description:
When people think of South India, they often picture spice trade routes, classical music, folk dances, and a coastline that has connected India with the world for centuries. Follow that coastline west into Karnataka and you'll reach a quieter stop near Ankola: Gabit Keni Beach. Life here revolves around the Arabian Sea, with fishing boats setting out before dawn and returning with the day's catch.

The beach is named after the Gabit fishing community. It's an easy stop while exploring the Uttara Kannada district, especially alongside Gokarna, Karwar, and the historic Mirjan Fort. Birdwatchers may spot coastal birds near the stream, while photographers often stop by during the softer light of early morning. Why not sample local cuisine? Fresh fish curries, squid fry, and prawn dishes are popular at eateries around Ankola. Before you leave, make time for a fresh seafood meal—it may end up being as memorable as the beach itself.

bing-57525.jpg.title: Atlantic puffin holding a wild iris in his beak in Elliston, Newfoundland, Canada
bing-57525.jpg.headline: Atlantic puffin in Elliston, Newfoundland, Canada
bing-57525.jpg.description:
As morning breaks over Elliston, a small seabird appears with a wild iris held across its bill. The scene looks almost like a gift, yet biologists say Atlantic puffins are not known to offer flowers to their mates during courtship. The colourful bill, which becomes brightest in the breeding season and fades later in the year, helps make the photograph memorable. Even their feet turn brighter.

Across Canada, puffins breed mainly on the coasts and islands of Newfoundland and Labrador. They spend most of their lives on the open Atlantic and return to land to raise a single chick in a burrow or rocky crevice. Both parents incubate the egg and deliver food. Their diet consists largely of capelin, sand lance and other small fish, which they catch underwater by using their wings as paddles. Puffins can even carry several fish at once, using backward-pointing spines on the tongue and palate to keep their catch from slipping away.

bing-57535.jpg.title: The Roy Thomson Hall, Toronto, Ontario
bing-57535.jpg.headline: Plot twist pending. 51st Toronto International Film Festival
bing-57535.jpg.description:
Ready for eleven days of movie mania? TIFF starts today, and Toronto is slipping into festival mode: coffee in one hand, screening schedule in the other. The event began in 1976 as the Festival of Festivals, giving Canadian audiences access to standout films from around the world. Fifty-one editions later, Roy Thomson Hall, along with other venues, is once again welcoming premieres, filmmakers and crowds hoping to catch the next big conversation before everyone else does.

This year's lineup features 293 films, with 'Being Heumann' by Siân Heder opening the festival and 'Villeneuve: The Rise of a Legend' by Yan Lanouette Turgeon bringing it to a close. Along the way, audiences can expect gala premieres, documentaries, shorts, industry events and late-night discussions that continue well beyond the theatre doors. One of the most entertaining TIFF traditions is the race for the People's Choice Award, where ordinary cinemagoers help decide which film leaves Toronto with the loudest buzz. So, which film gets your first popcorn at the festival?

bing-57536.jpg.title: Aerial view of Olvera, Andalusia, Spain
bing-57536.jpg.headline: A patchwork from above. Aerial view of Olvera, Andalusia, Spain
bing-57536.jpg.description:
Ever wondered why Andalusia is one of Spain's best-known regions? Flamenco, tapas, Moorish architecture, and extensive olive groves all play a part. Beyond its famous cities, you'll find historic places like Olvera. Surrounded by more than 2 million olive trees, this village developed as a strategic frontier settlement shaped by centuries of change. The Castle of Olvera still watches over the town, while the Church of Our Lady of the Incarnation dominates the skyline below. Visit La Cilla Cultural Center to discover Olvera's medieval history and traditions.

Hungry? Try 'gazpacho,' a chilled tomato soup; 'jamón ibérico,' Spain's famous cured ham; or the 'torta de aceite,' a crisp olive oil biscuit. For a scenic walk or bike ride, head to the Vía Verde de la Sierra, a former railway line turned popular trail. Watch your step on the steep cobbled streets—your camera might stay steady, but your footing may not! As the saying goes, 'poco a poco'—little by little. Slow down, wander, and let Olvera reveal itself.

bing-57543.jpg.title: Castelmezzano, provincia di Potenza in Basilicata, Italia
bing-57543.jpg.headline: La bellezza dei villaggi
bing-57543.jpg.description:
Castelmezzano, in provincia di Potenza (Basilicata, Italia), non si vede finché non ci sei dentro: si arriva attraversando una galleria e all'uscita il borgo compare all'improvviso, incastrato tra le guglie di arenaria delle Dolomiti Lucane.

Le case si arrampicano l'una sull'altra a 750 metri di quota, collegate da scale e vicoli che salgono fino ai resti del castello normanno-svevo. Da lì arriva anche il nome, Castrum Medianum, il castello di mezzo, perché stava tra due fortezze vicine. Una scalinata scavata nella pietra porta all'antico posto di vedetta, con la valle del Basento sotto i piedi.

Il paese conta circa ottocento abitanti, fa parte dei Borghi più belli d'Italia ed è una delle due stazioni del Volo dell'Angelo, il cavo d'acciaio che porta a Pietrapertosa sospesi nel vuoto. Un borgo da guardare dal basso e, se hai coraggio, anche dall'alto.

bing-57545.jpg.title: The bay of Villefranche-sur-Mer, Alpes-Maritimes, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France
bing-57545.jpg.headline: Where the Mediterranean reigns supreme. Villefranche-sur-Mer, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France
bing-57545.jpg.description:
In September, the French Riviera is bathed in softer light, and the Mediterranean vegetation begins to regain its vibrancy. Along the coast, rosemary, wild thyme and Aleppo pine scent the air, while sailboats drift across the sheltered waters of Villefranche-sur-Mer.

The town's spectacular bay is one of the deepest natural harbours in the Mediterranean, allowing large ships to anchor close to shore. Above the waterfront, pastel-coloured buildings climb the hills, while the 16th-century Fort Saint-Elme stands as a reminder of the town's strategic past. Wander through the old streets and you can discover Rue Obscure, a covered medieval passageway once used for defence and shelter.

Villefranche-sur-Mer has also inspired artists and filmmakers. Jean Cocteau transformed the Chapel of Saint Peter in 1957, covering its interior with colourful murals celebrating the lives of local fishermen. With its deep blue waters, historic streets and Mediterranean vegetation, the town blends natural beauty, heritage and Riviera charm.

bing-57548.jpg.title: The Flight 93 National Memorial Visitor Center near Shanksville, Pennsylvania
bing-57548.jpg.headline: A legacy of heroism. 25th anniversary of September 11, 2001
bing-57548.jpg.description:
Some journeys never reach their destination yet change the course of history. The Flight 93 National Memorial Visitor Center near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, tells the story of one such flight. It honors the 40 passengers and crew members whose actions on September 11, 2001, became a defining moment of courage.

The memorial's design speaks as powerfully as its exhibit. Its concrete walls, visitor center, and outdoor observation platform align with the actual flight path of United Flight 93. The surrounding landscape forms the 'Crescent of Embrace,' gently curving around the sacred crash site. A narrow entrance walkway opens onto an overlook above the field and hemlock grove where the plane came down. A glass panel bears the inscription, 'A common field one day, a field of honor forever.'

Inside, the exhibit intentionally excludes the hijackers and shines its focus exclusively on the passengers and crew. Their story endures because their decision to fight back is believed to have prevented the plane from reaching its intended target, making their sacrifice a legacy of heroism.

bing-57557.jpg.title: Interior of the Royal Albert Hall, London
bing-57557.jpg.headline: A finale worth singing about. Last Night of the Proms
bing-57557.jpg.description:
What happens when a grand classical concert lets its hair down? The Last Night of the Proms. The finale of the annual BBC Proms turns London's Royal Albert Hall into a joyful, flag-waving party, where world-class music meets quirky costumes, inflatable toys and enthusiastic singalongs.

The Proms began in 1895, and the Last Night gradually developed its distinctive traditions. Today, Prommers arrive waving Union Jacks and other flags, wearing everything from flag-covered suits to Viking helmets, and occasionally brandishing inflatable bananas or squeaky ducks. A traditional favourite, Henry Wood's 'Fantasia on British Sea-Songs' often gets the crowd stamping and whistling, while favourites including 'Jerusalem,' 'Rule, Britannia!' and Elgar's 'Land of Hope and Glory' turn the finale into one enormous chorus.

Getting a seat is another part of the ritual. One way is the five-concert ballot, which requires fans to attend at least five other Proms concerts before applying for Last Night tickets. Other options include a smaller public ballot, whole-season passes and limited day-of standing returns.

bing-57560.jpg.title: California sea lions hunting a sardine bait ball, offshore Mexico, Pacific Ocean
bing-57560.jpg.headline: Masters of the surf and shore. California sea lions, offshore Mexico, Pacific Ocean
bing-57560.jpg.description:
A day at the beach is rarely quiet when California sea lions are around. With their booming barks, playful personalities, and a knack for stealing the spotlight, these marine mammals know how to put on a show.

Found along the Pacific coast from British Columbia to Mexico, California sea lions are among the few animals that seem just as comfortable on land as they are in the water. Adult males are easy to spot thanks to the distinctive forehead bump, or sagittal crest. Unlike true seals, they rotate their hind flippers forward, allowing them to 'walk' or even run on all fours. In the ocean, they power through the water with their large front flippers, reaching speeds of up to 25 mph. They're also famous for jugging—floating upright with their flippers raised above the surface to help regulate their body temperature.

Whether lounging on shore or gliding through the waves, California sea lions are among the most charismatic animals along the Pacific coast.

bing-57565.jpg.title: Vista general del pelotón durante la 77ª Vuelta a España 2022, Etapa 21, Palacio de Cibeles, Madrid, España
bing-57565.jpg.headline: La meta está en el sur. La Vuelta a España
bing-57565.jpg.description:
Este domingo la Vuelta a España se despide en Granada (España), y no en Madrid, como sugiere esta imagen del pelotón rodando frente al Palacio de Cibeles. La edición de este año no pasa ni cerca de la capital y reserva su último acto a los pies de la Alhambra.

La etapa son 99,4 km con salida y meta en la propia ciudad, pero conviene olvidarse del paseo tranquilo de otros años. Tras un primer bucle por el área metropolitana, el pelotón entra en un circuito urbano que encadena hasta cinco pasos por la rampa del alto de la Alhambra, un muro corto y exigente que muchos ya comparan con las subidas a Montmartre del último Tour.

Con la colina de la Alhambra, «la roja» según su nombre árabe, y Sierra Nevada como telón de fondo, el maillot rojo se resolverá en uno de los escenarios más reconocibles del país.

bing-57572.jpg.title: Cadini di Misurina, Dolomites, Veneto, Italy
bing-57572.jpg.headline: A reef above its station. Cadini di Misurina, Dolomites, Veneto, Italy
bing-57572.jpg.description:
The image captures the jagged skyline of Cadini di Misurina at sunrise in Veneto, northeastern Italy. Visitors heading toward nearby Tre Cime di Lavaredo often come for the famous route only to find their attention hijacked by the Cadini. Part of the Dolomites, these needle-like peaks reaching more than 9,300 feet at their highest point seem sculpted for drama. The twist? They started out as ancient coral reefs.

Around 250 million years ago, this region lay beneath a warm tropical sea. As the African and Eurasian tectonic plates collided, the seabed was thrust thousands of feet into the sky, preserving shells and other marine fossils in cliffs now explored by hikers instead of fish.

At sunrise and sunset, the Dolomites glow pink and orange in the Alpine phenomenon known as 'enrosadira,' making these former reefs appear almost lit from within. Today, this UNESCO World Heritage Site preserves one of geology's most improbable stories. From coral reef to mountain skyline, few places have traveled farther.

bing-57574.jpg.title: 川辺のコスモス
bing-57574.jpg.headline: 今日はコスモスの日
bing-57574.jpg.description:
今日 9 月 14 日はコスモスの日。「愛情」や、「優美」、「謙虚」、「調和」など、コスモスにはさまざまな花言葉があり、ホワイトデーからちょうど半年となるこの日に、恋人や家族にコスモスの花を贈り感謝や愛情を伝える日とされています。「秋桜」とも書かれるコスモスは、秋を代表する花として親しまれています。早咲きや遅咲きなどでいくつかの品種があるものの、一般的には 9 月から 10 月中旬ごろまでが見頃の時期です。

川辺に咲くピンクや白のコスモスが、水面にきらめく陽光を浴び、その繊細な姿で秋の深まりを告げています。メキシコを原産とするこの花は、明治時代に日本へ渡来し、秋を代表する花の一つとして定着しました。

bing-57584.jpg.title: Field of kochia plants, China
bing-57584.jpg.headline: Where toughness takes root. Field of kochia plants, China
bing-57584.jpg.description:
In today's image, kochia plants spread across the landscape in China in shades of green and deep red. Native to parts of Eurasia, kochia was introduced to the United States in the late 1800s as an ornamental plant and a source of material for broom making. Its ability to withstand drought, heat, saline soils, and low rainfall helped it spread across the Great Plains and much of the American West.

Growing quickly from seed, a single plant can reach several feet tall in one season and produce thousands of seeds. Young plants have been used as forage for livestock, particularly in dry regions where other vegetation is scarce. While admired for its striking colors and resilience, kochia is also known to farmers as a hardy weed that can be difficult to control. From American prairies to the vibrant fields seen here in China, it remains a remarkable example of nature's adaptability.

bing-57593.jpg.title: Red-and-green macaws
bing-57593.jpg.headline: Survival of the flashiest. Red-and-green macaws
bing-57593.jpg.description:
Evolution occasionally favours maximalism. Just look at these red-and-green macaws with their scarlet plumage, vivid green wings and blue flight feathers. Their lives unfold across tropical South America, in a routine that connects fruit, seeds and soil in ways that are easy to miss from the ground.

Among the world's largest parrots, red-and-green macaws can reach about a metre from beak to tail. Oversized bills pry open tough fruits and nuts, while swallowed and discarded seeds help new plants take root. The plumage helps individuals communicate, recognise one another and stand out in the crowded rainforest.

Their social lives are just as colourful. Macaws mate for life and rarely stray far from their partners, communicating through calls that ring across the canopy. They're also among the bird world's brainiacs, pairing curiosity with the problem-solving skills parrots are known for. With bright feathers, formidable beaks, lifelong partnerships and a knack for turning lunch into reforestation, subtle was never the assignment.

bing-57596.jpg.title: Fort Union National Monument, New Mexico
bing-57596.jpg.headline: A crossroad of cultures. Hispanic Heritage Month
bing-57596.jpg.description:
Today marks the first day of Hispanic Heritage Month, a nationwide celebration honoring the histories, cultures, and contributions of Americans with roots in Spain, Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central and South America. Observed each year from September 15 to October 15, the month begins on a date that coincides with the independence anniversaries of several Latin American nations, including Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua.

The image shows Fort Union National Monument in northeastern New Mexico, a place where many stories of the American Southwest intersect. Once a major outpost on the Santa Fe Trail, Fort Union stood along a route that carried not only goods and travelers, but also ideas, languages, and traditions between cultures.

As Hispanic Heritage Month begins, sites like Fort Union remind us that the nation's story has been shaped by centuries of cultural exchange. From food and music to language, art, and community traditions, Hispanic influences continue to enrich everyday life across the United States.

bing-57608.jpg.title: Polar bear cubs playing in Svalbard, Norway
bing-57608.jpg.headline: The Arctic's new explorers. Polar bear cubs playing in Svalbard, Norway
bing-57608.jpg.description:
Two polar bear cubs pick their way across the snow in Svalbard, a remote Norwegian archipelago of glaciers, mountains, and frozen fjords deep in the Arctic Ocean. This wild landscape is part of the Barents Sea region, home to one of the world's largest polar bear populations, with around 2,600 bears.

For these youngsters, every outing is an adventure. They explore a world shaped by drifting sea ice, towering ice fronts, and months of darkness followed by endless summer daylight. Playful wrestling matches and mock chases may look like games, but they help prepare the cubs for life in one of Earth's most challenging environments.

Svalbard is one of the best places in the world to see polar bears, yet it is also among the fastest-warming regions on the planet. As sea ice conditions change, local bears have shown a remarkable ability to adapt, but their future remains closely tied to the frozen landscapes that define the High Arctic.

bing-57620.jpg.title: Sorine windmill and vineyards, Santenay wine region, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
bing-57620.jpg.headline: A toast to the harvest. Santenay wine region, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
bing-57620.jpg.description:
Each year, late summer and early fall bring one of France's most anticipated traditions: the 'vendanges,' the grape-picking season. The timing varies from one wine region to another and depends on weather conditions, sun exposure, and the ripeness of the fruit. For many vineyards, harvest is still a hands-on effort, with teams carefully selecting bunches destined for some of the country's most celebrated wines.

The scene is especially striking in Santenay, at the southern end of Burgundy's Côte de Beaune. Here, rows of vines stretch across rolling hills beneath the Sorine windmill, a restored 19th-century landmark that overlooks the surrounding countryside and vineyards, as seen in today's image.

Harvesting grapes has shaped French life for centuries. Its importance even echoes in the French Republican calendar, which named its opening month after the gathering of the crop—a reminder of how deeply winemaking is woven into the nation's history. As baskets fill and the vineyards glow with autumn color, the season blends agriculture, heritage, and celebration into a uniquely French ritual.

bing-57625.jpg.title: San Sebastián, Guipúzcoa, País Vasco, España
bing-57625.jpg.headline: Una costa de película. Festival Internacional de Cine de San Sebastián
bing-57625.jpg.description:
Hoy arranca en San Sebastián (Guipúzcoa, País Vasco, España) la 74.ª edición de su Festival Internacional de Cine: nueve días en los que la ciudad cambia el ritmo de las olas por el de las alfombras rojas.

Nacido en 1953, el Zinemaldia es el único certamen español con categoría A de la FIAPF, la misma que Cannes, Venecia o Berlín, y el gran escaparate del cine en español. El Kursaal concentra las galas y la Sección Oficial, que compite por la Concha de Oro, mientras el Victoria Eugenia, el Teatro Principal y Tabakalera reparten el resto de secciones.

Y luego está el decorado: la bahía de la Concha, el monte Urgull y una ciudad que se recorre a pie de pintxo en pintxo. Aquí, en septiembre, las colas para entrar al cine forman parte del paisaje tanto como el olor a mar.

bing-57632.jpg.title: Winnats Pass, Peak District National Park, England
bing-57632.jpg.headline: Through the heart of the pass. Winnats Pass, Peak District National Park, England
bing-57632.jpg.description:
A long, winding road cuts through rocks more than 300 million years old in England's Peak District. As if that geological timescale were not remarkable enough, the road passes through Winnats Pass, a narrow limestone gorge whose towering cliffs reveal the ancient seas that once covered this part of Britain.

Yet Winnats Pass is only one highlight of the Peak District National Park, Britain's first national park. Here, green limestone valleys give way to sweeping gritstone moorlands, while hidden cave systems run beneath the hills. Visitors can hike along dramatic ridges, explore underground caverns once worked by lead miners, and wander through picturesque communities such as Castleton and Bakewell. Few places in England pack so much geological diversity and outdoor adventure into a single landscape. Whether viewed from a windswept hilltop or from the depths of a cavern, the Peak District is a place where every turn reveals something new.

bing-57638.jpg.title: Oktoberfest München, Bayern
bing-57638.jpg.headline: O’zapft is!. Eröffnung des Oktoberfests
bing-57638.jpg.description:
Mit dem traditionellen Ruf „O’zapft is!“ beginnt heute in München das 191. Oktoberfest. Bevor sich die Festzelte füllen, richtet sich der Blick auf einen Moment, der jedes Jahr mit Spannung erwartet wird: den Anstich des ersten Bierfasses im Schottenhamel-Festzelt. Erst mit dem Anstich gilt die Wiesn offiziell als eröffnet. Wie viele Schläge der Münchner Oberbürgermeister dafür benötigt, gehört längst zu den meistbeachteten Details der Eröffnung.

Das Oktoberfest blickt auf eine über 200-jährige Geschichte zurück. Es geht auf die Feierlichkeiten zur Hochzeit des bayerischen Kronprinzen Ludwig und Prinzessin Therese im Jahr 1810 zurück. Aus dem einstigen Fest vor den Toren Münchens entwickelte sich das größte Volksfest der Welt. Die nach der Braut benannte Theresienwiese ist bis heute Schauplatz dieser Tradition.

In den kommenden Wochen prägen Festzelte, Fahrgeschäfte, Blasmusik, Trachten und bayerische Spezialitäten das Bild der Stadt. Doch unabhängig von allen Neuerungen beginnt auch die 191. Wiesn wie schon Generationen zuvor: mit dem Anstich des ersten Fasses und zwei Worten, die in Bayern jeder kennt.

bing-57639.jpg.title: A Borgo Marinari, sul Golfo di Napoli, Campania, Italia
bing-57639.jpg.headline: Porta fortuna, San Gennà
bing-57639.jpg.description:
Oggi Napoli (Campania, Italia) festeggia san Gennaro, il suo patrono: il 19 settembre è la data più sentita del calendario cittadino, con celebrazioni nel Duomo, bancarelle nei vicoli e una città che resta in strada fino a notte.

L'immagine però porta sul mare, a Borgo Marinari: una manciata di case, barche ormeggiate, circoli nautici e ristoranti storici sull'isolotto di Megaride, ai piedi del Castel dell'Ovo, nel quartiere San Ferdinando. Il borgo nacque a metà dell'Ottocento per ospitare i pescatori di Santa Lucia, e oggi ci si arriva a piedi attraversando l'istmo artificiale che unisce l'isolotto alla terraferma.

Megaride è il punto in cui, secondo la tradizione, approdarono i coloni greci e nacque il primo insediamento da cui si sviluppò la città; in epoca romana l'isolotto ospitava una dipendenza della villa di Lucullo. Un fazzoletto di terra che tiene insieme mito, mare e vita quotidiana.

bing-57644.jpg.title: Alphorn players, Bavaria, Germany
bing-57644.jpg.headline: The Alpine sound of Oktoberfest. Oktoberfest, Germany
bing-57644.jpg.description:
As Oktoberfest opens today, visitors arriving in Bavaria, Germany may hear a sound even older than the famous festival itself: the deep, resonant voice of the alphorn. This traditional Alpine instrument is closely linked to the culture of Bavaria, Austria, and Switzerland, where it once helped shepherds communicate across mountain valleys.

An alphorn is a long wooden wind instrument, typically about 11.5 feet in length. Usually crafted from spruce, it has no valves, keys, or finger holes. Instead, musicians create different notes by carefully controlling their breath and lip tension through a wooden mouthpiece.

Today, alphorn players perform at folk celebrations, cultural events, and Oktoberfest gatherings, keeping a centuries-old tradition alive. Its warm, echoing tones blend beautifully with the scenery of the Alpine region, offering a link to rural life and local heritage. For many festivalgoers, the alphorn provides a memorable reminder that Oktoberfest celebrates Bavarian culture as much as food, music, and community.

bing-57645.jpg.title: Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, Brazil
bing-57645.jpg.headline: Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, Brazil
bing-57645.jpg.description:
Think you know what a desert looks like? Lençóis Maranhenses National Park might change your mind. Along Brazil's Maranhão coast, huge white dunes sit beside freshwater lagoons, creating a landscape that changes with the seasons. Established as a national park in 1981 and recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2024, it covers more than 156,000 hectares (about 386,887 acres) and stretches along 80 kilometres of coastline. The dunes are shaped by prevailing winds, while seasonal rains collect in the hollows between them. Some lagoons last only through the wet season, while others remain year-round, including Lagoa da Esperança.

The Lençóis Maranhenses National Park also includes beaches, mangroves and restinga vegetation, with connections to the Cerrado, Caatinga and Amazon biomes. From Barreirinhas, visitors can take guided 4x4 tours to lagoons such as Lagoa Azul and Lagoa Bonita. Beyond its striking scenery, the park supports plants and wildlife adapted to an environment shaped by both sand and seasonal water.

bing-57648.jpg.title: Eiffel Tower at sunset, Paris, France
bing-57648.jpg.headline: The tower that won Paris over. Eiffel Tower, Paris, France
bing-57648.jpg.description:
No other city is nearly as romanticised as Paris. Yet the French capital's history has not always been as rosy as the sunset glowing behind the Eiffel Tower. Built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, or the World's Fair, which marked the centennial of the start of the French Revolution, the tower was originally intended to serve as the fair's entrance centrepiece. Designed by engineer Gustave Eiffel and his team, the iron landmark rose more than 300 metres above the Champ de Mars and became the tallest structure in the world at the time.

Many locals criticised the bold design, but it quickly captured the public's imagination. During the World's Fair, millions came to see the monument and enjoy panoramic views unlike any they had experienced before.

Today, visitors can stroll along the Seine and explore old neighbourhoods and museums throughout a city that continues to reinvent itself. As evening falls and the Eiffel Tower glows against the night sky, it remains a powerful symbol of French creativity, ambition and resilience.

windows-spotlight-1006.jpg.title: Pink salt formations sunset lagoon
windows-spotlight-1006.jpg.headline: The blushing lagoon
windows-spotlight-1006.jpg.description: The salts gathered in this serene basin find themselves sprinkled on dishes across Europe, from fish and chips to fine filets. Torrevieja, Spain, exports around 300,000 tons of salt a year, harvested from these saline lagoons set just off the Mediterranean. The salt's rosy tone isn't owed only to the fiery sunset: Halobacterium and algae called Dunaliella salina, both of which thrive in hypersaline habitats, combine here to create a cloudy, pervading pink. To make matters pinker still, flamingos are among the many birds that converge on the lagoons to scavenge in the shallow saltwater.

windows-spotlight-1008.jpg.title: Turquoise Sea Mangroves
windows-spotlight-1008.jpg.headline: Hot springs, cool seas
windows-spotlight-1008.jpg.description: The name of this place, Waiwera, is a Māori word for 'hot water,' even though we're looking down at the chilly South Pacific. The small coastal town is so titled for its thermal springs, and was once a busy vacation spot featuring numerous waterslides built around 25 steamy soaking pools. Formerly New Zealand's largest water park, Waiwera Hot Pools bustled in its heyday, but was shuttered in 2018 and bulldozed in 2023. The namesake springs still bubble away, though, just a couple minutes' walk from the jade-tinted ocean—a natural waterpark that's never closed.

windows-spotlight-101.jpg.title: Seagull, wet beach, pink purple sunset sky, ocean waves
windows-spotlight-101.jpg.headline: Bird meets beach
windows-spotlight-101.jpg.description: Did you know the name 'seagull' doesn't refer to any specific bird? More properly just called gulls, the scavenging coastal flyers we commonly call seagulls are various members of the avian family Laridae. And the world of gulls is a crowded one: The planet is populated (overrun, some beleaguered beachgoers might say) with no fewer than 50 gull species. Gulls populate shores of all climates, from the Arctic to the Antarctic to the tropics—so it's a wonder our lucky gull pal got this wide Queensland beach all to itself. After all, while these social birds rarely lack for company, we all need some me time now and then.

windows-spotlight-1010.jpg.title: Turquoise Coral Reef Shoreline
windows-spotlight-1010.jpg.headline: Coral shores
windows-spotlight-1010.jpg.description: Seen here at an extreme low tide, these exposed corals compose part of the reef that creates the storied surf break of Uluwatu, Bali. This Indonesian isle sits deep within the Coral Triangle—a vast region astride the Pacific and Indian oceans that includes the world's most biodiverse marine zones. Spread across more than 17,500 tropical islands, Indonesia alone contains 18% of the world's coral reefs and about 70% of coral species, making the country a key front in efforts to preserve these endangered ecosystems.

windows-spotlight-1015.jpg.title: Dolomite mountain peaks, valley fog, sunset, Dolomites, Italy
windows-spotlight-1015.jpg.headline: Above the fog
windows-spotlight-1015.jpg.description: The gorgeous Dolomite mountains of northeastern Italy share their name with a hard sedimentary rock that's found in abundance here. But which is named for which? In fact, both the rock and the range take their name from a person: Déodat de Dolomieu, an 18th-century geologist who grew up in the Alps and was among the first to describe the mineral.This fog-shrouded section of the Dolomites stands within Tre Cime di Lavaredo National Park, a swath of protected land named for a three-pronged peak not seen in this shot. The rugged park is ringed with hiking trails where folks can survey the slopes alongside locals like marmots and chamois.

windows-spotlight-1021.jpg.title: Snow-capped Teton Range River Reflection, Grand Teton National Park
windows-spotlight-1021.jpg.headline: A river ran through it
windows-spotlight-1021.jpg.description: This mountain range's crooked profile is no stranger to the camera. A favourite subject of the pioneering nature photographer Ansel Adams, it's also been the backdrop in Hollywood Westerns, including the classic "Shane." You'll find great views of the Tetons all over this national park, but some of the best are from here on the floodplain surrounding the Snake River. This spot, Schwabacher Landing, was once a popular launch for rafters and canoers, but was cut off from the main flow as the river changed course. Now it's better known for calm, reflective waters and busy resident beavers, at least until the rushing Snake slithers this way again someday.

windows-spotlight-1023.jpg.title: Autumn snow-capped Fitz Roy mountain reflection, Los Glaciares National Park, Argentina
windows-spotlight-1023.jpg.headline: A mirrored mountain
