Stretching almost a quarter-mile over what's now Gyeongju's Andong Dam, it still holds the record as Korea's longest wood pedestrian bridge. The span is just one piece of Gyeongdeok's legacy as a modernizer who advanced Buddhist art and design and helped centralize a formerly feudal government. Marvels like Bulguska Temple and Seokguram Grotto began construction during his reign, setting the stage for Gyeongju's present renown as a 'museum without walls.'

windows-spotlight-1180.jpg.title: Boats, turquoise ocean, white sand, Spice Islands
windows-spotlight-1180.jpg.headline: Sailing the Spice Islands
windows-spotlight-1180.jpg.description: Traditional sailboats called dhows ply Zanzibar's azure seas, adding a dash of accent color to this wash of blue-green. The small dhows seen here are for fishing or leisure, but larger ones once shipped goods all over the Indian Ocean—with their sleek, sturdy hulls, shipping heavy goods from fresh fruit to solid gold became a breeze. What coveted commodity made Zanzibar a heavyweight exporter? Spices. Cultivating cloves, cinnamon, and other seasonings, this island group in Tanzania has been a titan of trade for over a millennium.

windows-spotlight-11801.jpg.title: Reddish-brown Highland cattle, Scottish Highlands
windows-spotlight-11801.jpg.headline: A Highlander says hi
windows-spotlight-11801.jpg.description: Just as happy nibbling on sparse upland grasses as they are gorging from a fattening trough, Highland cattle are prized by farmers everywhere for their adaptability. First bred as early as the 6th century to weather northern Britain's harsh conditions, the brawny beef breed thrives at almost any latitude from Scandinavia to the Southern Hemisphere. But the scruffy specimen seen here dwells right in its eerily beautiful ancestral home: the Scottish Highlands.

windows-spotlight-11802.jpg.title: Saguaro cactus, tower of thorns, blue sky
windows-spotlight-11802.jpg.headline: Tower of thorns
windows-spotlight-11802.jpg.description: You've likely seen this stately cactus used as a symbol of Mexican or American Southwest culture. But perhaps not from this low angle, which really underscores what towering heights the saguaro can reach. Native to the Sonoran Desert, these multi-pronged, spiky spires can grow higher than 40 feet and, after soaking up a heavy monsoon rain, may weigh up to 4,800 pounds. The desert's isolated-yet-heavy downpours allow the saguaro to store vast amounts of water that keep it standing proud through long droughts.

windows-spotlight-11805.jpg.title: Moorland fields, hedgerows, sea, Porlock, Exmoor National Park, Somerset, England, United Kingdom
windows-spotlight-11805.jpg.headline: Moor to love
windows-spotlight-11805.jpg.description: As you may have guessed from the name, the region of Exmoor in southwest England is known for its expansive moorlands. Besides its signature heaths, Exmoor contains blanket bogs and ancient woodlands within its more than 18,000 acres. And as shown in our image, Exmoor incudes land long settled and cultivated—here we see fields and houses on a ridge overlooking Porlock Bay. This area is part of Exmoor's 267 square miles set aside in 1954 as a national park. Folks have long liked living in the Exmoor area—it's been populated since at least the Mesolithic era.

windows-spotlight-11810.jpg.title: Desert Highlands
windows-spotlight-11810.jpg.headline: Hot, hot highlands
windows-spotlight-11810.jpg.description: The intrepid photographer who trekked to this out-of-the-way Saharan highland could have hogged the beauty all to themselves, so we're thankful they chose to share. These are the Hoggar Mountains, a dramatic desert skyline of pitted peaks and volcanic spires sculpted over time by wind and erosion. The range is home to Mount Tahat, the highest point in Algeria, and the remote Assekrem plateau, long used as a retreat for hermit monks. Despite their harsh, hot conditions, the Hoggars support desert-adapted wildlife and nomadic Tuareg communities who've traversed these lands for ages.

windows-spotlight-11811.jpg.title: Black-headed Hemispingus with purple berries
windows-spotlight-11811.jpg.headline: Tearful or cheerful?
windows-spotlight-11811.jpg.description: Given its cheerful chirps and animated behavior, it's a bit unexpected that the lacrimose mountain tanager's name means tearful or sorrowful (it's probably in reference to the teardrop-like yellow markings beneath the bird's eyes). The colorful passerines known as tanagers are the second-largest bird family in the world, making up about 4% of all bird species and roughly 12% of those found in Central and South America. The latter stat includes the lacrimose mountain tanager, which thrives in the northern Andean countries of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela.

windows-spotlight-11813.jpg.title: Martian River Delta
windows-spotlight-11813.jpg.headline: Of microbes and Mars
windows-spotlight-11813.jpg.description: Though this crater lake is among the deepest in Türkiye, its crystal shallows are the main draw for most. Lake Salda's wide white-sand beaches are havens for swimmers and sunbathers—and have even caught the attention of NASA scientists. Much of the mineral-rich shore is encrusted with microbialites: fossilized microbe mats that represent some of Earth's earliest known life. Before the Perseverance rover was sent to Mars in 2020 to explore the Jezero Crater—once also a crater lake—researchers studied Salda's microbialites to better understand the shapes that extinct microscopic Martians might've taken.

windows-spotlight-11820.jpg.title: Red and Dark Volcanic Peaks, Lake Reflection, Laguna Miscanti, Chile
windows-spotlight-11820.jpg.headline: Like on Mars?
windows-spotlight-11820.jpg.description: A long, long time ago on a planet not so far away, the scenery might have looked like this. Billions of years back, Mars was likely dotted with frigid rivers and lakes similar to Laguna Verde here, as now-dormant Martian volcanoes fumed and rumbled like Licancabur, the cinder-cone giant to our right. Scientists frequent this high-altitude stretch of the Bolivia-Chile border seeking to solve the mysteries of the red planet's past.In fact, this western section of South America could be called Earth's most extraterrestrial spot: The adjacent Atacama Desert—the world's driest—has been a testing site for Mars rovers and other NASA gear because it's so similar to the surface of Mars today.

windows-spotlight-11821.jpg.title: Grand Teton Oxbow Bend alpenglow reflection, Grand Teton National Park, Wyoming
windows-spotlight-11821.jpg.headline: Around the bend
windows-spotlight-11821.jpg.description: The mirror-calm surface of the Snake River reflects the majesty of the Teton mountain range here at Oxbow Bend, a favorite spot for wilderness photographers. Within the borders of Wyoming's Grand Teton National Park, these mountains are a protected habitat, as are the Snake River and the wetlands it supports. These lush wetlands make up only one of the park's several ecological zones. The different ecosystems range from the high slopes of the treeless alpine tundra, to the densely forested subalpine zone, and finally open out to a vast sweep of sagebrush plains and wetlands.

windows-spotlight-11822.jpg.title: Yellow-headed Verdin
windows-spotlight-11822.jpg.headline: Sharp observations
windows-spotlight-11822.jpg.description: If you've spent any time birdwatching, you might have marveled at some species' ability to stick effortless landings on thorny plants without suffering painful pokes. Puncture-proof landing techniques are often seen in passerine birds with desert habitats—like this verdin, native to the American Southwest and northern Mexico. These aridity-adapted avians are so lightweight that most cactus spines can't penetrate their tough toes, which are covered in hard scales and contain few nerve endings. On top of that, the birds boast highly evolved spatial awareness that tells them exactly where their landing gear can get a safe grip.

windows-spotlight-11830.jpg.title: Agricultural fields and forests
windows-spotlight-11830.jpg.headline: Fields of plenty
windows-spotlight-11830.jpg.description: This overview of the fields in San Cristobal, Paraguay, is one of countless finely detailed images available in the Microsoft Planetary Computer. This vast, cloud-powered database lets scientists see a whole timeline of crisp satellite captures and environmental data for any location in the world. By analyzing this data, scientists can explore better ways to manage natural resources. For example, by comparing images and data with year-over-year crop yields, a scientist could find environmental clues as to why some years are more productive than others.

windows-spotlight-11834.jpg.title: Llama at Inca citadel, Machu Picchu, Peru
windows-spotlight-11834.jpg.headline: Llama in a lofty locale
windows-spotlight-11834.jpg.description: This llama is visiting a world-famous landmark that its ancestors helped build. During the Inca Empire's construction of Machu Picchu between the 15th and 16th centuries, llamas were the pack animal of choice for hauling building materials to the 7,710-foot-high work site. Despite their gawky looks, llamas' surprising agility and long, grippy toes made them more than up to the task. And once the lofty citadel was established, llamas stayed productive…quite literally. The maize crops grown here, part of an agricultural revolution that ushered in the Incas' golden age, were fertilized largely by llama poop.

windows-spotlight-11836.jpg.title: Fanad Head Lighthouse, rocky coast, sunset, County Donegal, Ireland
windows-spotlight-11836.jpg.headline: A longstanding light
windows-spotlight-11836.jpg.description: The Irish Sea just off of Howth Head in County Dublin has long been notorious for shipwrecks, and a beacon has been planted on this promontory since the 17th century. Charles II commissioned the first, a simple square tower and coal-fired lamp. The next was built in 1814, a bit farther south and set lower to avoid being obscured by fog. This is the lighthouse that still stands today, though with many improvements added over the years—it's especially notable for being the first in Ireland to use a gas-powered beacon in the mid-19th century, and the last in the country to be automated, in 1996.

windows-spotlight-11838.jpg.title: Kiwi-shaped spit, Farewell Spit, New Zealand
windows-spotlight-11838.jpg.headline: A kiwi-shaped spit
windows-spotlight-11838.jpg.description: This overview of New Zealand's kiwi-shaped Farewell Spit is one of countless finely detailed images available in the Microsoft Planetary Computer. This vast, cloud-powered database lets scientists see a whole timeline of crisp satellite captures and environmental data for any location in the world. By analyzing this data, scientists can explore better ways to manage natural resources. For example, a scientist could match shots of Farewell Spit year-over-year with historical wind and tidal data to show how and why its dune-lined shores have shifted over time.

windows-spotlight-11843.jpg.title: Big Ben Houses of Parliament Westminster Bridge Archway Night, London, United Kingdom
windows-spotlight-11843.jpg.headline: Clock talk
windows-spotlight-11843.jpg.description: Somewhat like the distinction between England, the United Kingdom, and Great Britain, the naming of London's most famous landmark can be a bit befuddling if you're not in the know. Well, here's the high tea: 'Big Ben' refers specifically to the 13-ton Great Bell housed in what's been officially called Elizabeth Tower since 2012 (the Diamond Jubilee year of Queen Elizabeth II). Before that, in no-nonsense British fashion, the tower was simply titled the Clock Tower. Still, perhaps ever since its first chime in 1859, Londoners have referred to the bell, clock, and tower alike as Big Ben. But not the whole building, which comes with its own naming ambiguity: You can call it either the Palace of Westminster or Houses of Parliament.

windows-spotlight-11845.jpg.title: Acacia tree Giraffe silhouette orange sunset
windows-spotlight-11845.jpg.headline: A shadow on stilts
windows-spotlight-11845.jpg.description: If this Maasai giraffe wasn't silhouetted by the sunset, we'd be seeing its telltale spots—a jagged, leaflike pattern unlike the smooth-edged tessellations pasted upon most giraffes. While all giraffes are technically classed as subspecies of Giraffa camelopardalis, the Maasai giraffe's genetics are distinct enough that some scientists say it should be its own species. Recent research shows more DNA diversity among giraffes than once thought, suggesting the Giraffa genus should include up to eight full-fledged species, not just one.

windows-spotlight-11854.jpg.title: Tall waterfall, multicolored rock cliff, tropical forest
windows-spotlight-11854.jpg.headline: 'Swiss' mists
windows-spotlight-11854.jpg.description: A wisp of a waterfall in southeastern Paraguay paints a baby-blue streak against reddish cliffs clad in greenery. The star of our shot is known as Salto Suizo, meaning 'Swiss Falls'—maybe a reference to the many veil-like Alpine plunges found in far-off Switzerland. Such steep drops are far less common in this South American nation mostly defined by plains and marshland. Here in the Ybytyruzú highlands, you'll find several exceptions, but Suizo's twin tiers top them all at about 200 feet in total height.

windows-spotlight-1186.jpg.title: Reservoir Walk, Curved Dam, Green Forest
windows-spotlight-1186.jpg.headline: A relaxing reservoir walk
windows-spotlight-1186.jpg.description: Tucked into seemingly every corner of Hong Kong SAR, from the mainland peninsula to its numerous islands, you'll find artificial reservoirs created to quench a booming population's thirst in this region that's short on natural freshwater. The metropolis innovatively uses seawater for such applications as toilet flushing, but its drinking and irrigation water is mostly delivered from elsewhere in China, then stored in reservoirs built into basins and bays throughout the bustling region. Ho Pui Reservoir, seen here from a drone's perspective, is a popular destination in the mountains, with a hiking trail that traverses right over the curving dam.

windows-spotlight-11861.jpg.title: Red yellow paraglider, snow mountains, clouds
windows-spotlight-11861.jpg.headline: Extra elevation
windows-spotlight-11861.jpg.description: As long as you bundle up really, really well, paragliding is an all-season sport. Winters don't get much harsher than up here in the Austrian Alps, but our photo subject proves anything is possible with a few extra layers. They're soaring above Achen Lake, a popular area for aerial sports thanks to its high launching points, gusty winds, and reliable thermals—rising columns of warmer air that paraglider pilots catch to generate lift.

windows-spotlight-11872.jpg.title: Illuminated Stone Chhatri, Gadisar Lake, Jaisalmer
windows-spotlight-11872.jpg.headline: Oasis outpost
windows-spotlight-11872.jpg.description: With a little artificial lighting, the 'Golden City' of Jaisalmer, India, stays golden even in blue hour. Not far from the western border with Pakistan, Jaisalmer is a lively oasis in the Thar Desert. On the outskirts of the city lies Gadisar Lake, an oasis within an oasis. First excavated in the 12th century to capture precious rainwater, the lake fills seasonally, with water pooling below small temples near the shore. Though it's remote, Jaisalmer relies heavily on tourism. Visitors are drawn to the many ornate historical buildings perched on the lake and lining the streets.

windows-spotlight-11874.jpg.title: Dark brown llamas, light brown young llama, mountains
windows-spotlight-11874.jpg.headline: Llamas of a different color
windows-spotlight-11874.jpg.description: If KISS needs a new mascot, we've found the right animal for the job—and she'd make a great roadie, too. This llama family, especially mama llama's 'face paint,' illustrates the varied colors these glammed-up camelids come in. About 22 shades, including white, black, and a spectrum of browns and grays, combine to create countless coat styles even within a single llama herd. This makes the llama overall less suited to wool production than its cousin the alpaca, which typically appears in one color per herd—but the llama's appeal comes with its multi-purpose nature. While not usually uniform in tone, llama wool still makes for fine, warm clothing, and in addition, the llamas' larger size makes them ideal livestock guardians and beasts of burden.

windows-spotlight-11876.jpg.title: Blue illuminated cable-stayed bridge at night
windows-spotlight-11876.jpg.headline: Buffalo in Belgium?
windows-spotlight-11876.jpg.description: It's believed that the city of Ghent got its name from an old Celtic word for 'confluence,' and that description is especially appropriate today. When Stone Age people first settled the area, two rivers met here, now called the Scheldt and the Lys. Millennia of human modification later, Ghent is intercut with an intricate network of countless canals. Of course, with many watercourses comes the need for many bridges—more than 250 of them. This one, the cable-stayed Ottergem Bridge, spans the Ringvaart (a sort of uber-canal connecting most of the city's waterways) next to the home stadium of soccer club K.A.A. Gent. Since the team's nickname is the Buffalos—in homage to an early-1900s visit by Buffalo Bill's Wild West show—the bridge is popularly called the 'Buffalo Bridge.'

windows-spotlight-11880.jpg.title: Piedra del Peñol Staircase, Guatapé, Antioquia, Colombia
windows-spotlight-11880.jpg.headline: Whose rock is it anyway?
windows-spotlight-11880.jpg.description: The last century of this lone stone hulk's 65 million years has brought some changes—and that staircase running up its side like stitches on a baseball is just one of them. Visitors who climb 700-plus steps to the top of El Peñón de Guatapé are rewarded with a view over the flooded valley below, a tangle of countless inlets, straits, and bays that came about in the 1970s when a hydroelectric dam was built. Forced to higher ground, the nearby towns of Guatapé and El Peñol soon developed a rocky rivalry: On the other side of the rock, a prominent graffito seeming to read 'GI' remains after a Guatapé denizen attempted to brand it for his hometown—only for El Peñol residents to stop him before he finished writing the 'U.'

windows-spotlight-11881.jpg.title: Lone pine tree on sea stack, rocky beach, anchored boats, Platja de sa Boadella
windows-spotlight-11881.jpg.headline: Beach, boats, and boulders
windows-spotlight-11881.jpg.description: A scraggly, stone-bound pine marks the northeast end of a busy bay in Catalonia, Spain. Tossa de Mar, a community of about 5,500 set on the glamorous Costa Brava, is popular with beachgoers and boaters alike: It's not uncommon to see dozens of sleek watercraft anchored in the bay or beached on the soft sand. On the beach's opposite end, a medieval castle overlooks the seaside, accenting the modern resort town with a touch of history. If that's not far enough back in time for you, Tossa de Mar is also home to Roman ruins dating to the 1st century BCE.

windows-spotlight-11884.jpg.title: Dalian Bay Bridge Night, Dalian
windows-spotlight-11884.jpg.headline: A cross-sea convenience
windows-spotlight-11884.jpg.description: Before the long, curving bridge in our photo opened in 2015, residents of the western reaches of Dalian, China, had to contend with heavily congested surface streets to reach the city center. The area's steep topography left few options for a new freeway on land, so engineers looked to the sea. The first ground-anchored suspension bridge built in China, the Xinghai Bay Bridge lets travelers zip across more than 4 miles of water off the city's southern coast, its double-decker highways connecting with commuter tunnels on either side.

windows-spotlight-11890.jpg.title: Dark-spotted whale shark, remoras, blue ocean
windows-spotlight-11890.jpg.headline: A fishy friend group
windows-spotlight-11890.jpg.description: Whether it's aware or not, this whale shark is about to become these flanking fishes' very own commuter bus. While they bear the ominous nickname 'sharksucker,' they're actually not even an annoyance to the deep-sea juggernaut. In fact, the bond between remoras and larger fish like sharks is a classic example of symbiosis, either commensalism (where one animal benefits from the relationship, and the other is neither helped nor harmed) or mutualism (where both animals benefit). In this case, the remora reaps rewards by attaching to the larger animal via a suction cup on its underside, hitching a free ride to conserve energy. Research also suggests the friendship isn't one-sided, as the suction-cup action may help remove parasites and dead skin from the shark.

windows-spotlight-11891.jpg.title: Helix Bridge multi-color lighting, Singapore
windows-spotlight-11891.jpg.headline: Flying colors?
windows-spotlight-11891.jpg.description: A modern twist on the triangular truss bridge accents a city known for a high-flying pastime. The Atal Pedestrian Bridge in Ahmedabad, India, was designed in homage to the colorful traditional kites flown here on Makar Sankrānti, an Indian public holiday held each January to mark winter's end. Here in Gujarat state, the celebration is known as Uttarayana: a two-day bash that locals spend months preparing for, featuring mass kite flights, kiting competitions, and other kite-centric events. As Gujarat's biggest city, Ahmedabad hosts the International Kite Festival, drawing kite flyers from across the globe to decorate the skies.

windows-spotlight-11892.jpg.title: Crashing Ocean Waves on Rocky Breakwater
windows-spotlight-11892.jpg.headline: Wet and wild
windows-spotlight-11892.jpg.description: The southwesternmost stretch of the Indian subcontinent has been known as the Malabar Coast for more than a millennium. Crossing four modern Indian states (including this one, Kerala), the beachy strip between the Western Ghats mountain range and the frothy Indian Ocean is one of the wettest parts of the country, and the first to receive monsoon rains each year. The extreme seasonal weather powers the Western Ghats' rich rainforests, home to 30% of all plant and animal species found in India—including more than 300 threatened ones. Another regional rarity: a special coffee variety known as Monsooned Malabar. These coffee trees are exposed to heavy rain and winds for months, resulting in a swollen, pale bean with almost no acidity.

windows-spotlight-11894.jpg.title: Turquoise Water, Winding Tidal Channels, Shark Bay, Western Australia
windows-spotlight-11894.jpg.headline: A byway for brigands
windows-spotlight-11894.jpg.description: Most who visit Quintana Roo are seeking the Caribbean beaches of Cancún or Cozumel, or the crystal-clear cenotes of Tulum. Further down the coast and a little ways inland, another watery destination awaits: Lake Bacalar, a long, thin freshwater lake that's one of Mexico's largest. Straight across from the town of Bacalar, a narrow channel connects the main lake to Lake Mariscal, a small lagoon to the east. This waterway is known as the Canal of the Pirates, as it was used by bands of buccaneers who hid out on Mariscal between raids on local Spanish settlements. Fortunately, today the canal is more popular with kayakers and paddleboarders than with plunderers and pillagers, so your booty is safe here.

windows-spotlight-11895.jpg.title: Temporary Waterpark, Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, Brazil
windows-spotlight-11895.jpg.headline: A temporary waterpark
windows-spotlight-11895.jpg.description: Lençóis Maranhenses National Park receives close to 50 inches of rain annually, and about 70% of that falls during the rainy season between January and May. The rainwater fills the troughs between the dunes, and an impermeable layer of rock beneath the sand prevents drainage, causing numerous lagoons to form. Temporary as they are, the ribbonlike lakes beckon swimmers and other watersports enthusiasts—like these kiteboarders—to enjoy them before they evaporate. Which they do quickly: Once the dry season hits, the pools lose up to 3 feet of depth per month until the next rain cycle replenishes them.

windows-spotlight-11897.jpg.title: Galtaji Temple ornate facade, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India
windows-spotlight-11897.jpg.headline: Spa for the spirit?
windows-spotlight-11897.jpg.description: The Galtaji temple complex is tucked into a ravine between rocky hills outside Jaipur, India, covering more than half a mile of inclined terrain. A cold spring high in the hills spills down to fill seven bathing pools called kunds, set amid the temples at varying elevations. These waters are considered holy in Hinduism, and Galtaji draws pious folks from across India to soak in the kunds. (The sliver of water at the bottom of our photo is Galta Kund, which is considered the holiest of all.) Besides Hindu pilgrims and curious tourists, you'll find another, more mischievous cohort here: A pack of several dozen rhesus macaques, known as the Galta Gang, lives in the temples, often swiping snacks and shiny objects from unwary travelers.

windows-spotlight-11898.jpg.title: Whitehaven Beach Whitecaps, Australia
windows-spotlight-11898.jpg.headline: Whitehaven whitecaps
windows-spotlight-11898.jpg.description: In this high-altitude view of Whitehaven Beach, the Coral Sea's rolling breakers appear as tiny, white brushstrokes over an aquamarine watercolor wash. Found on Whitsunday Island—the largest of the 74 islands in the Whitsundays region—this Queensland beach is covered with some of the purest white silica sand in the world, spread over more than 4 miles. That gives visitors plenty of space to indulge in a wide range of activities. Some will swim, while others snorkel, take a hike through the forest, or relax on the sand with a good book. At the western edge of the Great Barrier Reef, and relatively close to the Australian mainland, the Whitsundays are a popular destination for adventure travelers and lazy sunbathers alike.

windows-spotlight-11902.jpg.title: Blue Jay on Pebbles with Water Reflection
windows-spotlight-11902.jpg.headline: Why the flat top?
windows-spotlight-11902.jpg.description: If it wasn't for the distinguishing blue markings, it might be hard to identify this stout passerine in profile. We're used to seeing blue jays with telltale crests on the tops of their heads, since those feathers go up when the bird is in an alert or aggressive state. Which is often: Some birders even scorn blue jays as 'backyard bullies' that chase other species away from feeders. But this belligerent behavior has an upside, as blue jays may also pester birds of prey, helping keep the predators at bay while smaller birds party on. During less action-packed days, you might catch a jay with its crest down while foraging (like our photo subject) or preening.

windows-spotlight-11903.jpg.title: Hierve el Agua, Oaxaca
windows-spotlight-11903.jpg.headline: Oaxacan wonder
windows-spotlight-11903.jpg.description: It's hard to tell from this perspective, but this otherwise unassuming dead tree sits right on the edge of a steep precipice. This lake isn't really a lake but one of several pools that emerge here from a mountain spring, trickling down the cliffside to create a permanent, calcified 'waterfall' of mineral deposits. This natural landmark of Oaxaca, Mexico, is called Hierve el Agua, meaning 'the water boils,' but the water here isn't hot—the name just refers to the bubbly action of the cold springs.

windows-spotlight-11907.jpg.title: Green Aurora Borealis, Snow-capped Mountains, Lake Reflection, Red Canoe, Spirit Island, Maligne Lake, Jasper National Park, Alberta, Canada
windows-spotlight-11907.jpg.headline: Great green north?
windows-spotlight-11907.jpg.description: The pine-lined Spirit Island, one of the most commonly photographed sights in Canada, rises from glassy glacial waters under an uncommonly intense aurora. Here on Maligne Lake, the largest natural lake in Jasper National Park and the Canadian Rockies, cruise boats offer tourists their own opportunity to snap close-ups of the famous island between spring and fall. Alternatively, if that red canoe in our shot is calling your name, you can grab a rental from the north end of the lake. But if Spirit Island is your goal, set aside a full day and get pumped to paddle hard: From the boathouse, it's about a 9-mile trip each way.

windows-spotlight-11908.jpg.title: Las Lajas Sanctuary, Ipiales, Nariño, Colombia
windows-spotlight-11908.jpg.headline: A gorge-spanning sanctuary
windows-spotlight-11908.jpg.description: As breathtaking as any of Europe's grand basilicas, this canyon-crossing landmark lies an ocean away from the 'Old World.' Rising 330 feet above the Guáitara River in the wilds of southwestern Colombia, the Sanctuary of Las Lajas is built against a rock face that serves as the interior's back wall and bears a mural of Mary, which long predates the sanctuary and is claimed by some to be miraculous in origin. While no one knows who painted the mural or exactly how long it's been there, the site has drawn pious South American pilgrims since the 18th century, and was home to a series of small shrines and chapels before the current basilica was finished in 1949.

windows-spotlight-11909.jpg.title: Roanoke River Lighthouse sunset, Edenton, North Carolina
windows-spotlight-11909.jpg.headline: A beacon reborn
windows-spotlight-11909.jpg.description: On this North Carolina island best known for a 16th-century colony that mysteriously vanished, a lost lighthouse lives on in replica. The Roanoke Marshes Lighthouse is a reconstruction of a screw-pile light that stood from 1877 to 1955 in the middle of Croatan Sound, several miles from here on Roanoke Island's opposite side. After its decommissioning, a failed attempt at moving the light sent it sinking to the bottom of the sound. Completed by history-conscious locals in 2004, the reconstructed light now houses a free museum and features a Fresnel lens similar to the original beacon's.

windows-spotlight-11910.jpg.title: Coyote Buttes, Arizona
windows-spotlight-11910.jpg.headline: Bodacious buttes
windows-spotlight-11910.jpg.description: Striking sedimentary streaks paint pictures of bygone eons in this far-flung red-rock paradise. Arizona's 280,000-acre Vermilion Cliffs National Monument includes several protected wilderness sites, including the Coyote Buttes seen here. From midair it's a feast for the eyes, but the pièce de résistance is tucked deep in the monument's cuts and canyons: A whorled sandstone formation known as 'The Wave' lies at the end of a rugged route amid the striped stone stacks. Come prepared, though—you'll want plenty of water and supplies for the mostly trail-free route, as well as a hiking permit (only a small number are offered via a daily lottery).

windows-spotlight-11911.jpg.title: White sand sandbank, turquoise water, boats
windows-spotlight-11911.jpg.headline: A beachy bank
windows-spotlight-11911.jpg.description: Off the southern coast of Zanzibar, near the fishing village of Kizimkazi, lies a fleeting island of white sand surrounded by turquoise waters. This is Pungume Sandbank, a (sometimes) dry spot in the sea that's a popular stop for boat tours and snorkelers. At low tide, the bank emerges like a mirage, offering a perfect spot to relax, swim, or picnic in the middle of the Indian Ocean. The area is also known for dolphin sightings and coral reefs teeming with colorful marine life.

windows-spotlight-11914.jpg.title: Balanced Rock, Joshua Tree National Park
windows-spotlight-11914.jpg.headline: A well-balanced park
windows-spotlight-11914.jpg.description: Although the titular trees are justly celebrated, this desert region's geology is every bit as unusual as its flora. An ecologically sensitive area, Joshua Tree was protected as a national monument beginning in 1936, before gaining park status in 1994. It may be one of the nation's younger national parks, but Joshua Tree's distinctive monzogranite formations, featuring balancing stones and bedrock stacks cracked in geometric patterns, date back around 10 million years. Set where the high-elevation Mojave Desert and the lower Colorado Desert meet, the park is about three hours east of Los Angeles by car and welcomes more than 3 million visitors in a typical year.

windows-spotlight-11923.jpg.title: Taj Mahal, Mosque, Jawab, Golden Mist, Agra, India
windows-spotlight-11923.jpg.headline: The Taj's twin neighbors
windows-spotlight-11923.jpg.description: Wreathed in mist and blushing with sunlight, the Taj Mahal is a clear standout in this city full of pristinely preserved Mughal architecture. Also remarkable are two lesser-known buildings that flank the famed marble mausoleum, lurking outside of frame in most iconic photos of the locale. The western building, nearer to us in this shot, serves as a mosque, while the further one is a jawab (meaning 'answer'): a near-identical ornamental structure built to complete the complex's symmetry.

windows-spotlight-11928.jpg.title: Chand Baori Geometric Steps, Abhaneri, Rajasthan, India
windows-spotlight-11928.jpg.headline: Get in your steps
windows-spotlight-11928.jpg.description: This multi-directional staircase looks a bit like an M.C. Escher mindbender found its way into reality, but the seemingly infinite steps had a practical purpose in the past. Known as a baori, vav, or stepwell, this type of chamber was dug deep enough to penetrate the water table, filling it up like a well. During dry periods when levels were low, people could use the stairs to reach the water far below. Originating in the 7th century, stepwells of various shapes and sizes are found all over western India and other arid parts of South Asia. The pictured Panna Meena Ka Kund, a 16th-century stepwell in Jaipur, is a classic example of the geometric architecture that appears in these useful public works.

windows-spotlight-11941.jpg.title: Cast away
windows-spotlight-11941.jpg.headline: Cast away
windows-spotlight-11941.jpg.description: It looks a bit like this boat is just doodling lines on the sea surface, but there's a little more depth to it than that. That squiggly scribble is actually the outline of a large cast net, an ancient tool used to snare whole schools of fish in shallow water. Below the surface, weights pull the walls of the net toward the sea bottom, trapping fish in a circular 'cage' before the net is closed and pulled up, ideally packed tight with the tasty swimmers. This boat is fishing for anchovies off the coast of Vietnam, but the method is used worldwide to target many types of bite-sized seafood.

windows-spotlight-11944.jpg.title: Volcano, lake, blue wooden pier, Lake Atitlán, Guatemala
windows-spotlight-11944.jpg.headline: A volcanic view
windows-spotlight-11944.jpg.description: To the south and west of Central America's deepest lake, a trio of stratovolcanoes dominates the serrated mountain skyline. We're seeing Volcán San Pedro from the small inlet of Lake Atitlán that separates it from the other two of the triplets: Volcán Tolimán and Volcán Atitlán. Long regarded as one of Guatemala's can't-miss sights, Lake Atitlán is terrifically beautiful but troubled: Serious pollution problems developed here throughout the 20th century, culminating in the 2000s with harmful cyanobacteria blooms. Efforts to clean Atitlán's shores and divert wastewater from the lake are ongoing, largely led by indigenous Maya people. Tourists are always welcome to help—grab a trash bag!

windows-spotlight-11945.jpg.title: Purple sea of mist, forested mountains, golden orange sunset sky
windows-spotlight-11945.jpg.headline: 'Sea of mist'
windows-spotlight-11945.jpg.description: This dreamy view comes from the Aiyerweng Skywalk, a mountaintop lookout in Betong, Thailand, where early risers are rewarded with a glowing ocean of clouds. Known as the 'sea of mist,' this phenomenon occurs when cool morning air traps fog in the valleys below, creating a surreal landscape of floating peaks. Located in the far south of Thailand near the Malaysian border, Betong is a lesser-known gem with a rich cultural mix and lush highland scenery.

windows-spotlight-11946.jpg.title: Spotted Owlet peeking from hollow tree stump
windows-spotlight-11946.jpg.headline: Boo! I mean, who!
windows-spotlight-11946.jpg.description: Picture an owl in a tree—is this not quite what you had in mind? Well, our peeking pal here is a bit eccentric in the wide, wise world of owls. Unlike their nocturnal cousins, burrowing owls are often active in broad daylight, spending most of their time on the ground and preferring cozy hidey holes to high perches in the forest canopy. Though not built to do their own burrowing, these owls are great recyclers, happy to nest in abandoned prairie dog and badger burrows, hollowed-out stumps and logs, and other makeshift lairs.

windows-spotlight-11953.jpg.title: Colorful Illuminated Cave with Water Reflection
windows-spotlight-11953.jpg.headline: A light show down below
windows-spotlight-11953.jpg.description: The scenery of Guangxi extends even below the region's resplendent surface, its steep karst geology concealing a magical world underground. Though nature carved it, Reed Flute Cave's splendor has been lightly assisted by humans: First artificially lit in the post-World War II era, today it's wired up with a rainbow of electric lights that illumine the cave's natural mirror pond, accenting an already fantastical aura. The cave's name comes not from its flute-like stalactites and stalagmites (and even columns like the one in this shot) but from the bamboo-like reeds that grow just outside of it, long used to make traditional xiao flutes.

windows-spotlight-11954.jpg.title: Red beach turquoise water mangroves, Broome
windows-spotlight-11954.jpg.headline: Swept off to Broome
windows-spotlight-11954.jpg.description: Broome, Western Australia, is certainly a colorful place, and not just for the contrast created by its red beaches and green mangrove forests. On this far-flung peninsula in the Kimberley region, offbeat occupational options abound. Some examples: Pearl farmer at one of Roebuck Bay's two major oyster farms. Paleontologist studying local dinosaur footprints—some of the largest ever found. Camel tour guide leading a mini-caravan on the beach each sunset. Outdoor projectionist at the world's oldest open-air cinema. The list goes on—ready to start your job hunt?

windows-spotlight-11958.jpg.title: Gurudongmar Lake, Snow-capped Himalayan peaks, Sikkim, India
windows-spotlight-11958.jpg.headline: Elevated peace
windows-spotlight-11958.jpg.description: Situated amid imposing Himalayan peaks, Gurudongmar Lake is one of the highest bodies of water in the world, with its surface about 17,000 feet above sea level. Part of the multiethnic Indian state of Sikkim—a rugged patch between Nepal and Bhutan that remained an independent kingdom until 1975—the lake is held sacred by both Buddhists and Sikhs. That this place is good for the spirit is hard to deny: Whether you're here under a clear summer sky and the shade of Khangchengyao's peak, or wandering amid mists that hug Gurudongmar's frozen shores, there's hardly a more solemn place on planet Earth.

windows-spotlight-11959.jpg.title: Park Güell Porter's Lodge House mosaic roof, Barcelona
windows-spotlight-11959.jpg.headline: An offbeat legend's legacy
windows-spotlight-11959.jpg.description: The architect Antoni Gaudí spent his long career adding imaginative accents to the Spanish city he called home. Barcelona was historically known as a gritty center for shipping and heavy industry, and Gaudí saw the expansive city as a canvas for his unusual approach to building design. Marked by intricate mosaics and undulating shapes inspired by natural forms, 14 of Gaudí's buildings and complexes now dot the Catalan capital. These include the garden-lined Park Güell (where the pictured pavilion stands at the entry gates) and his magnum opus: the beautifully bizarre Sagrada Familia.

windows-spotlight-11960.jpg.title: Isla Incahuasi, Salar de Uyuni, Bolivia
windows-spotlight-11960.jpg.headline: Briny flats, spiny isle
windows-spotlight-11960.jpg.description: Isla Incahuasi is one of many 'islands' on the high Andean salt 'sea' called Salar de Uyuni. This unusual landscape in Bolivia is a 4,086-square-mile salt flat, the world's largest, and is covered by a thick salt crust over a brine pool heavy with lithium. Isla Incahuasi is actually the top of an extinct volcano reaching up from the middle of the salt flat and is spiked all over with tall pasacana tree cacti. Far back in its history, Isla Incahuasi was surrounded by water: Roughly 40,000 years ago the area was one gigantic lake, and this ancient volcano was submerged beneath it. That explains the coral-like fossil deposits found scattered on the isle.

windows-spotlight-11963.jpg.title: Coastal Sea Arch Blue Hour
windows-spotlight-11963.jpg.headline: Window to the sea
windows-spotlight-11963.jpg.description: We're peering through the Arch of Portitxol, a striking rock formation near the historic fishing center of L'Escala, Spain. Formed by wind and wave erosion, it's a view humans have appreciated since antiquity. Roman ruins not far from here indicate that people were catching and preserving fish from the local Mediterranean waters as long ago as 575 BCE. Today, the arch is a favorite among photographers and travelers exploring the glitzy Costa Brava.

windows-spotlight-11964.jpg.title: Praia das Catedrais sea arches sunset, Galicia, Spain
windows-spotlight-11964.jpg.headline: Sun's out, buttresses out
windows-spotlight-11964.jpg.description: As Catedrais is one of the most beautiful and mysterious beaches in northern Spain. It's on the famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage route and its official name is Aguas Santas (Holy Waters) beach. It's also known as As Catedrais because its arches, thought to have been carved by the action of salty water and wind over millions of years, look like the buttresses of a Catholic church. However, some geologists have argued that these arches and caves are not entirely natural but are the remains of an ancient Roman gold mine, and believe certain formations suggest they were created by humans rather than nature.

windows-spotlight-11969.jpg.title: Rhinoceros grazing in green grassland
windows-spotlight-11969.jpg.headline: Helping horns?
windows-spotlight-11969.jpg.description: This gentle, horned giant is just one of the iconic—and endangered—African species protected here at the Ol Pejeta Conservancy in the heart of Kenya. The southern white rhinoceros, once nearly extinct, has made a slow comeback thanks to conservation efforts like those at Ol Pejeta. Sadly, its northern counterpart is in a much tougher spot: Najin and Fatu, a mother-daughter pair of northern white rhinos who also live in Ol Pejeta, are the last of their species on Earth. But they might have a lifeline left: Biologists aim to bring the species back from the brink by implanting northern rhino embryos into southern rhino surrogate mothers.

windows-spotlight-11970.jpg.title: Desert tracks, sand dunes, rock formations, golden hour, Tadrart
windows-spotlight-11970.jpg.headline: Tracks on the Tadrart
windows-spotlight-11970.jpg.description: Welcome to Tadrart Rouge, a swath of the Algerian Sahara noted for its iron-rich red sands. This remote area is a favorite among off-road enthusiasts, and you'll often see 4x4 tracks weaving through towering dunes and surreal rock formations. Long before these adventurers arrived, the area was something of an arts district: Prehistoric petroglyphs number in the thousands here, chronicling the civilization that once flourished in this section of the Sahara. Most of these drawings date back to the Green Sahara era, and depict wildlife like giraffes and elephants that thrived here before the rivers ran dry.

windows-spotlight-11976.jpg.title: Bighorn Ram, Ovis canadensis
windows-spotlight-11976.jpg.headline: Back from the brink
windows-spotlight-11976.jpg.description: Bighorn sheep once roamed the Western United States by the millions: Native American petroglyphs depict impossibly long caravans of the sheep, and Lewis and Clark spotted them often along their trailblaze to the Pacific. Overhunting and habitat loss brought the bighorn's US population as low as 15,000 at one point, but it's since climbed back to 70,000 or so. Some of the first work to save bighorns was done right here in Arizona (this specimen was seen in Saguaro National Park). Local boy scouts led the state's first bighorn conservation push in 1936, when only about 150 sheep survived in the state, compared to today's 6,000.

windows-spotlight-11977.jpg.title: Watercolor layered sandstone cliffs, Jervis Bay, New South Wales, Australia
windows-spotlight-11977.jpg.headline: Watercolor walls
windows-spotlight-11977.jpg.description: A short trail off the Maria Island coast road will bring you to this singular sandstone overhang carved by crashing waves. The Painted Cliffs are perhaps the most impressive natural sight on this small, mountainous island off mainland Tasmania's eastern edge, presenting a Triassic geology only seen on this short stretch of shore. What caused the cliffs' rosy blush? Iron oxide (that is, rust) percolated through porous sediment layers and stained them from within, probably carried by rainwater from prehistoric monsoons. Eventually, the power of the ocean eroded the cliff face to reveal a warm wash of color. The erosion continues to this day, so visitors should exercise caution when exploring near the fragile cliffs.

windows-spotlight-11978.jpg.title: Diwan-i-Aam, Red Fort, Delhi, India
windows-spotlight-11978.jpg.headline: An audience with emperors
windows-spotlight-11978.jpg.description: The towering Red Fort, housed amidst the bustling streets of Old Delhi, echoes the grandeur of India's history. Commissioned by the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in the mid-17th century, it is named for its red sandstone walls, boasting a blend of Persian, Timurid, and Indian architectural styles. From the majestic Lahori Gate to the intricate designs of the Diwan-i-Khas private reception hall, each alcove tells a story. Our image features a view of the carved columns and ceiling of another audience hall—the Diwan-i-Am. It served as a gathering place where the public could bring concerns and petitions to the emperor.

windows-spotlight-1198.jpg.title: Brooklyn Bridge car light trails sunset, New York City
windows-spotlight-1198.jpg.headline: A bridge between boroughs
windows-spotlight-1198.jpg.description: As pedestrians tramp over the upper deck of the Brooklyn Bridge, past waving trinket sellers and countless love locks, the lower decks thrum with five lanes of endless New York City traffic. Back when the bridge opened, carriages and buggies were a much bigger congestion concern than cars: The Big Apple icon welcomed its first crossings over the East River way back in 1883, after a dangerous, daring, and decade-spanning construction process. Now more than 100,000 motor vehicles a day cross this main connection between Manhattan (up ahead, with One World Trade Center peeking through the bridge's steel cables) and NYC's most populous borough of Brooklyn (behind us to the southeast).

windows-spotlight-11986.jpg.title: Prismatic peaks
windows-spotlight-11986.jpg.headline: Prismatic peaks
windows-spotlight-11986.jpg.description: High in the Peruvian wilds, Vinicunca—also known as Rainbow Mountain—unfurls its vibrant stripes like a geological tapestry. This natural marvel stands at over 16,500 feet above sea level and owes its varied hues to a rich mineral composition: rust-red iron oxide, olive-green phyllite, chalk-white limestone, mustard-yellow sulfur, and more. Once hidden beneath layers of ice, this watercolor landscape was revealed in the 2010s as Vinicunca's glacier melted away entirely. A bad sign for the climate, but a boon for tourism—the painted peak became a bucket-list item virtually overnight, despite its hard-to-reach setting deep in the Andes.

windows-spotlight-11992.jpg.title: Blue Mountain Lake, Illuminated Village, Snow-capped Peaks, Alps
windows-spotlight-11992.jpg.headline: A blue gem in the Alps
windows-spotlight-11992.jpg.description: Nestled at the foot of the Brenta Dolomites, Lake Molveno stands out like a sapphire in the rough—except when blue hour adds an azure aura to the whole landscape. The teal-tinted alpine lake has multiple Blue Flag beaches, recognized for high standards of water quality and environmental management—making it a favorite for green-minded travelers. The town of Molveno, set upon the steep shore, offers a charming base for exploring nearby Adamello Brenta Natural Park—home to brown bears, ibexes, and golden eagles.

windows-spotlight-11993.jpg.title: Alpine Ibex on rocky mountain slope
windows-spotlight-11993.jpg.headline: Against steep odds
windows-spotlight-11993.jpg.description: Though this Alpine ibex is a resident of France, you can bet your bottom Euro its ancestors come from Italy. Overhunted for centuries, this species of amply horned goats saw its numbers reduced to around 100 animals by the late 1800s. That small population resided in Italy's Gran Paradiso region near the French and Swiss borders, and most Alpine ibexes in the wild today are descended from them (a classic population bottleneck). It was a close call with a good outcome—but not without consequence. Even though the species is now considered least-concern with an estimated 50,000 living individuals, it's extremely low in genetic diversity, making it more vulnerable to disease than before.

windows-spotlight-11995.jpg.title: Snow-capped mountain lake reflection
windows-spotlight-11995.jpg.headline: Lake or spelling test?
windows-spotlight-11995.jpg.description: More than 400 lakes lurk in the rugged folds of Bolivia's stark Andean topography, and if their sheer numbers weren't tough enough to keep track of, their many names are liable to bamboozle the unprepared traveler. This lake's name is variously written as Huayna Khota, Chojña Qota, Ch'uxña Quta, and a variety of spellings in between. For place names in Bolivia, this is a common phenomenon: Officially styled as the Plurinational State of Bolivia, the nation constitutionally enshrines dozens of Indigenous tongues and dialects as languages of the law.

windows-spotlight-120.jpg.title: Glacial Ice Fragments on Black Sand Beach, Diamond Beach, Iceland
windows-spotlight-120.jpg.headline: An iceberg's remains
windows-spotlight-120.jpg.description: Glistening ice crystals slowly melt onto dark volcanic sands here in the Land of Fire and Ice. Known in English as Diamond Beach, this remarkable stretch of southeast Iceland's shore sits where a large lagoon—made up of meltwater from Breiðamerkurjökull glacier—empties to the Atlantic. The constantly calving glacier leaves the lagoon filled with icebergs floating to and fro, breaking apart as they crash into each other. Smaller fragments flow out of the lagoon and wash up as 'diamonds' to decorate the carbon-black beach.

windows-spotlight-12003.jpg.title: Golden Hour Coastal Rocks Ocean Waves
windows-spotlight-12003.jpg.headline: A gem of a coast
windows-spotlight-12003.jpg.description: Bermagui, a small town on Australia's Sapphire Coast, is known for its rugged beauty and dramatic seascapes. This long-exposure image captures the rocky shoreline at dawn, where waves crash against ancient stone formations under a pastel sky. The coastline here was shaped by volcanic activity and erosion, creating churning chasms and jagged outcrops that are a magnet for photographers and nature lovers. An ocean-fed rock pool carved into the cliffs, known as the Blue Pool, is a symbol of Bermagui and an extra-scenic swimming experience.

windows-spotlight-12004.jpg.title: San Juan de Duero Monastery Cloister ruins, Soria, Spain
windows-spotlight-12004.jpg.headline: Sacred silence
windows-spotlight-12004.jpg.description: The skeletal remains of the Church of Santa Eulalia in Palenzuela, Spain, evoke an eerie beauty. Built between the 13th and 15th centuries in a Gothic style, the church once served as the ceremonial heart of the small town. Today, its pointed arches and crenellated tower stand in silent testimony to centuries of devotion, decline, and repurposing. After the church fell into disuse in the 19th century, stones from the structure were scavenged to build roads and other public works. Yet its grandeur persists, still evoking a near-spiritual awe.

windows-spotlight-12005.jpg.title: A bubbly bevvy's birthplace
windows-spotlight-12005.jpg.headline: A bubbly bevvy's birthplace
windows-spotlight-12005.jpg.description: The Veneto Region's name relates to its most famous locale, Venice, but we're in quite a different world than that city of canals and islets. Here in the region's uplands, just 30 miles north of Venice, the Prosecco Hills unfurl in a patchwork of vineyards and winding roads. This aerial view captures Val Bona, a prized corridor of the wine country where DOCG-certified Prosecco Superiore is born. The rolling terrain and temperate climate make this UNESCO-listed landscape ideal for cultivating Glera grapes—the sparkling soul of Italy's favorite fizz.

windows-spotlight-12006.jpg.title: White Sand Beach Turquoise Ocean Coastal Granite Rocks Parked Vehicle
windows-spotlight-12006.jpg.headline: Between the tides
windows-spotlight-12006.jpg.description: On the southern coast of Western Australia, Wylie Bay offers a surreal blend of white sand, turquoise surf, and rugged granite outcrops. This aerial view captures the freedom of beach driving, a popular pastime here in Esperance, where the sand is packed solid enough to support vehicles and the scenery is simply spectacular. Just be sure to check the tides before you go lest you get stuck on a sandbar or swamped in rising seawater. Missed your low-tide time window? Nearby Wylie Bay Rock offers a different angle, rewarding those who hike to the top with an oceanic panorama.

windows-spotlight-12009.jpg.title: Geological Rock Formation Coastal Beach
windows-spotlight-12009.jpg.headline: A geologist's paradise
windows-spotlight-12009.jpg.description: Rising from smooth, shiny sands, the Glasshouse Rocks stand just a stone's throw from the town of Narooma, Australia. These sea stacks are a small remnant of tectonic plate movements that happened almost 500 million years ago, and they aren't the only ultra-ancient attractions here on Surf Beach. Pillowy stone beds also line the shore, evidence of volcanic flows flash-frozen in their tracks by the waves. Another remarkable formation (nicknamed Kangaroo Rock for its profile resembling the animal) bears distinctive chevron folds: zigzagging sediment layers buckled by incredible tectonic pressure.

windows-spotlight-12010.jpg.title: Sunrise wetland trees reflection
windows-spotlight-12010.jpg.headline: One wild wetland
windows-spotlight-12010.jpg.description: The Pantanal is a crucial and distinctive South American ecosystem covering a vast territory of around 54,000 to 81,000 square miles, depending on the season. The majority of the wetlands sit in the Brazilian state of Mato Grosso do Sul, but they push beyond the borders into Bolivia and Paraguay. The name for this massive alluvial plain comes from the Portuguese word pântano, which translates roughly to 'swamp.' And boy, they aren't kidding: During the rainy season—November to March—as much as 80% of the Pantanal is submerged. So visit during the 'dry' season, from around April to October, when the lower water levels make visible the vast array of wildlife in the region.

windows-spotlight-12012.jpg.title: A ghost's post?
windows-spotlight-12012.jpg.headline: A ghost's post?
windows-spotlight-12012.jpg.description: Though keepers tended its light between 1776 and 1844, the Point of Ayr lighthouse has sat derelict ever since. Over the years, this former beacon on the northernmost beach in Wales has gained a reputation for apparitions: Some have claimed to see ghostly figures on the tower's circular balcony, and a stainless steel 'ghost keeper' sculpture stood at the railing for a time in the early 2010s. The shiny statue was relocated after a short stay, so nowadays if you notice someone leaning on the ringed rail, you may just be seeing things…or are you?

windows-spotlight-12014.jpg.title: Whisky Bay Granite Boulders Sunrise, Wilsons Promontory National Park, Victoria, Australia
windows-spotlight-12014.jpg.headline: A spiritedly named bay
windows-spotlight-12014.jpg.description: To prepare for this 'Prom,' you're better off buying a good pair of hiking shoes than booking a limo. 'The Prom' is a local nickname for Wilsons Promontory National Park, which covers 125,000 acres in the southernmost part of Australia's mainland. The ocean-washed mirror in our photo is Whisky Bay, one of many tucked-away beaches on the peninsula, located about 10 miles from South Point (the park's aptly named southern extremity). Reachable by a short yet rugged ramble, the beach is bound by wave-sculpted boulders that frame expansive views of the Bass Strait. The small islands visible from here are part of a protected area for seabirds, and the waters in between make up a large marine reserve.

windows-spotlight-12015.jpg.title: Green Poisonous Leaves with Water Droplets
windows-spotlight-12015.jpg.headline: Do not eat!
windows-spotlight-12015.jpg.description: When it comes to names, this poisonous plant possesses a plethora, from pleasant to pejorative: False hellebore, bear corn, devil's bite, poor Annie, and tickleweed are just a few of them. Scientifically termed Veratrum viride, this perennial features large, gently curved leaves arranged in neat spirals on stalks up to 6 feet tall, and produces large bunches of attractive yellow-green wildflowers. Though pleasing in appearance, it's a focus of caution for foragers in the eastern United States and Canada, as young Veratrum viride leaves resemble those of the sought-after wild leek.

windows-spotlight-12017.jpg.title: Tindhólmur Sea Stack, Vágar Cliffs, Faroe Islands
windows-spotlight-12017.jpg.headline: Staggering crags
windows-spotlight-12017.jpg.description: Sitting in the cold North Atlantic Ocean between Iceland and Norway, the Faroe Islands are certainly off the beaten path. Indeed, their surreal and colossal landscapes possess a transcendent, dreamlike quality. One of the best places to experience the Faroes' staggering sense of wonder is a spot just off the coast of Vágar, one of the archipelago's 18 islands. The islet of Tindhólmur is indeed spectacular, even by the Faroe's high standards: Its shape appears sculpted by a giant cleaver and it boasts not one, but five serrated peaks. The island is uninhabited and privately owned, so visitors need permission, a hired guide, and a sturdy boat to reach this otherworldly locale.

windows-spotlight-12018.jpg.title: Tawny Puma lying on grassy ground
windows-spotlight-12018.jpg.headline: Puma power
windows-spotlight-12018.jpg.description: What we call the species Puma concolor depends on where we live. In North America, these cats are usually called cougars or mountain lions. Here in South America's Torres del Paine National Park, they're pumas. This national park stretches across 935 square miles in the southern Patagonia region of Chile and provides a great habitat for pumas, which hunt guanacos and the other deer-like ruminants that munch on the grassy plains of the park. Scientists frequent Torres del Paine to study the pumas, as the large population presents a good opportunity for easy observation.

windows-spotlight-12023.jpg.title: Jaguar in water among aquatic plants
windows-spotlight-12023.jpg.headline: Big cat spotted!
windows-spotlight-12023.jpg.description: Jaguars once ranged from the Southwestern United States to Patagonia, but nowadays, more than half of them live in the Amazon Basin. Just outside that mighty river's reaches, this big kitty is haunches-deep in a different waterlogged habitat: the Pantanal, a swampy section of South America renowned as the biggest wetland in the world. Here in this biodiversity hotbed, jaguars top a food chain comprising 150-plus local mammal species. Critters advised to watch out for these hungry feline neighbors include giant anteaters, capybaras, tapirs, and howler monkeys.

windows-spotlight-12026.jpg.title: Fisherman's Bastion and Matthias Church, Night, Budapest
windows-spotlight-12026.jpg.headline: A bastion in Budapest
windows-spotlight-12026.jpg.description: Though Budapest, Hungary, traces its history to medieval times and beyond, much of its current cityscape took shape near the turn of the 20th century. The turreted barrier in the foreground of our photo is part of the Fisherman's Bastion, completed in 1902 to replace the walls first built on this hillside near the Danube in the 1700s. Behind the bastion rises the studded steeple of Matthias Church, built in the 14th century and restored in the 19th (though local lore dates the original structure all the way back to the year 1015). Within the same walkable complex, you'll find another famed structure with a history of renovations and additions: Buda Castle.

windows-spotlight-12027.jpg.title: Spire of sandstone
windows-spotlight-12027.jpg.headline: Spire of sandstone
windows-spotlight-12027.jpg.description: India, and especially its capital region of Delhi, is known for its sandstone structures from forts to palaces to temples—but the Qutb Minar stands above them all. Rising 238 feet, the tower was built at the turn of the 13th century by the Ghurid dynasty, a Central Asian power that had just seized control of northern India and brought Islamic customs with them. The Qutb Minar served as both a symbol of their victory (a short-lived one, as their rule was upended by the year 1215) and as a minaret: a tall structure from which a muezzin performs the call to prayer. Today the tower itself is closed for entry, but its grounds are a popular tourist attraction open to visitors of all faiths.

windows-spotlight-12028.jpg.title: Park Güell Hypostyle Hall, Barcelona, Spain
windows-spotlight-12028.jpg.headline: Believe the hypostyle
windows-spotlight-12028.jpg.description: It sounds like the name of some futuristic fashion fad, but the term 'hypostyle' really comes from ancient Greek. It refers to a large hall with a column-supported roof, in this case a ceiling covered in tiny tiles and intricate mosaics. The Hypostyle Room is the apter of two names given to this pavilion in Park Güell, Barcelona, designed by Antoni Gaudí in the early 1900s. Its other name, the Hundred Columns Chamber, is catchy but inaccurate: The always-unorthodox Gaudí removed columns from the regular pattern to create a more open feel, so there's just 86 of them.

windows-spotlight-1203.jpg.title: Person silhouette on reflective water sunset
windows-spotlight-1203.jpg.headline: Water walker?
windows-spotlight-1203.jpg.description: We're witnessing a miraculous sight, but not the walk-on-water kind. It may look like this silhouetted subject is striding on the surface of a mountain lake, but that's actually just an inch or two of water. When rains fall here on the Bonneville Salt Flats, they form a mirror that stretches up to 40 square miles over the tightly packed saline surface. Some 17,000 years ago, this magical illusion wouldn't have been possible: Back then, the basin lay under hundreds of feet of water as Lake Bonneville covered what's now northwest Utah.

windows-spotlight-12032.jpg.title: Shanghai Tower, Shanghai World Financial Center, Skyscrapers, Clouds, Twilight, Shanghai
windows-spotlight-12032.jpg.headline: Tall, taller, tallest
windows-spotlight-12032.jpg.description: The skyscrapers in our picture, at the core of Shanghai's Lujiazui business district, are the only three supertall buildings in the world located virtually adjacent to each other. Jin Mao Tower (left, 1,380 feet) was mainland China's tallest building from 1999 until the Shanghai World Financial Center (right, 1,614 feet) opened in 2007 and took the title. Shanghai Tower (center, 2,139 feet) topped out in 2013, becoming one of the tallest skyscrapers in the world. From its observation deck at 1,800 feet, visitors can overlook the Bund—the historic financial district built by European powers in the 1800s—and far beyond, with views reaching almost 40 miles on clearer days.

windows-spotlight-12033.jpg.title: Lotus Temple, Delhi, India
windows-spotlight-12033.jpg.headline: A petal-topped temple
windows-spotlight-12033.jpg.description: Elegant building design is a hallmark of the Bahá'í Faith, and this might be the grandest example. The Lotus Temple, located in the Indian capital of New Delhi, shares characteristics with other Bahá'í Houses of Worship, like its nine-sided floor plan and austere interior free of pictures or other likenesses—not to mention its racking up of design awards since its 1986 opening. Its architect Fariborz Sahba modeled the structure after the lotus blossom, a national symbol of India sacred to both Hindus and Buddhists, and the 'petals' are clad in Greek marble quarried from the same source as the Parthenon. The Bahá'í interfaith tradition welcomes all people inside, and up to 5 million admirers and worshippers visit each year.

windows-spotlight-12037.jpg.title: Grutas de Tolantongo thermal pools, mountain valley, Hidalgo, Mexico
windows-spotlight-12037.jpg.headline: Soaking in the view
windows-spotlight-12037.jpg.description: The rock pools that spill over this slope resemble natural travertine formations—and indeed, they're fed by warm springs that have trickled down these valley walls for millennia. But the Grutas (Grottoes) de Tolantongo resort is largely human-made, developed in the 1970s by local farmers who resolved to transform this untraveled Hidalgo hollow into a tourism destination. In addition to dozens of relaxing pools with transfixing views, visitors can head to the valley floor for a cool dip in the Tolantongo River, a mineral-rich flow shrouded by the tree canopy below.

windows-spotlight-12039.jpg.title: Redfish Lake Sawtooth Mountains Reflections, Idaho
windows-spotlight-12039.jpg.headline: Redfish reflections
windows-spotlight-12039.jpg.description: Tucked below the Sawtooth Mountains' towering summits, Little Redfish Lake glows with alpine serenity. This high-altitude Idaho lake, fed by glacial runoff and surrounded by pine forests, is a haven for nature lovers and fishing enthusiasts seeking a tranquil, motorboat-free retreat. The 'Redfish' name alludes to the sockeye salmon that once gathered here by the thousands during spawning season, seeming to tint the water with their pinkish-red coloration. Starting in the mid-20th century, the salmon run was decimated by environmental factors such as dams built upriver from the lake. However, healthy populations of bass and trout still attract anglers in ample numbers.

windows-spotlight-12043.jpg.title: Hercílio Luz Bridge Sunset, Florianópolis, Santa Catarina, Brazil
windows-spotlight-12043.jpg.headline: The 'Magic Island'
windows-spotlight-12043.jpg.description: Split between Santa Catarina Island and the cloud-shrouded mainland in the distance, Florianópolis anchors a metro area of well over a million people in southeastern Brazil. With more than 40 beaches, this 'Magic Island' has been a popular tourist destination for many generations of South Americans. And the rest of the world is catching on fast: Nowadays, in terms of international visitors, Florianópolis consistently ranks in Brazil's top 5 cities. A celebrated surfing hub, the area offers a multitude of other adventures too, like paragliding and mountain biking.

windows-spotlight-12045.jpg.title: Red Jantar Mantar steps, archway, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India
windows-spotlight-12045.jpg.headline: Stairway to heaven?
windows-spotlight-12045.jpg.description: William Blake wrote, 'If the doors of perception were cleansed every thing would appear to man as it is, Infinite.' This door is actually just an ornamental hollow leading nowhere, but it's part of an instrument that's allowed many generations a glimpse into infinity. The Jantar Mantar of New Delhi, built in the 1720s on the order of Jai Singh II, is a complex of building-sized astronomical tools—including the structure we're seeing, which flanks a 70-foot-tall sundial aligned with Earth's axis. Other buildings on the grounds used strung wires to cast shadows or pinholes to track sunlight. Remarkable on its own, this is just one of five Jantar Mantar that Jai Singh—a known math and science buff—commissioned across his kingdom. Four still stand today, including this one, a larger one in Jaipur, and one each in Ujjain and Varanasi.

windows-spotlight-12046.jpg.title: El Jem Roman Amphitheater, El Jem, Tunisia
windows-spotlight-12046.jpg.headline: An ancient arena
windows-spotlight-12046.jpg.description: Smack in the center of El Jem, Tunisia, stands an ancient entertainment hub that happens to be one of Africa's best preserved Roman ruins. Built in the 3rd century CE when the city was known as Thysdrus, the Amphitheatre of El Jem sat as many as 35,000 spectators, making it one of the largest amphitheaters in the empire despite its remoteness. After the public's taste for gladiator battles faded, the structure was used as a fort, apartment complex, granary, and more throughout the centuries, becoming a UNESCO site in 1979.

windows-spotlight-12047.jpg.title: Pink Salt Lake
windows-spotlight-12047.jpg.headline: Pool of pink
windows-spotlight-12047.jpg.description: Though it does lie at the base of a volcano, that's not a pool of lava we're seeing. Flanked by vast, dry salt pans below the volcanic cone that shares its name, Laguna Carachi Pampa is a hypersaline lake on the Puna de Atacama, an expansive, arid plateau in central South America that's often compared to the surface of Mars. Unlike the Red Planet, this place is known to support life: The lake's red-hot coloration comes from microorganisms it hosts in its hypersaline waters. Larger life also finds ways to thrive here, such as flamingos that use it as a breeding ground—how's that for color coordination?

windows-spotlight-12049.jpg.title: Charcoal Coast
windows-spotlight-12049.jpg.headline: A charcoal-colored coast
windows-spotlight-12049.jpg.description: Indonesia is one of the planet's most volcanic countries, and its famed resort hotspot of Bali is no exception. This surfer's paradise is home to two currently active volcanoes, Agung and Batur, and its past is packed with volcanic activity—nearly every inch of Bali has been covered with magma at some point in geological history. Because of this, highly fertile soil is found all over the island, and black-sand beaches made of cooled and crumbled lava can be found on most every coast. This stretch of obsidian shore is part of Klungkung, Bali's smallest regency, which also includes the stunning Nusa Penida island group.

windows-spotlight-1205.jpg.title: Mirrored Maroon Bells, Colorado
windows-spotlight-1205.jpg.headline: Mirrored maroon
windows-spotlight-1205.jpg.description: Just outside the popular resort city of Aspen rise two of the Centennial State's most beloved fourteeners. Though the intense glow of a Colorado sunrise conceals their true colors in this photo, the picturesque Maroon Bells in the distance are named for the ruddy mudstone that composes them. Whatever hue they take on, the twin mounts reflected in Maroon Lake compose one of North America's most iconic photo ops. But like this photographer, you might have to wake up early to get an undisturbed shot: Drawing roughly 300,000 visitors a season, the Maroon Bells Scenic Area is one of the most visited sites in the Rockies.

windows-spotlight-12050.jpg.title: Frozen Abraham Lake, Snow-capped Mountains, Sunset Clouds, Abraham Lake, Alberta, Canada
windows-spotlight-12050.jpg.headline: Silent but lovely
windows-spotlight-12050.jpg.description: An epic Rocky Mountain setting and status as Alberta's biggest reservoir are only secondary claims to fame for Abraham Lake. Its main attraction? Well, look closely at the iced-over lake: See the bubbles embedded within? They're pockets of methane, a main ingredient in flatulence—in this case, it's gas passed by bacteria feeding from the lake bed. Each winter, a great bounty of these bottom burps are frozen in place by the bitter cold while making their way to the surface. Luckily, methane is odorless—contrary to popular belief—so even come the thaw, what's been dealt here won't be smelt.

windows-spotlight-12051.jpg.title: Green Rice Paddies, Tropical Forest, Bali, Indonesia
windows-spotlight-12051.jpg.headline: A sustainable legacy
windows-spotlight-12051.jpg.description: This lush, quilted landscape of rice fields is a visual testament to the millennium-old subak irrigation system, which harmonizes farming with ecology and spiritual life. Since the 9th century, Bali's freshwater supply has been managed by local co-ops each centered around Hindu water temples. From lofty sources like Lake Batur—considered Bali's main freshwater source, located about 20 miles north of this farm in Ubud—water spills downhill through networks of weirs and waterways to soak the rice terraces from the highest to the lowest. Flow is directed on a schedule carefully planned by the co-ops, so rice fields may spend a given season either fertile, like the prosperous paddy to our right, or fallow, like the unsown area to our left.

windows-spotlight-12056.jpg.title: Bridge over Braided Glacial River, Volcanic Plain, Iceland
windows-spotlight-12056.jpg.headline: Bridge over braided waters
windows-spotlight-12056.jpg.description: The Markarfljót River snakes through Iceland's southern highlands, carving a braided path across volcanic plains. This aerial view captures the river's many channels and the bridge that crosses them near Þórsmörk, a remote valley named after the Norse god Thor. Fed by glacial meltwater and flanked by rugged terrain, the Markarfljót is both a natural marvel and a vital link in Iceland's dramatic landscape. Visitors crossing this span are often bound for Seljalandsfoss, a waterfall that spills over the mouth of a cavern—those who venture inside will discover spectacular views.

windows-spotlight-12057.jpg.title: Layered Rock Gorge with River, Gujarat
windows-spotlight-12057.jpg.headline: A gorge in Gujarat
windows-spotlight-12057.jpg.description: The 36 states and territories of India are subdivided into around 800 different districts, and Kutch, in the western state of Gujarat, is the largest. Its name, also spelled Kachchh, means a land that alternates between wet and dry stages, such as the Rann of Kutch that makes up much of the district. Outside of the summer monsoon season, riverine features like the Kadiya Dhro gorge in our photo typically dry up. Also known as 'India's Grand Canyon,' Kadiya Dhro draws visitors whether or not its stream is flowing—but when it is, take care if you're tempted with a swim, as crocodiles have been spotted in the murky flow.

windows-spotlight-12059.jpg.title: Ocean coral reef beach waves
windows-spotlight-12059.jpg.headline: Joyous Réunion
windows-spotlight-12059.jpg.description: Roughly oval in shape, the overseas French territory of Réunion is lapped by the Indian Ocean on all sides. Here near the westernmost edge of this 970-square-mile isle, wide shelves separate the sandy shoreline from the wave break by as much as a quarter mile, leaving a long, calm stretch of shallows that's great for casual swims and dazzling snorkel sessions alike. Along with its fellow islands in the Mascarene chain, Réunion is one of the world's best places to observe marine life, with many biologists ranking it in the top ten biodiversity hotspots on Earth.

windows-spotlight-12065.jpg.title: Ocean waves and dark rocks on sandy shore
windows-spotlight-12065.jpg.headline: Risco business
windows-spotlight-12065.jpg.description: Corral del Risco is a rugged stretch of coastline near Punta de Mita, a resort town on Mexico's Pacific coast. This aerial view captures the raw beauty of the shoreline, where waves crash against boulders smoothed by centuries of erosion. The area is part of the Riviera Nayarit, a region known for its biodiversity, luxury resorts, and traditional fishing villages. The rock piles here are remnants of ancient lava flows, and the surrounding waters are rich with marine life, making this a popular area for snorkeling and diving. If you'd rather stay on dry land, Punta de Mita itself sits on a peninsula that offers panoramic views of Banderas Bay and the Marietas Islands.

windows-spotlight-12067.jpg.title: São Miguel das Missões Ruins, São Miguel das Missões, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
windows-spotlight-12067.jpg.headline: A mission abandoned
windows-spotlight-12067.jpg.description: Though its architecture is distinctively European, a peek at palm trees through this ruin's outer door hints at its wild New World setting. São Miguel das Missões was one of several missions established by the Jesuit order in the late 1600s near the triple frontier of Brazil, Argentina, and Paraguay. The missions' mission? To 'civilize' the local Guaraní people by bringing them into planned Catholic communities—an effort that only lasted until Spain expelled the order from the Americas in 1767. The missions' melding of Catholicism with Indigenous ways shaped the lasting culture of the region, with UNESCO recognizing several of the ruins (including São Miguel) as World Heritage Sites.

windows-spotlight-12068.jpg.title: Crescent City Connection, New Orleans, Louisiana
windows-spotlight-12068.jpg.headline: Bridging the Big Easy
windows-spotlight-12068.jpg.description: Although more than 20 miles of the Mississippi River wind past the city of New Orleans, only one bridge spans the mighty river within city limits. Well, really it's two. The twin spans of the Crescent City Connection, one westbound and one eastbound, connect central New Orleans with the city's 15th Ward. Better known as Algiers, this southeastern segment of the city packs a lot of history, having transformed from a hub of the slave trade to a unique center of African American and Creole culture—especially music. Brass bands first paraded the streets here in the 1870s, and numerous Algiers-born musicians were instrumental in the creation of jazz.

windows-spotlight-12070.jpg.title: Pelješac Cable-Stayed Bridge, Sunset, Pelješac, Croatia
windows-spotlight-12070.jpg.headline: Shortcut over the sea
windows-spotlight-12070.jpg.description: Until recently, reaching the cut-off corner of Croatia we see in the distance required doubling around a long, narrow bay, plus a double border crossing at the Herzegovinian coastal strip of Neum. That potentially hours-long ordeal is cut to about a 5-minute drive by the Pelješac Bridge, which spans roughly a mile and a half across this Adriatic inlet. The project was a political hot potato for years due to its potential limiting of shipping to Neum. But the pro-bridge crowd won out in the end, and the span was completed in 2022, recording 2 million crossings in its first year.

windows-spotlight-12073.jpg.title: Forth Bridge steel railway bridge sunset, Queensferry, Scotland
windows-spotlight-12073.jpg.headline: Span of steel
windows-spotlight-12073.jpg.description: Sounding like the makings of a tongue twister, the Firth of Forth is one of Scotland's most important bodies of water, bordering the country's capital Edinburgh near its opening to the North Sea.
