windows-spotlight-12681.jpg.title: Sunset-lit sandstone hoodoos, Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness, New Mexico, USA
windows-spotlight-12681.jpg.headline: Enchantment awaits
windows-spotlight-12681.jpg.description:
Stunning landscapes lit by spectacular sunsets are a signature look in the Land of Enchantment, but few places in New Mexico are quite as magical as the Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness. This landscape not far from the Four Corners is full of oddly shaped hoodoos, looking something like castle walls crowded with fantastical creatures and characters. Popular names for the sandstone figures follow this imaginative thread: The section of the wilderness in our photo is called the Valley of Dreams, populated by the Giant Mushroom, the Chocolate Penguin King, and more.

These distinctive hoodoos form through differential erosion. Softer rock layers erode faster than the harder caprock. The visible formations consist of sandstone and shale, revealing ancient geological strata. They belong to the Kirtland Formation, a fossil-rich area with evidence of ancient flora and fauna. The wilderness also protects a rare petrified wood forest. Visitors must explore this landscape on foot, a measure overseen by the Bureau of Land Management for preservation.

windows-spotlight-12683.jpg.title: Village in green valley, Western Pyrenees, France
windows-spotlight-12683.jpg.headline: Basque in the sun
windows-spotlight-12683.jpg.description:
Bridging two cultures while remaining steadfastly unique, the Basque Country sits on the border between France and Spain, largely nestled in the western Pyrenees. Set your translator app to French or Spanish here and you'll get along just fine, but if you really want to endear yourself to locals, learn a little Basque vocab. Unrelated to the Romance languages of the nations that govern this region, Basque is Europe's only true language isolate, with no known cousins in the linguistic world. Will your pintxos with a side of piperade washed down with txakoli taste even better if you order in Basque? Can't hurt to try.

The villages pictured here display a distinctive style. Traditional Basque farmhouses, known as baserri, feature prominent red-tiled roofs and white facades. These sturdy stone and timber structures have historically been the center of rural life. They were designed to house both families and livestock under one roof. This deep connection to the land defines the region's enduring cultural identity.

windows-spotlight-1269.jpg.title: Towers of tuff, cave dwellings, Cappadocia, Turkey
windows-spotlight-1269.jpg.headline: Towers of tuff
windows-spotlight-1269.jpg.description: For thousands of years, people in Cappadocia, Turkey, have literally carved out an existence within the 'fairy chimneys' that rise up across the region. These natural towers are made of soft tuff, formed from hardened volcanic ash. The rock is soft enough that Cappadocians dug innumerable caves into them. They used these caves as sheltered homes, churches, even entire underground communities that offered protection from frequent raids. Away from the city, these stone spires crowd the landscape. But in the town of Uçhisar, they blend in with the many caves on the hill, some of which are used as dwellings to this day.

windows-spotlight-12691.jpg.title: Morning mist over Krün valley, Bavarian Alps, Germany
windows-spotlight-12691.jpg.headline: Small town, big summits
windows-spotlight-12691.jpg.description:
This pastoral Bavarian village isn't just surrounded by some of Germany's highest peaks, it's hosted the highest echelons of governance from around the globe. The town of Krün has twice welcomed heads of state from the Group of Seven—Germany, France, Italy, Japan, Canada, the United States, and the United Kingdom—for their annual G7 summit. Not far from the humble hamlet, another summit casts its shadow: Zugspitze rises as the tallest mountain in the Bavarian Alps and all of Germany.

The misty valley, dotted with small traditional barns, gives way to the sunlit peaks of the Karwendel range. This extensive range forms the core of the Karwendel Nature Park, the largest protected area in the Eastern Alps. Diverse ecosystems thrive across its alpine meadows, dense forests, and high-altitude rocky slopes. These imposing limestone summits define the region's character, creating a striking contrast with the gentle, fog-shrouded valleys below.

windows-spotlight-12692.jpg.title: El Morro Fortress, San Juan, Puerto Rico
windows-spotlight-12692.jpg.headline: Seaside citadel
windows-spotlight-12692.jpg.description:
Its weathered appearance gives it an almost ancient feel, but El Morro Fortress last saw military use as recently as 1961. The fortified lookout at the edge of San Juan does have some centuries under its stony belt, dating to 1539 when Puerto Rico was still held by Spain (itself ruled by Holy Roman Emperor Charles V). Despite ensuing political twists and turns back in Europe, Spain kept its hold on Puerto Rico until the Spanish-American War in 1898, after which this highly strategic gateway to the Caribbean became a territory of the United States. Part of the National Park Service since the US Army retired it as a base, El Morro Fortress was also designated a UNESCO site in 1983.

The fortress's robust construction features thick walls and a unique star-shaped design, a hallmark of 16th-century military engineering. These elaborate defenses, including multiple levels of firing platforms, were designed to withstand naval attacks from the Atlantic Ocean. Its strategic location controlled access to San Juan Bay, making it a critical stronghold in protecting Spanish colonial interests. Today, the site serves as a tangible record of the region's enduring geopolitical significance.

windows-spotlight-12696.jpg.title: Symphony of the Stones, Garni Gorge, Armenia
windows-spotlight-12696.jpg.headline: A soaring 'symphony'
windows-spotlight-12696.jpg.description:
The Garni Gorge can be appreciated from both near and far. Get a wide enough perspective and you'll enjoy splendid views of a rugged and green river canyon in central Armenia. Venture into the gorge itself and fantastic geological wonders await—chief among them are cliffs known as the Symphony of the Stones. Massive basalt columns stand out from hill faces in neat, soaring rows, resembling the ranks of pipe organs. The site was formed through a process called columnar jointing. It's easy to get close to this marvel—or even get partway beneath it—as the photographer who captured our image did.

The Azat River, flowing through the Garni Gorge, reveals these impressive columnar basalt cliffs. This entire lower basin of the Azat River, including the geological features and nearby cultural sites, is designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The river's erosive power over millennia has shaped the canyon, bringing these distinctive volcanic rock formations into view. This interplay of natural forces and human history defines a remarkable landscape in central Armenia.
windows-spotlight-12696.jpg.copyright: © Denny van der Vaart/iStock/Getty Images Plus

windows-spotlight-1275.jpg.title: Multiple waterfalls, green mountains, lake, Poço da Alagoinha, Flores Island, Azores, Portugal
windows-spotlight-1275.jpg.headline: The 'lost Eden'
windows-spotlight-1275.jpg.description: Some describe this part of Flores Island as unspoiled perfection; others call it a 'lost Eden.' Here at Ribeira do Ferreiro, dozens of waterfalls tumble down soaring, steep basalt cliffs carpeted in lush greenery, with some falls flowing into a wide pond. One reason this landscape remains pristine is due to its remote location. The Azores island chain is an autonomous region of Portugal, set some 850 miles west of the Portuguese mainland in the Atlantic Ocean. Another reason for the Edenic vibe? In 2007, UNESCO declared the entire island of Flores a Biosphere Reserve. The designation helps to balance commercial interests with ecological concerns and aims for sustainable development.

windows-spotlight-1277.jpg.title: Karst islands, reefs, Raja Ampat, West Papua, Indonesia
windows-spotlight-1277.jpg.headline: Above the reefs
windows-spotlight-1277.jpg.description: Looming just off Bird's Head Peninsula, the Raja Ampat island chain sits smack in the middle of the Coral Triangle—a vast region astride the Pacific and Indian oceans that includes the world's most biodiverse marine zones. Of all the coral species that build reefs, more than three-quarters are found in pockets of the Triangle, though it covers less than 2% of the world ocean's total area. Raja Ampat is renowned as one of the top hotspots for seeing aquatic life, particularly as a place where divers can swim with both reef-dwelling and oceangoing manta rays—two populations seldom seen together.

windows-spotlight-1279.jpg.title: Candy-striped Cape Hatteras Lighthouse Milky Way, Buxton, North Carolina
windows-spotlight-1279.jpg.headline: A candy-striped light
windows-spotlight-1279.jpg.description: While immigrating to the soon-to-be United States in 1772, Alexander Hamilton escaped a close call when his ship nearly sank off North Carolina's Outer Banks. So when the young nation's lighthouses were later placed under Treasury Secretary Hamilton's authority, this was the first area he recommended for a new one. 'Hamilton's Light' lasted until just after the Civil War, when the current Cape Hatteras Lighthouse was built. The tallest lighthouse in the United States from base to top, it had to be painstakingly relocated in 1999 from unstable ground just a few paces from shore. Now set 1,500 feet inland, the 210-foot tower is one of the tallest structures ever moved.

windows-spotlight-128.jpg.title: Drive if you dare
windows-spotlight-128.jpg.headline: Drive if you dare
windows-spotlight-128.jpg.description: Drive carefully or this wild car ride might make you seasick. Winding from the mainland across numerous islands, Norway's 5-mile Atlanterhavsveien (Atlantic Road) is known for its dizzying roller-coaster feel as it carries car traffic mere feet above the ocean. Storseisundet Bridge, the span at the center-bottom of our image, curves and arches steeply to create a famous optical illusion that makes travelers feel they're cruising straight into oblivion. But if you prefer less deceptive sights, take in our bird's-eye view. There's nothing illusory about this spectacular scenery.

windows-spotlight-1285.jpg.title: Orange Red Yellow Agate Streaks
windows-spotlight-1285.jpg.headline: Winning streaks
windows-spotlight-1285.jpg.description: Countless generations of geologists, pro and amateur alike, have sought the storied and striated agate. The philosopher and rockhound Theophrastus named it for the Achates, a river in Sicily where he presumably found his first fine specimen. Of course, when this pioneering prospector was combing the riverbanks around 300 BCE, these were already some seriously ancient stones. While their many dense silica layers make agates difficult to date, some earned their first stripes during the Archean Eon that ended 2.5 billion years ago. That means they're just about as old as life on Earth itself!

windows-spotlight-1295.jpg.title: Winding Tongtian Road, Tianmen Mountain, Zhangjiajie
windows-spotlight-1295.jpg.headline: Twists of Tongtian
windows-spotlight-1295.jpg.description: Hairpin turns, all 99 of them, make driving Tongtian Avenue something of a hair-raising adventure, even for the most experienced motorist. This wildly curvy route is also called the 'Avenue Leading to the Sky' and for nearly 7 miles it snakes toward the top of Tianmen Mountain in China's Hunan Province. There's an alternate way up, but it's not much better for the faint of heart: What's considered the world's longest high-mountain cable car system ascends over 4,000 feet.

windows-spotlight-1297.jpg.title: Old wooden pier, smooth sea, sunset
windows-spotlight-1297.jpg.headline: Peering over smooth seas
windows-spotlight-1297.jpg.description: Corinthia is a regional unit of Greece, located in the Peloponnese region. Those are the dry geographical facts, but the region's historical legacy is an altogether more interesting story. World powers began battling for control over this area thousands of years ago. Most were eyeing the strategic Corinth Isthmus connecting the Peloponnese peninsula to mainland Greece. The Ancient Greeks attempted to carve a passage through the land bridge (where's Zeus when you need him?) for an easier transit of the 8,320-square-mile peninsula. It wasn’t until 1893 that technology caught up with ambition and a canal was dug for maritime passage. The ensuing development in the region has led parts of Corinthia to become essentially suburbs of Athens.

windows-spotlight-1299.jpg.title: Orange Ocellaris Clownfish Green Sea Anemone
windows-spotlight-1299.jpg.headline: Found you!
windows-spotlight-1299.jpg.description: This little striped fish may have just been spotted, but it has little to fear in the arms of its magnificent anemone pal here. Unlike their predators, clownfish are immune to anemone venom, so these friendly tendrils are a fortress from which the clownfish can feed on plankton and other small organisms. In exchange, the fish helps circulate water around the anemone, keeps its tentacles clean, and wards off anemone-eating butterflyfish. Once a clownfish finds a host anemone, it rarely leaves, so these benthic buddies' partnership runs deep.

windows-spotlight-13.jpg.title: White Desert chalk pillars, sunset, White Desert National Park, Egypt
windows-spotlight-13.jpg.headline: Stoic stones
windows-spotlight-13.jpg.description: Reminiscent of the American Southwest's red sandstone, but standing an ocean away and then some, these statuesque stones will appear several shades paler in the brightness of midday. We're seeing just three of the countless limestone pillars that burst through the sand—often in curious shapes—here in Egypt's White Desert. It takes hours to drive here from any major city in the country, but whether whitewashed by noonday sun or painted in ochres by a light-brushed horizon, it's worth a bit of an expedition.

windows-spotlight-130.jpg.title: Magenta Flower Field Sunset, Paarl
windows-spotlight-130.jpg.headline: Pretty Paarl
windows-spotlight-130.jpg.description: Nature lovers, foodies, and history buffs can all find appeal in this place whose name means 'pearl.' Here in Paarl, South Africa, an extensive network of trails traverses mountainsides and meadows alike, offering wanders amid wildflowers as well as high vistas of the city. Mild in climate, Paarl is also a major center in the Cape Winelands, where you'll find the country's finest vineyards. Finally, cementing its place in national history, Paarl is where then-future President Nelson Mandela was finally released from prison in 1990, heralding the end of apartheid.

windows-spotlight-1304.jpg.title: Bugaboo Spire sunset, Bugaboo Provincial Park, British Columbia, Canada
windows-spotlight-1304.jpg.headline: What's in a weird name?
windows-spotlight-1304.jpg.description: Touted as North America's equivalent of the French Alps, the granite spires of the Bugaboos tower over glaciers in eastern British Columbia. How did the mountain range get its offbeat name? A late-19th century gold rush gone wrong led disappointed prospectors to deem the area a 'bugaboo,' their term for a dead end. What gold seekers abandoned, mountaineers soon championed, and one after another the flinty spires were summited. The last of the Bugaboos to be conquered is seen here in our image—Snowpatch Spire was first summited in 1940. This peak, along with the rest of the range, lies within Bugaboo Provincial Park.

windows-spotlight-1308.jpg.title: White Chalk Cliffs of Dover, Dover, Kent, England
windows-spotlight-1308.jpg.headline: Chalk talk
windows-spotlight-1308.jpg.description: The blank canvas that lines England's southeast coast has inspired not only poets and musicians, but also one of Great Britain's oldest known names. Easily seen from French shores here at the English Channel's narrowest point, the chalky White Cliffs of Dover are easily spotted from mainland Europe. So it's thought that the classical name 'Albion' (likened to a Greek word for white) arose from how ancient visitors described the cliffs. Chalk it up to strong first impressions!

windows-spotlight-1310.jpg.title: Kirkjufell Mountain, Kirkjufellsfoss Waterfall, Sunset, Iceland
windows-spotlight-1310.jpg.headline: Iceland aglow
windows-spotlight-1310.jpg.description: Like most Icelandic landmarks, this series of short waterfalls boasts incredible beauty as well as a tongue-twister name: Kirkjufellsfoss. It's less tricky when you break it down: 'Kirk' means church, 'fell' means mountain, and 'foss' means waterfall, summing up to 'church mountain waterfall.' Between the falls and the distant Atlantic rises the church mountain itself, Kirkjufell, piercing the sky like a cathedral spire. Though there's no official tally, Kirkjufell is considered the most photographed mountain in Iceland (of course, Kirkjufellsfoss often makes a cameo appearance). This 1,500-foot peak is used to being a standout: During the Ice Age it was a nunatak, or glacial island, its summit untouched by the encroaching ice all around it.

windows-spotlight-1312.jpg.title: Arco Naturale, Capri, Italy
windows-spotlight-1312.jpg.headline: March to the arch
windows-spotlight-1312.jpg.description: The namesake of soft drinks and short pants alike, this Italian island has a shoreline defined by cliffs and caverns. On the opposite end of Capri from the island's most famous attraction—the eerie yet romantic Blue Grotto—a sweeping stone arch overlooks the azure Tyrrhenian Sea. The Arco Naturale, itself a collapsed grotto, is only reachable on foot—but rising less than a mile from the center of Capri village, it's not a hard hike for those who seek a unique panorama.

windows-spotlight-1313.jpg.title: Sunlit grassy highland cliffs
windows-spotlight-1313.jpg.headline: A vast highland's edge
windows-spotlight-1313.jpg.description: Most of southern Africa is bounded by steep cliffs that drop sharply near the coast, and nowhere is the contrast between high plateau and low plains more clear than the Amphitheatre. While it comprises just three of the roughly 600 miles of mountainlike cliffs called the Drakensberg, this sheer section of the Great Escarpment plummets more than 4,000 feet straight to the lowlands—so it's as stunning from below as from above. Scan the Amphitheatre's nooks and crannies and you may catch a glimpse of Tugela Falls, by some measures considered the world's tallest waterfall.

windows-spotlight-1319.jpg.title: Turquoise Braided Tidal Bay
windows-spotlight-1319.jpg.headline: A brush-stroke bay
windows-spotlight-1319.jpg.description: While this might look like a masterpiece from the Museum of Modern Art's walls, we're actually on the opposite side of the world from West 53rd Street. Our aerial shot shows Shark Bay, the westernmost point in Australia—a spot known not only for its 28 species of sharks, but also for two other lifeforms of interest. One is the dugong, or sea cow, a cousin to the manatee that numbers more than 10,000 within the bay. The other is less cute (not to mention less alive) but perhaps even more fascinating: Layered microbial fossils called stromatolites—the remains of some of the oldest known organisms—dot the shallows of the bay.

windows-spotlight-132.jpg.title: Sand dunes and lagoons
windows-spotlight-132.jpg.headline: Where dunes meet lagoons
windows-spotlight-132.jpg.description: These sand dunes only exist because the ocean is so close by, but that's not saltwater we're seeing. Brazil's remote Lençóis Maranhenses National Park is famous for its freshwater lagoons, which fill the dips and valleys amid the dunes each rainy season. Whether you witness them from high above or jump right in for a swim, the interlocking crystalline pools form a surrealist masterpiece that's forever in flux. The lagoons, slowly but surely, will evaporate into shallow puddles by autumn, only to be replenished when stormy weather returns next spring and summer.

windows-spotlight-1320.jpg.title: Schreckhorn mountain reflected in Bachalpsee, Swiss Alps
windows-spotlight-1320.jpg.headline: Alpine bliss
windows-spotlight-1320.jpg.description: Mountaineer Alfred Wills' ascent of the Wetterhorn (the leftmost mountain in our picture) in 1854 is said by some to have kicked off the golden age of Alpinism, when many local summits were first conquered by pioneering climbers. Here on the shores of Bachalpsee (aka Lake Bachalp), we're not getting quite as close to the blue Swiss sky—though we're still 7,400 feet up amid the Bernese Alps. And on a crisp alpine day like this, Bachalpsee mirrors the imposing peaks of the Wetterhorn, Schreckhorn, and Finsteraarhorn, making their snowy summits feel almost within reach.

windows-spotlight-1321.jpg.title: Rock-cut cave city, Cappadocia, Turkey
windows-spotlight-1321.jpg.headline: Cave city
windows-spotlight-1321.jpg.description: Cappadocia, Türkiye, is famed for its 'fairy chimneys,' pillars of soft tuff formed from compacted volcanic ash. Starting with the Hittites about 3,800 years back, people have dug innumerable caves into the tuff. Serving as homes, churches, and even entire underground communities, the caves gave protection from frequent raids in this former crossroads of empires. Marked by ancient carvings and wall art, many of Cappadocia's caves are used as dwellings or lodging even today.

windows-spotlight-1333.jpg.title: Kuang Si Falls, Red Foliage, Turquoise Pools, Luang Prabang, Laos
windows-spotlight-1333.jpg.headline: Foot of the falls
windows-spotlight-1333.jpg.description: We're just seeing the lowermost of multiple tiers that make up this terraced waterfall ensconced in autumnal colors. Though it's a ways out of frame, you can almost hear the Kuang Si Falls' main cascade roaring as it plummets 200 feet into the pools above. Here at the lower levels, the falls are generally gentle and end in calm turquoise pools. If you happen to be here in Laos during the country's hot, humid summer, good news: Some of the pools are open for swimming, so this sightseeing stop comes complete with a nice cooldown.

windows-spotlight-1338.jpg.title: Múlafossur Waterfall, Gásadalur, Vágar Island, Faroe Islands
windows-spotlight-1338.jpg.headline: A tall fall in two parts
windows-spotlight-1338.jpg.description: Fossá Waterfall tumbles twice over huge, terraced cliffs totaling over 400 feet high before forming a churning channel to the sea. Following the road that hugs Streymoy's eastern shore, drive north for about 45 minutes from the capital Tórshavn and the Faroe Islands' tallest cascade is impossible to miss. Indeed, you can watch it pass right under the roadway before it joins the salty strait separating Streymoy from Eysturoy—the next-largest chunk of land in this remote region of Denmark.

windows-spotlight-134.jpg.title: Chureito Pagoda Mount Fuji Sakura, Japan
windows-spotlight-134.jpg.headline: Sakura season
windows-spotlight-134.jpg.description: How much Japanese iconography can we jam into one photo? Here we see the iconic Mount Fuji and Chureito Pagoda framed by spring cherry blossoms, called sakura in Japanese. Viewing them is a beloved tradition here that involves gatherings, festivals, and just spending time outdoors beneath these blooming canopies—national pastimes collectively known as hanami. Since cherry trees at different latitudes bloom at different times, the Japanese Meteorological Agency tracks the cherry blossom front across the country each spring, giving partiers and picnickers a chance to plan ahead.

windows-spotlight-1344.jpg.title: Three scruffy brown capybaras in water
windows-spotlight-1344.jpg.headline: Scruff squad
windows-spotlight-1344.jpg.description: The capybara is most associated with wet, tropical wilderness like the Amazon Rainforest, but its range extends to every country in South America except Chile. It's one of well over a hundred mammal species found here on the massive flooded grassland known as the Pantanal—a biodiversity hotbed at the intersection of Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay. The world's largest rodent happily adapts to urban habitats, too, so it's hardly an uncommon sight in the continent's many growing metropolises.

windows-spotlight-1349.jpg.title: Atuh Beach rock formations, sunrise orange pink sky, water reflection, Nusa Penida, Bali, Indonesia
windows-spotlight-1349.jpg.headline: In before the tourists
windows-spotlight-1349.jpg.description: Bali's persistent sunshine has to start somewhere. Why not ease into a day of swimming, surfing, or snorkeling with a gentle sunrise on a quiet beach? Here on Nusa Penida—an island in Indonesia's Bali province that's many times smaller than the main island—you might even get a nice swath of seashore to yourself. Plus you'll be getting a sneak preview of the sunny day to come, since Nusa Penida lies east of most of Bali's tourism hotspots.

windows-spotlight-1353.jpg.title: Sigiriya Rock Fortress, Sri Lanka
windows-spotlight-1353.jpg.headline: Fortress over the forests
windows-spotlight-1353.jpg.description: Though this scene reminiscent of 'The Lion King' is actually set nowhere near the savannahs of Africa, its grand granite subject bears the name Sigiriya, or Lion Rock. And like Mufasa reigned supreme from his high perch, King Kashyapa I held this high point as his seat of power during the 5th century. While the fortress was near impenetrable, it was far from stealthy: the 400-foot-high, 100-foot-wide western face of Lion Rock was once covered in colorful frescoes. Though most of these murals have worn away, the intricate ruins topping the tower remain, accessible by climbing more than 1,200 stairs.
windows-spotlight-1353.jpg.copyright: © Tuul & Bruno Morandi/The Image Bank/Getty Images

windows-spotlight-136.jpg.title: Coastal Road, Farmland, Rocky Shore, Turquoise Ocean, Azores
windows-spotlight-136.jpg.headline: Above the Azores
windows-spotlight-136.jpg.description: The ring road that circles the island of Terceira only wends its way along the shoreline at a few points throughout the 50-mile drive, mostly cutting inland through pastures and farms. One of nine islands that make up the Azores—an overseas realm of Portugal—Terceira is full of terraced fields that farmers use for raising crops and grazing cattle. Though tourism has overtaken agriculture as Terceira's economic driver, the dairy farming tradition remains strong here, producing milk and cheeses that are much sought after on the mainland.

windows-spotlight-1363.jpg.title: McWay Falls beach cove, Big Sur, California
windows-spotlight-1363.jpg.headline: Roadside attraction
windows-spotlight-1363.jpg.description: Whether wrapped in winter fog or bathed in summer sun, this stream's subtle spill into the sea is a favourite sight for people cruising the Big Sur stretch of California State Route 1. You can see McWay Falls all-year-round, as long as this famous highway holds up. Here, where the mountains meet the eroding ocean, landslides sometimes force extended closures. Before one such landslide in 1983, McWay Falls plummeted directly into the Pacific, but now it lands on the beach before trickling into the waves. Visitors may be tempted to scramble down for a closer look, but authorities warn against this due to the still-unstable cliffs.

windows-spotlight-1366.jpg.title: Red sandstone buttes, reservoir, dark clouds, sunset, Lake Powell
windows-spotlight-1366.jpg.headline: Of droughts and dams
windows-spotlight-1366.jpg.description: When completely filled, Lake Powell's coastline is longer than the West Coast of the mainland United States, its sinuous shape outlining almost 2,000 miles of shore along the Arizona-Utah border. The 21st century has been hard on the nation's second-largest reservoir, though, with the southwestern megadrought leaving it below a quarter of its capacity at times (evidenced by the 'bathtub rings' visible here). Though popular for recreation, Lake Powell—and the Glen Canyon Dam that creates it—is a focus of debate: Many environmental groups say the lake should be drained to restore the Colorado River's natural flow.

windows-spotlight-137.jpg.title: Circular coral reef with outrigger boat, Palawan, Philippines
windows-spotlight-137.jpg.headline: A pearly province
windows-spotlight-137.jpg.description: The Philippines' largest province sticks out from the crowd of islands that forms most of the nation. The long, skinny finger of Palawan stretches southwestward more than 350 miles, its coral-rimmed islands, lagoons, and bays showcasing seas of rich, pearly turquoise. Speaking of pearls, hunting that satiny gem was once a major industry in Palawan. Boats not unlike this bangka used to haul pearl divers into waters up to 100 feet deep, where they'd freedive to find abundant oyster and clam beds. One pearl harvested here in the 1930s, presumably from a giant clam, has been hailed as the largest in the world at over 14 pounds.

windows-spotlight-1370.jpg.title: A marble marvel
windows-spotlight-1370.jpg.headline: A marble marvel
windows-spotlight-1370.jpg.description: It'll take a boat ride across a mountain-ringed glacial lake to get this view of Chile's Cuevas de Marmol, or Marble Caves. From our photo you might guess this is a vast, gaping cavern. In reality, though, you may have to duck as your boat passes under its low-slung stone ceilings. Reflecting blue hues from the glacial waters, the swirling patterns of the cavern walls have been revealed over the past 6,000 years as waves carved these marbled maws into the lakeside cliffs.

windows-spotlight-1375.jpg.title: El Capitan Merced River Starry Night, Yosemite National Park, California, USA
windows-spotlight-1375.jpg.headline: Quick, make a wish!
windows-spotlight-1375.jpg.description: Did you spot the shooting star photobombing this iconic shot? Night or day, Yosemite National Park is widely considered one of the most spectacular natural places in the United States. Though it covers a vast swath of surrounding mountains and forests, most visitors spend the bulk of their visit in the Yosemite Valley, a portion of which is featured in our image. Here in the valley, the Merced River flows below two of the most renowned sites in Yosemite: El Capitan and Half Dome.

windows-spotlight-1376.jpg.title: Motion in the ocean
windows-spotlight-1376.jpg.headline: Motion in the ocean
windows-spotlight-1376.jpg.description: The name Kaikōura comes from the Māori word for a local ocean delicacy: southern rock lobster, also known as crayfish or kōura. The seafood catch here is indeed plentiful, as are opportunities to see massive marine wildlife like sperm whales and orcas. Even more popular are Kaikōura's dusky dolphins, who gather by the hundreds and impress crowds with their acrobatics.
windows-spotlight-1376.jpg.copyright: © Cultura RF/Ben Pipe Photography/Image Source/Getty Images

windows-spotlight-1378.jpg.title: Bull Moose, Mountains
windows-spotlight-1378.jpg.headline: Moose in the mountains
windows-spotlight-1378.jpg.description: As spring unfolds in Colorado, the backwoods teem with life small and large. We'd say this bull moose belongs in the second category. Moose trounce their deer relatives in size, with bulls weighing up to three-quarters of a ton. And while this hulking hoofer's velvety antlers are still sprouting, they may soon span more than 6 feet. Northerly states like Maine and Alaska boast far bigger moose populations, but Colorado's contingent stands strong at roughly 3,000 and is one of the fastest growing.

windows-spotlight-1380.jpg.title: Colorful hillside town, medieval castle, Liguria
windows-spotlight-1380.jpg.headline: Lovely Liguria
windows-spotlight-1380.jpg.description: While the Italian region of Liguria is known for its lovely coastal cities and towns, you'll find charm to equal the seaside if you head inland. Villages known as comunes dot hill and dale here, and some are just as steeply situated as those on the sea cliffs. The sloping comune in our photo, Ameglia, lies between the Magra River and Gulf of La Spezia, built on a hillside topped with a well-preserved medieval castle.

windows-spotlight-1382.jpg.title: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque illuminated arches reflecting pool, Abu Dhabi
windows-spotlight-1382.jpg.headline: A truly grand place
windows-spotlight-1382.jpg.description: While it was really built just a few decades ago, there's no denying the old-world grandeur of this palatial exterior. The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, built between 1994 and 2007, is a crowning achievement in modern Arabic architecture and the largest mosque in the United Arab Emirates. Intended as a center for unity and education, the 30-acre complex boasts vast public libraries of not only Islamic scholarship but also works by scientists, artists, and others from across the globe. Inside, impossibly large décor abounds—including a German-made chandelier measuring 33 feet across and weighing 9 tons, and a 60,000-square-foot Iranian woven carpet containing more than 2 billion knots.

windows-spotlight-1384.jpg.title: Meteora Monastery, Meteora, Greece
windows-spotlight-1384.jpg.headline: A pious, precarious place
windows-spotlight-1384.jpg.description: Like the other five surviving monasteries of Meteora, Rousanou isn't as given to solitude as it used to be. The 20th-century addition of convenient staircases opened these contemplative complexes to curious tourists. But before that, ascetics and their daring visitors had to ascend and descend ladders to get here—or be hauled up and lowered down by nets and ropes, the same way food and other necessities were delivered. Ease of transit isn't the only big modern change for Rousanou: While originally a home for male monks, nowadays it hosts a convent of nuns.

windows-spotlight-1387.jpg.title: Stars over Sam Phan Bok
windows-spotlight-1387.jpg.headline: Stars over Sam Phan Bok
windows-spotlight-1387.jpg.description: Sam Phan Bok, known as Thailand's Grand Canyon, is a huge rock reef that lies under a river and emerges during the dry season when the water level drops. Its name translates to '3,000 holes,' alluding to the crypts and depressions that define the riverine ravine. It's set in the easternmost part of Thailand: Ubon Ratchathani, a landlocked province bordering Laos and Cambodia. It's a bit far-flung, so the lush monsoon forests and national parks in the area are low on light pollution—making this stellar Milky Way shot possible.

windows-spotlight-1388.jpg.title: Bamburgh Castle silhouette sunset beach, Northumberland, England
windows-spotlight-1388.jpg.headline: A castle in profile
windows-spotlight-1388.jpg.description: This island's characteristically cloudy skies don't usually let much sun through, but when they do, spectacular silhouettes can be seen against the crimson horizon. From its promontory post on England's northeast coast, Bamburgh Castle gets a sneak preview of the sunrise over Britain each morning. This long-ago domain of Sir Lancelot—or so say the legends—has seen many, many of them. The castle itself has only stood since the 12th century, but it sits on a spot first settled about 12,000 years back.

windows-spotlight-139.jpg.title: Humpback whale underwater
windows-spotlight-139.jpg.headline: Hello, humpback
windows-spotlight-139.jpg.description: This friendly humpback whale was spotted near the archipelago of Tonga, but you don't need to travel all the way to the South Pacific to witness these giants at play. Highly migratory, humpbacks have a range that covers the entire global ocean except the very coldest Arctic waters. Sticking close to the surface and making relatively shallow, short dives, humpbacks frequently breach in spectacular fashion, making them perhaps the world's most popular sight for whale watchers.

windows-spotlight-1398.jpg.title: Sediment-rich coastal estuaries, Kimberley Western Australia
windows-spotlight-1398.jpg.headline: Watercolor wilderness
windows-spotlight-1398.jpg.description: This overview of sprawling tidal flats in Derby, Australia, is one of countless finely detailed images available in the Microsoft Planetary Computer. This vast, cloud-powered database lets scientists see a whole timeline of crisp satellite captures and environmental data for any location in the world. By analyzing this data, scientists can explore better ways to manage resources and combat climate change. Here in northwestern Australia, for example, a scientist might observe changes in the coastline over time to track effects of the region's 40-foot tides—the highest on the continent.

windows-spotlight-1401.jpg.title: Na Pali Coast Green Cliffs Beach, Kauai, Hawaii
windows-spotlight-1401.jpg.headline: Paddle-in paradise
windows-spotlight-1401.jpg.description: Whether witnessed from the air or the sea, this Hawaii state park is a spectacular sight to behold—and a coveted one at that. To access this land of spiny cliffs and slender valleys on the island of Kauai, you'll need advance reservations to hike in. Otherwise you'll have to see it either from high above like this, or from the water by sailing or paddling in. The park's name, Nā Pali Coast, refers to the ridges' abrupt, 4,000-foot rise from the beach: Nā pali translates from Hawaiian to mean 'high cliffs.'

windows-spotlight-1403.jpg.title: White Windmill, Fuerteventura, Canary Islands
windows-spotlight-1403.jpg.headline: An easygoing isle
windows-spotlight-1403.jpg.description: Though we're indeed in Spain, we're about a thousand miles from the plains of La Mancha where the fictional Don Quixote tilted at windmills like this one. Fuerteventura is the second largest by area of the Canary Islands, a Spanish overseas holding since 1405 even though it's much closer to Morocco. Despite its size, Fuerteventura is home to less than 1% of the Canaries' population (most reside on Tenerife or Gran Canaria), so breathing room is ample on the windy isle.

windows-spotlight-1404.jpg.title: Colorful Glowing Spinning Carnival Ride, Night
windows-spotlight-1404.jpg.headline: Garden glow
windows-spotlight-1404.jpg.description: The kaleidoscope of light and motion in our image comes courtesy of two things: Long-exposure photography and an annual festival put on in the heart of Paris. Every year from June to August the Festival of the Tuileries adds towering amusement rides and cotton candy to the historic Tuileries Garden. (We're seeing a swinging chair ride in the center of our image here.) Queen Catherine de Medici commissioned a grand garden in 1564 to complement her royal residence, the Tuileries Palace. Following the French Revolution, the garden became a public park, and has since served as a beloved gathering place for locals and visitors to the City of Light.

windows-spotlight-1407.jpg.title: Ancient Mudbrick Heri Es-Souani Royal Granaries, Meknes, Morocco
windows-spotlight-1407.jpg.headline: A vast past pantry
windows-spotlight-1407.jpg.description: Fez, Marrakesh, Rabat, and this city, Meknes, constitute the Imperial Cities of Morocco, the nation's four historical capitals. Meknes had its brief turn from 1672 to 1727, when Sultan Ismail Ibn Sharif fortified it as his seat of rule, centered on an imposing kasbah. Adjoining the kasbah's grounds are the weathered ruins of the Heri es-Swani, expansive grain silos that once supplied the city and now stand as a mazelike monument to a moment in Morocco's past.

windows-spotlight-141.jpg.title: Coastal Dunes, Sado Estuary, Portugal
windows-spotlight-141.jpg.headline: A dominant dune
windows-spotlight-141.jpg.description: This overview, showing France's Great Dune of Pilat at low tide, is one of countless finely detailed images available in the Microsoft Planetary Computer. This vast, cloud-powered database lets scientists see a whole timeline of crisp satellite captures and environmental data for any location in the world. By analyzing this data, scientists can explore better ways to manage natural resources. For example, a scientist could match shots of Pilat year-over-year with historical wind and tidal data to show how and why the Great Dune has shifted over time.

windows-spotlight-1412.jpg.title: Mount Otemanu ocean sunset, Bora Bora, French Polynesia
windows-spotlight-1412.jpg.headline: Standing alone
windows-spotlight-1412.jpg.description: The name Tahiti may bring to mind beautiful beaches and a laid-back island lifestyle. But a trip to French Polynesia's largest island isn't complete without a peek at this landmark peak. Towering over this part of the world at 7,352 feet, Mont Orohena is the most topographically isolated mountain in the world that isn't a fourteener. Since the nearest landmass to Tahiti is relatively flat Australia, Orohena is the highest point in a 2,500-mile radius. So if you reach the summit on a clear day, get ready for a long, uninterrupted view over the sunny South Pacific.

windows-spotlight-1416.jpg.title: Manarola colorful cliffside village at night, Cinque Terre, Italy
windows-spotlight-1416.jpg.headline: One down, four to go
windows-spotlight-1416.jpg.description: Even if you thoroughly wander Manarola's towering, twisting topography, you'll have only explored a fifth of this spectacular region. Consisting of Manarola and four other villages on Italy's northwest coast, Cinque Terre ("Five Lands") is a national park and UNESCO World Heritage Site that's visited by more than 2 million people a year. Precariously terraced and sloping straight to the Ligurian Sea shore, the cluster of villages is only accessible by train, boat or trail. Who said paradise would be easy to reach?

windows-spotlight-1420.jpg.title: Tre Cime di Lavaredo, Lago Antorno, golden autumn light, Dolomites, Italy
windows-spotlight-1420.jpg.headline: Triplet peaks
windows-spotlight-1420.jpg.description: If you're headed to Italy, you're probably eager to feast your eyes on old masters' paintings between plates of pasta. But should you wander off the beaten path and trade gourmet grub for trail mix, you'll marvel at masterpieces even more ancient. Here in the Dolomites, an Italian subrange of the Alps, the rugged landscape is a match for any found in Austria or Switzerland.If mountains are nature's masterpieces, the one up ahead is a triptych. Though appearing like a single mountain from this viewpoint on the shores of Lake Antorno, the Three Peaks of Lavaredo are actually a majestic trio, popular with photographers from any angle.

windows-spotlight-1422.jpg.title: Fairytale Castle Neuschwanstein, Schwangau, Bavaria, Germany
windows-spotlight-1422.jpg.headline: The Fairytale King's castle
windows-spotlight-1422.jpg.description: Sometime during his 1864-1883 reign, King Ludwig II of Bavaria grew tired of bickering ministers, international scheming, and dreams of empire building—in short, politics. A big fan of music and drama, especially Richard Wagner's vivid operas about German mythic heroes, the king had a flair for the fantastical. And though his focus on frivolous pursuits rather than matters of state earned him a chiding nickname, 'The Fairytale King,' the castle he left as his legacy is one of Germany's most beloved symbols.Construction began on Neuschwanstein Castle in 1868, and though it was never finished, it's one of the world's most visited castles, drawing almost a million and a half people per year. And it's a pop culture landmark just as much as a historical one: The famous castle at Disneyland in California was directly inspired by Neuschwanstein.

windows-spotlight-1425.jpg.title: Twelve Apostles Sunset, Victoria, Australia
windows-spotlight-1425.jpg.headline: Towering twins
windows-spotlight-1425.jpg.description: The state of Victoria's shores form the southernmost stretch of Australia's coast, with hundreds of miles of picturesque coastline flanking the metropolis of Melbourne. There's no better way to experience it than the Great Ocean Road, a 150-mile seaside highway winding westward from Melbourne's suburbs to this region called the Shipwreck Coast—aptly titled for the more than 600 vessels its depths have claimed. When the hungry waves are calm, this spot just below the Gibson Steps—a cliffside staircase leading 230 feet down to the beach—is a great place to take in a sunset framed by the coast's signature sea stacks. These twins are often mistaken as part of the famous Twelve Apostles formation nearby, but they're actually a separate group named Gog and Magog.

windows-spotlight-1426.jpg.title: Sunrise mist Two Jack Lake Mount Rundle reflection, Banff National Park, Alberta, Canada
windows-spotlight-1426.jpg.headline: A tale of two Jacks
windows-spotlight-1426.jpg.description: Though it's really a humble arm of the much larger Lake Minnewanka, this body of water is so nice they named it…well, not twice, but after two different folks. Two Jack Lake was named in 1959 in honor of two late local celebrities: Jack Watters, once a bigwig at the local coal mine, and 'Captain Jack' Stanley, who ran a boat concession on the lake. Its placid surface presenting a perfect reflection of Mount Rundle, Two Jack is a great alternative destination if you wish to dodge the crowds of nearby Lake Louise and Moraine Lake.

windows-spotlight-143.jpg.title: Blue ice, snow-covered island, bare trees, Norway
windows-spotlight-143.jpg.headline: Norwegian exposure
windows-spotlight-143.jpg.description: Thanks to the North Atlantic Current (an extension of the warm Gulf Stream), Norway is actually quite temperate for its high latitude. That hardly means Norwegians are spared Boreas' bite: Here in the lowlands near Oslo, locals pay for their warm summers with long, dark winters and thick layers of snow and ice. But as the Nordic saying goes, there's no bad weather, just bad clothes—so bundle up and get to work on that snow fort!

windows-spotlight-1434.jpg.title: Flock of Pink Flamingos in shallow water at sunset
windows-spotlight-1434.jpg.headline: A bird's paradise
windows-spotlight-1434.jpg.description: Clear across the Yucatán Peninsula from Caribbean resorts like Cancún, you'll find the town of Celestún set along the shallow Gulf of Mexico. As with the opposite coast's tourist hotspots, you'll meet many colorful types here. Flocks of snowbirds, the occasional year-rounder. But we're not talking about hard-partying vacationers: During winter, these warm, mangrove-bounded waters host not only flamingos but also herons, pelicans, and many other migratory birds. In all, more than 300 bird species make the Ría Celestun Biosphere Reserve home at least part of the year.

windows-spotlight-1435.jpg.title: Temple of Peace, Arched Bridge, Canal, Sanssouci Park, Potsdam, Germany
windows-spotlight-1435.jpg.headline: Peace in the park
windows-spotlight-1435.jpg.description: The Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm may be in Germany, but its 18th-century design follows the English model that was trendy at the time: a mix of arboriculture and architecture that follows the flow of natural spaces, shunning the curated symmetry of French or Italian gardens. English gardens are often grand in scope, and this World Heritage Site is no exception at 36,000 acres. The park even includes a castle, plus dozens of other buildings and bridges for its million-plus yearly visitors to discover. Shown here is the wrought-iron Agnes Bridge framing the Venus Temple, one of numerous neoclassical structures in the park.

windows-spotlight-1437.jpg.title: Flysch rock formations, Zumaia, Basque Country, Spain
windows-spotlight-1437.jpg.headline: Stone squiggles
windows-spotlight-1437.jpg.description: Looking like layers of lasagna as they're exposed by the tide, these wavy formations were snapped not in Italy but on the northern coast of Spain. This distinctive pattern of shallow rocky ridges, known as flysch, arose during a process called orogeny: the birth of mountains. As tectonic plates smashed together and were thrust upward to form the Basque Country's coastal peaks, landslides crashed down the new slopes and created powerful currents when they entered the water. Sediment was compressed against the seafloor by these currents, resulting in rigid strips of rock that deformed into undulating shapes as the fault settled.

windows-spotlight-1439.jpg.title: Blue-footed Booby chick
windows-spotlight-1439.jpg.headline: Fuzz to feathers
windows-spotlight-1439.jpg.description: The smallest member of the booby and gannet family, the red-footed booby still cuts a pretty strong figure in the sky, with a wingspan  around 5 feet. Of course, it's going to be a while before this little seabird chick takes flight. First it'll need to shed its baby fuzz to make way for that first coat of feathers. All red-footed booby chicks start out covered in white down, but as they mature their plumage takes on a brown, white, or multicolored morph depending on the individual's genetics. Regardless of feather pattern, though, adults of both sexes sport the species' signature ruby-red stompers.

windows-spotlight-1442.jpg.title: Forest Island Turquoise Lake Sunset
windows-spotlight-1442.jpg.headline: Any buccaneers here?
windows-spotlight-1442.jpg.description: Don't expect to meet Long John Silver on this pirate-hook islet. Treasure Island, aka Flynn Island, may look tropical with its sandy shores and set against a soothing sunset, but it's actually located in the northern part of Michigan's mitten. Hunting for Captain Flint's treasure may be futile here at Higgins Lake, but those who cast lines off these sandbars will find other riches: Perch, trout, and even toothy northern pike await anglers' baited hooks within these chilly waters.

windows-spotlight-1446.jpg.title: Three Giraffes Savanna Sunset
windows-spotlight-1446.jpg.headline: Tall trio
windows-spotlight-1446.jpg.description: A towering trio looks on as a watercolor sunset washes the vast veld they call home. The world giraffe population is estimated at a little over 100,000, and several thousand of them live here in Kruger National Park. Founded in 1926 as South Africa's first national park, Kruger is one of Africa's biggest game reserves at more than 7,500 square miles. In addition to South African giraffes (one of nine giraffe subspecies), the huge park protects robust populations of rhinos, elephants, lions, and more.

windows-spotlight-1452.jpg.title: Multi-colored Beach Huts on Coastal Dunes
windows-spotlight-1452.jpg.headline: Shacks on the strand
windows-spotlight-1452.jpg.description: Dozens of small shelters skirt busy beaches here at the seaside resort of Southwold, England, whether built on boardwalks above the beach or plopped right on the sand like these. Owning one of these convenient day-use huts is a pricey prospect, as they fetch well over 100,000 British pounds on the market. But many can be rented for a reasonable fee, offering a kitchenette and shady, private lounge space for a long day at the coast. Each hut has a name as unique as its paint job, from White Swan to Jabba the Hut.

windows-spotlight-1454.jpg.title: Herd of buffalo grazing by river
windows-spotlight-1454.jpg.headline: Where the buffalo ruminate
windows-spotlight-1454.jpg.description: For bison, summer is always a great time to put on a few extra pounds before winter comes—but even when looking to beef up, bison still order the salad. Grazers of grass and other wild brush, these great American ungulates are also ruminants: Their specialized digestive systems process and metabolize food extremely slowly, squeezing as many calories as possible out of a few mouthfuls of grass. Every little bite helps for this lumbering, hungry herd—there's a long Yellowstone winter ahead of them.

windows-spotlight-1455.jpg.title: Orange and Red Desert Dunes
windows-spotlight-1455.jpg.headline: Durable dunes
windows-spotlight-1455.jpg.description: Most of the United Arab Emirates' 11 million-plus people live in the urban cluster at the nation's northeast corner, including global cities like Dubai and Abu Dhabi. But here we see a much sleepier sector: The Rub' al Khali, or Empty Quarter. The world's largest erg, the quarter covers 250,000 square miles of the lower Arabian Peninsula with countless dunes, many reaching over 800 feet tall. Packed tight and soaked deep down with groundwater, these mountains of sand tend to keep their shape in spite of the fierce desert winds that whip their surface.

windows-spotlight-1456.jpg.title: Tangled Mangrove Delta, Sundarbans
windows-spotlight-1456.jpg.headline: A tangled delta
windows-spotlight-1456.jpg.description: This overview of the intricate Ganges Delta is one of countless finely detailed images available in the Microsoft Planetary Computer. This vast, cloud-powered database lets scientists see a whole timeline of crisp satellite captures and environmental data for any location in the world. By analyzing this data, scientists can explore better ways to manage resources, combat climate change, and track population growth. Here in Bangladesh, the need for better understanding of climate change is greater than ever, as rising sea levels pose a threat to as many as six million homes in the densely populated country.

windows-spotlight-1461.jpg.title: Northern Saw-whet Owl perched on mossy rock
windows-spotlight-1461.jpg.headline: Little but loud
windows-spotlight-1461.jpg.description: The northern saw-whet owl's name hearkens to bygone days when it shared the Northwoods with roving lumberjacks and fur trappers. The grizzled forest workers likened this tiny owl's call—a high, sharp series of hoots often repeating for hours—to the familiar sound of a whetstone honing a saw tooth by tooth. Though best recognized for making noise, the pint-size predator is great at hearing it, too: As with many owl species, the saw-whet's ears are asymmetrical in structure and placement, allowing it to triangulate upon prey with fierce precision using sound alone.

windows-spotlight-1462.jpg.title: Lake Bled Island Church and Castle, Slovenia
windows-spotlight-1462.jpg.headline: An island sanctuary
windows-spotlight-1462.jpg.description: Though the island that supports it is only accessible via traditional flat-bottomed boats (or by trudging over ice during winter), a lonely church at the center of Slovenia's Lake Bled gets plenty of visitors. At this popular marriage venue watched over by Bled Castle (perched on a bluff at the right of our photo), tradition holds that the groom must carry the bride up all 99 steps to the church's tower and ring its bell, which is said to grant wishes. It's an out-of-the-way setting within what some might call an out-of-the-way country. But if you ask us, Slovenia deserves a spot on any great European tour itinerary.

windows-spotlight-1464.jpg.title: Cracked Salt Flat, Mountains, Blue Sky
windows-spotlight-1464.jpg.headline: A salty spectacle
windows-spotlight-1464.jpg.description: Different folks will see different things when they gaze on the big, beautiful blank canvas of the Bonneville Salt Flats. To a chef, it's reassurance that the world's most important seasoning is in high supply, as 90% of the surface here is plain old table salt. To a filmmaker, it's anything from a distinctive Utah establishing shot to a surreal sci-fi setting. And to a daredevil on wheels, it's the perfect wide-open space for impressive stunts: The land speed record has been broken here multiple times.

windows-spotlight-1470.jpg.title: Red Lighthouse, Pier, Sunset, Holland, Michigan
windows-spotlight-1470.jpg.headline: Small beacon, big city
windows-spotlight-1470.jpg.description: Marking a point where the Milwaukee River meets Lake Michigan, this lighthouse stands quite close to the downtown heart of the city it's named for. First lit in 1872, the steel lighthouse had keepers until 1926, and was fully automated in 1939. Although the tower itself isn't open to visitors, the pier is easily accessible, and the dark red structure stands out against water and sky in an especially photogenic way. Lighthouse lovers will appreciate the location: From Milwaukee Pierhead Light one can easily spot both Kenosha North Pier Light and Milwaukee Breakwater Light.

windows-spotlight-1475.jpg.title: Historic Portland Head Light sunset, Cape Elizabeth, Maine
windows-spotlight-1475.jpg.headline: Historic headland
windows-spotlight-1475.jpg.description: The Portland Head Light rises from a rocky cape not within the same-named Maine municipality but in nearby Cape Elizabeth. The lighthouse is older than the state itself: It was first lit in 1791, when Maine was still a part of Massachusetts, George Washington was president, and the beacon's fuel was whale oil. Portland Head was among the earliest federally funded projects in the United States, completed with a $1,500 appropriation passed by congress at President Washington's urging.

windows-spotlight-1477.jpg.title: Faro di Capo Zafferano, Sicily, Italy
windows-spotlight-1477.jpg.headline: Not so rotten
windows-spotlight-1477.jpg.description: On a clear day, this rough-hewn Irish harbor islet is quite a pleasant place, contrary to its unsavory label. Rotten Island's name isn't meant to be descriptive, though: It's an anglicized version of the name Naomh Rotain, a hermit who's said to have made his home here. His stay is likely a legend, but once the Rotten Island Lighthouse was built in 1838, up to 11 people lived here at a time to tend it. Over time, advancing technology meant fewer and fewer keepers were needed, and by 1959, keeping the beacon lit only required an occasional visit. Today the island is uninhabited and the lighthouse fully automated, a frequent sight on the many cruises that dock in nearby Donegal.

windows-spotlight-148.jpg.title: Cliff lighthouse, Winding road light trails, Starry night ocean
windows-spotlight-148.jpg.headline: Not-so-straight and narrow
windows-spotlight-148.jpg.description: In this long exposure photo, the snaking light trails of modern car headlamps complement the shine of a Mediterranean beacon built in 1893, while ancient stars set the night even more alight. This shot was likely taken in the offseason, since the road to Formentor Lighthouse is closed from about June to September to relieve tourism-fueled traffic jams. But summertime visitors can still walk, cycle, or charter a shuttle to this 19th-century tower that marks the northernmost cape of Majorca.

windows-spotlight-1484.jpg.title: Red Sunset Water, Silhouetted Ducks
windows-spotlight-1484.jpg.headline: Of ducks and depths
windows-spotlight-1484.jpg.description: These ducks in a row are among the many waterfowl who gather here on Lake Tahoe, which even in winter never fully freezes due to its massive depth and volume. Other flocks found on this ample alpine lake: Sailors, swimmers, anglers, and nature lovers of all types. On shore, you'll find hordes of hikers trekking the trails, foodies enjoying fine dining, and gamblers trying their luck at lakeside casinos. And each winter, even set between two warm states (California and Nevada), this elevated area becomes a powdery paradise for skiers, snowboarders, and even snow tubers.

windows-spotlight-1486.jpg.title: Safdarjung's Tomb reflecting pool, Delhi, India
windows-spotlight-1486.jpg.headline: Twin to the Taj?
windows-spotlight-1486.jpg.description: Here in India's capital region, Mughal architecture spans centuries. The pictured Safdarjung's Tomb was built in 1754, more than 120 years after the distant Taj Mahal, from which much of its design was borrowed. In contrast, the nearby Red Fort in central Delhi was built in the 1630s, the same decade as the Taj. Even closer to Safdarjung's Tomb is another Mughal mausoleum, Humayun's Tomb—the palatial garden-tomb complex that inspired all others to come when it was built way back in 1565.

windows-spotlight-149.jpg.title: Gentoo penguin, Antarctica
windows-spotlight-149.jpg.headline: Flightless, but resourceful
windows-spotlight-149.jpg.description: While gentoo penguins are native to the oceanic islands that speckle the sub-Antarctic, our photo subject is one of a sizeable population living on mainland Antarctica. Gentoo colonies on the icy continent are clustered at the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula, a bustling penguin metropolis shared with chinstrap, emperor, and Adélie penguins. Unfortunately, this part of Antarctica is warming faster than any part of the world besides the North Pole—threatening Adélies, for example, which mostly eat krill attracted to ice-borne algae. On the brighter side, gentoos are noted for their ability to change their habits, finding new food sources and breeding locations in response to climate change. This flexibility has helped them become the fastest—and only—growing population of penguins in the Antarctic region.

windows-spotlight-1492.jpg.title: Purple coral polyps
windows-spotlight-1492.jpg.headline: Purple polyps
windows-spotlight-1492.jpg.description: Acropora is a genus of hard coral including more than a hundred species, some known as elkhorn or staghorn corals for the antlerlike texture of their multitudinous polyps. Acropora species' tough exoskeletons and fast growth are critical to living reef structures across the globe, with Acropora found in the Pacific and Indian oceans as well as the Caribbean. While these carapaced Cnidarians come in a seemingly endless palette of colors, purple specimens like this are considered quite rare.

windows-spotlight-1495.jpg.title: Minack Theatre, Porthcurno, Cornwall
windows-spotlight-1495.jpg.headline: The stage by the sea
windows-spotlight-1495.jpg.description: Set right against the crashing waves of the English Channel, the Minack Theatre in Porthcurno, Cornwall, lies just a few miles from England's westernmost and southernmost points. As many as 80,000 people per year squeeze into this steep, stone-hewn space to see spectacular interpretations of Shakespeare's plays. Perhaps as compelling a story as any drama seen here was the life of Rowena Cade, who founded the Minack on her property in 1932. Rowena not only offered up part of her cliffside estate to the community for open-air theater productions, she eagerly built the stage and seating herself. Cutting stones and mixing concrete by hand, she and a few friends added to the theater a little at a time until her death in 1983, just shy of age 90.

windows-spotlight-1496.jpg.title: Hot air balloons tea fields sunrise
windows-spotlight-1496.jpg.headline: Soaring over tea fields
windows-spotlight-1496.jpg.description: After changing hands several times in the ensuing centuries, Beaumaris eventually fell into ruin. But today’s visitors likely won't notice anything amiss, as the castle is still impressively looming and large, having been restored beginning in 1925. And as we can see in our image, Beaumaris even comes complete with the requisite medieval moat.

windows-spotlight-1497.jpg.title: That Wanaka Tree, yellow leaves, snow-capped mountains, Lake Wanaka, New Zealand
windows-spotlight-1497.jpg.headline: A dangerously famous tree
windows-spotlight-1497.jpg.description: This arboreal oddball may live all alone in the waters of Lake Wanaka, but it gets plenty of visitors. Known all over social media as #ThatWanakaTree, this thirsty willow's curious placement in a splendid setting has made it a South Island icon—and a global destination for those seeking a perfect selfie.All that attention isn't always such a great thing, though. Since its rise to online fame, That Wanaka Tree has been damaged at various times by careless climbers and saw-wielding vandals. (That large, low-hanging limb in our picture? Yeah, that's gone now.) And to make matters worse, the cold water here makes for slow regrowth, meaning the tree's injuries will show for years. So if you make your way to this spot someday, by all means snap a shot with this remarkable resident of the Southern Alps—but look, don't touch!

windows-spotlight-15.jpg.title: Rocky peak of Mount Segla, Norway
windows-spotlight-15.jpg.headline: The spire of Segla
windows-spotlight-15.jpg.description: The lush inland of Senja, a large island off mainland Norway, is bounded by toothy coastal mountains. None of them make for a better viewpoint than Mount Segla. Its unmistakable, needle-like crag marks the end of a tough but rewarding trail from the fishing village of Fjordgård. Here we get a panoramic view of the mountain-lined bays and fjords that cut into this Arctic isle's northern coastline.

windows-spotlight-1507.jpg.title: Rock Arch Forest Overlook
windows-spotlight-1507.jpg.headline: Nature's masonry
windows-spotlight-1507.jpg.description: Cerro Arco, a singular stone arch in the wilds of Paraguay, almost looks like it was built out of boulders mortared together. And in a sense it was, though no human mason crafted it. The arch is made up of sandstone that long ago underwent silicification: Water rich in dissolved silica seeped into the cracks and voids within the sandstone, eventually drying into a sort of glue that strengthened the structure. Later, flowing water washed away the lower reaches of sediment where the silica didn't permeate, leaving this impressive crest of reinforced rock.

windows-spotlight-151.jpg.title: Fish River Canyon Sunset, Namibia
windows-spotlight-151.jpg.headline: Africa's grandest canyon
windows-spotlight-151.jpg.description: By sheer numbers, this Namibian ravine doesn't quite stack up against the more familiar Grand Canyon: At 100 miles long and 1,800 feet deep, Fish River Canyon is less than half the Arizona landmark's size. But as a master sculptor of scenery, the shallow and seasonal Fish River gives the mighty Colorado a run for its money. Along the Fish's banks, a 50-mile trail affords hikers incredible views for days (most tackle it in about five). And as further reward, the hot spring resort of ǀAi-ǀAis awaits at the trail's terminus.

windows-spotlight-1511.jpg.title: Color-splashed coastal path with red and white lighthouse and sea ice
windows-spotlight-1511.jpg.headline: A color-splashed coast
windows-spotlight-1511.jpg.description: Civil engineers in this icy East Asian port decided that this stark seaside park needed not only a guiding lighthouse but a smattering of warm color. Urban design is a big job in Dalian, a peninsular city in Northeast China known for its eclectic architecture and varied history. The British, Russians, and Japanese have all occupied Dalian in the last 200 years, and a hodgepodge of historical design styles can still be found amid the sleek modern cityscape. Perhaps most eye-catching is a neo-romantic hilltop castle—actually a luxury hotel built in 2002.

windows-spotlight-1514.jpg.title: Bamboo Forest Path, Arashiyama Bamboo Grove, Kyoto, Japan
windows-spotlight-1514.jpg.headline: A bamboo forest stroll
windows-spotlight-1514.jpg.description: Although visitors to this place may feel like they're a world away, they're actually only a stone's throw from urban hustle and bustle. Just beyond the western edge of Kyoto, Japan, lies the district of Arashiyama. The area is well known for beautiful natural scenery and attractions, including the Sagano Bamboo Forest. A walk along the paths of the forest is not just a visual treat—with daylight filtering through the thousands of green bamboo trunks—but a delight for the ears as well. As the wind blows through the forest, it creates a distinctive sound that is often cited as one of the most memorable aspects of the forest.

windows-spotlight-1517.jpg.title: Lounge leopard
windows-spotlight-1517.jpg.headline: Lounge leopard
windows-spotlight-1517.jpg.description: Not unlike its patterned coat, the leopard's range consists of bands and blotches on the world map, covering much of Africa and numerous pockets of Asia. As solitary animals, different leopards have different habits. Many are nocturnal, covering nearly 50 miles a night stalking prey before they slump on a limb or log, dangle a leg or two, and lounge the whole day away. That could well be the case for our cool cat friend here—though this bespeckled beast may just be enjoying a siesta between day shifts.

windows-spotlight-1518.jpg.title: Old Harry Rocks, Dorset, England
windows-spotlight-1518.jpg.headline: A history of Harrys
windows-spotlight-1518.jpg.description: Scoundrels and scallywags form the lineup of suspects behind the naming of the Old Harry Rocks. 'Old Harry' was an olden-days euphemism for the devil, but it's also possible the chalk sea stacks get their name from Earl Harold, a Viking raider who supposedly perished here and was turned into a stone pillar. In maybe the most convincing origin tale, Old Harry was Henry Paye, a pirate from nearby Poole who looted hundreds of French ships in the early 1400s and hauled the booty back to these parts.

windows-spotlight-1519.jpg.title: Yellow Feather Star on Coral Reef
windows-spotlight-1519.jpg.headline: Seafloor shrubbery
windows-spotlight-1519.jpg.description: Their name may sound like alien antagonists from a 'Star Trek' episode, but the crinoids have shared a home planet with us for quite some time. These filter feeders of Earth's final frontier date back about 480 million years in the fossil record, and stone landforms made up mainly of crinoid ossicles exist across the globe. Shrublike specimens such as this bright yellow fellow are commonly called feather stars, a nod to their fellow echinoderms the starfish. Others bound to long, thin stalks are known as sea lilies ('crinoid' comes from the Greek 'krinon,' which means lily).

windows-spotlight-1520.jpg.title: Zebra Stripes
windows-spotlight-1520.jpg.headline: Stripe science
windows-spotlight-1520.jpg.description: Why do zebras have stripes? As far as science is concerned, the answer's not in black and white. Originally it was thought that stripes camouflage the animals amid tall savannah grasses like those found here in Kenya. But research has suggested they also serve as a warning coloration, as reflective protection from hot sunlight, or even as a visual bug repellent. One thing we know for sure: Stripes help us identify zebras by species (like these plains zebras, recognizable by the stripes across their bellies) and even as individuals, because their stripe patterns are unique just like human fingerprints.

windows-spotlight-1525.jpg.title: Red Planet Mars
windows-spotlight-1525.jpg.headline: NASA's next stop?
windows-spotlight-1525.jpg.description: We Earthlings have long been fascinated by Mars. The red planet has inspired myriad myths and legends—as well as some fantastic science fiction. Since the early 1970s dozens of unmanned exploration vehicles have orbited the planet, or landed on its iron-rich soil. We've learned a great deal about Mars from this research, but the most exciting discoveries likely lay ahead, when humans will first touch down on another planet. Missions to Mars are in the development stages across government agencies and private tech companies alike. NASA has set a goal to get astronauts on Mars by the 2030s. (No word if Matt Damon is on board with the plan.)

windows-spotlight-1529.jpg.title: Skógafoss Waterfall, Green Northern Lights, Iceland
windows-spotlight-1529.jpg.headline: A film-famous fall
windows-spotlight-1529.jpg.description: Skógafoss plummets over sheer cliffs that long ago marked the land's end in this island country. Almost 200 feet tall—and about half as wide when flowing its hardest—the massive cascade roars where Iceland's coast once dropped straight off into the ocean. The coastline receded long ago, stranding the glacier-fed fall about 3 miles inland. Now it's a popular stop on Iceland's Ring Road, thanks partly to pop culture appearances in 'Game of Thrones' and the 'Thor' franchise.

windows-spotlight-153.jpg.title: Soda Lake Tufa Towers Stargazing, Mono Lake, California
windows-spotlight-153.jpg.headline: Soda lake stargazing
windows-spotlight-153.jpg.description: Whether you're right on the shore or passing high above it on Highway 395, Mono Lake is a bit of an eerie sight at night. Looking like something between termite mounds and alien skyscrapers, towers of tufa—a type of limestone that forms at cool temperatures, often underwater—lurk throughout the soda lake's shallows. Long ago the tufa towers were submerged, but streams feeding Mono Lake were diverted to Los Angeles in 1941. This dropped the endorheic lake's levels by many feet, exposing a surreal setting once exclusively enjoyed by the lake's unique brine shrimp.

windows-spotlight-1532.jpg.title: Classiebawn Castle, Mullaghmore, County Sligo, Ireland
windows-spotlight-1532.jpg.headline: A classy 'castle'
windows-spotlight-1532.jpg.description: Built on a small headland in County Sligo, Classiebawn Castle isn't so much a castle as a country manor. Classiebawn was commissioned and constructed in the late 19th century, when Ireland was marked by conflict but long after the age when castles dotted Europe as defensive bulwarks. Though short on military history, the estate offers a long-distance view of the beaches of Mullaghmore Peninsula and the wide Atlantic beyond.

windows-spotlight-1536.jpg.title: Tangled blue-green river delta
windows-spotlight-1536.jpg.headline: A tangled 'bay'
windows-spotlight-1536.jpg.description: Bahía Blanca, or White Bay, is the name given to this many-tendrilled body of water as well as the metro area that sits on it. Technically, it's not a bay but an estuary: a transitional waterway between a river (in this case the Napostá Grande Stream) and its opening to the sea, where saltwater and freshwater mingle to become brackish. The city built on the estuary—just 'Bahía' to its 300,000 or so residents—is one of several Argentine ports on the coast of Buenos Aires Province (which, somewhat misleadingly, doesn't include the national capital Buenos Aires).

windows-spotlight-1539.jpg.title: Caerphilly Castle, Moated Unfinished Fortress at Sunset, Caerphilly, Wales
windows-spotlight-1539.jpg.headline: The unfinished fortress
windows-spotlight-1539.jpg.description: King Edward I conquered North Wales in the 1200s, then built a ring of castles around it to defend his newly won territory. Beaumaris Castle is one of them—or, to be more accurate, nearly one of them. Before construction on Beaumaris was completed, the king's finances and attention were redirected to his military campaign in Scotland. The stout fortress was never fully finished—but the concentric design of walls within walls has been praised by historians as a triumph of medieval military architecture.

windows-spotlight-1540.jpg.title: Limestone Karst Peninsula, Turquoise Sea, Sandy Beach, Krabi, Thailand
windows-spotlight-1540.jpg.headline: Peninsular paradise
windows-spotlight-1540.jpg.description: When it comes to road tripping in this part of southern Thailand, the buck stops on the other side of that distant, rocky outcrop jutting into the sea. Thanks to those impassable crags, traffic here on the Railay Peninsula is limited to boats—usually scrappy long-tail boats hired from nearby cities. Though a bit hard to reach, Railay is beloved by beachgoers and enjoys a devoted following among rock climbers, so the peninsula is often abustle despite its isolation.
windows-spotlight-1540.jpg.copyright: © Tuul & Bruno Morandi/The Image Bank/Getty Images

windows-spotlight-1543.jpg.title: Pink Rhododendrons Mountain Sunset
windows-spotlight-1543.jpg.headline: Of roads and rhododendrons
windows-spotlight-1543.jpg.description: Amid the steeply rolling greenery of the Great Craggy Mountains, Catawba rhododendrons add a sprinkle of pink to mirror the blushing sunset. With roadside views like this, it's easy to see why the Blue Ridge Parkway is one of the nation's best regarded scenic drives. It's also one of the most widely accessible parts of the National Park System, given its fee-free entry and nearness to large East Coast cities. This combination of charm and convenience has made the parkway the most visited unit of the system by far, beating out flagships like Yellowstone and Yosemite by more than threefold.

windows-spotlight-1547.jpg.title: Lake Geneva cloud inversion, Switzerland
windows-spotlight-1547.jpg.headline: Of clouds and classic rock
windows-spotlight-1547.jpg.description: That's not Smoke on the Water, just clouds. But the Swiss town of Montreux (seen here from atop the Dent de Jaman) is where Deep Purple first recorded that famous rock riff. Not only that, it's where the story behind the song took place: The band was in town to record at Montreux Casino, but a few days before their studio session, a fan at a Frank Zappa concert launched a flare that set the casino on fire. No one was seriously hurt, but the venue burned to the ground as the band watched smoke billow over Lake Geneva. The rest is rock 'n' roll history—as any weary-eared guitar store clerk will affirm.

windows-spotlight-1548.jpg.title: White Travertine Terraces Sunset Reflections, Pamukkale
windows-spotlight-1548.jpg.headline: Mirrors in multitude
windows-spotlight-1548.jpg.description: The signature cloud-white shades of this Turkish geothermal landmark are only really brought out by the bright of day. Of course, when the warm waters of Pamukkale (translating to 'cotton castle') are flowing at high enough volume, daytime also brings out crowds clamoring for space in the springs. But as proved by this soaker-free shot, most of the travertine terraces' relaxing revelers retreat by sunset.

windows-spotlight-1551.jpg.title: Forested Peaks, Paraguay
windows-spotlight-1551.jpg.headline: Peaks of Paraguay
windows-spotlight-1551.jpg.description: What's in a name? In this case, a lot of the letter Y. The Ybytyruzú mountain range gets its name from Guarani, an indigenous language with 6.5 million speakers that's one of two official ones here in Paraguay. 'Ybyty' means mountain and 'ruzú' means big, and the name 'Big Mountains' is relatively accurate: Cerro Tres Kandú, the highest point in Paraguay, rises within the Ybytyruzú. While not an especially lofty peak at 2,762 feet, it's impressively prominent against the low plains that abut the range.

windows-spotlight-1555.jpg.title: Asperitas Clouds Sunset
windows-spotlight-1555.jpg.headline: Name that cloud
windows-spotlight-1555.jpg.description: Cloudgazers seeking familiar shapes might have a tough time with these altocumulus clouds over Australia: They have characteristics of both stratiformis (streaky or wavy) and floccus (woolly or tufted) clouds. If all that Latin has you suspecting something science-y going on here, you'd be right: Just like flora and fauna, clouds can be taxonomized by genus and species. The altocumulus genus has five distinctly shaped species—castellanus, floccus, lenticularis, stratiformis, and volutus—appearing at a wide range of elevations from 6,500 to 20,000 feet.

windows-spotlight-156.jpg.title: Red Kochia Pom-Pom Plains
windows-spotlight-156.jpg.headline: The pom-pom plains
windows-spotlight-156.jpg.description: Trimmed into neat spheres like so many big red bunny tails, these tinted tufts (a type of tumbleweed) are the life of the party here at this park in Japan's Ibaraki Prefecture. Bassia scoparia—also known as kochia, fireweed, or burning bush—takes on a deep crimson tone each autumn. Hitachi Seaside Park is carefully planted with seasonal flowers and shrubs, including kochia. Throngs of people attend the annual Kochia Carnival to wander winding paths amid the fall foliage—or view the blushing hills from up high on the park's Ferris wheel. Soon after the festivities, the plants dry out to release their seeds, which may be boiled and enjoyed as 'land caviar.'

windows-spotlight-1560.jpg.title: Red and Purple Rock Ridges
windows-spotlight-1560.jpg.headline: Ridges of red
