windows-spotlight-1560.jpg.description: Chiselled cliffs like this are a common sight here in Utah's curiously named Capitol Reef National Park. Neither underwater nor near any capitol building, the park is actually named after both its treacherous terrain (settlers used the term "reef" to refer to rocky ridges that made much of this area impassable) and its stately stone domes that bring to mind a famous landmark in Washington, DC. Those big white domes stand in stark contrast to rust-tinted cliffs like this one, owing to the park's unique and once highly active geology. Capitol Reef is composed of many distinct layers of sediment extending kilometres below the surface and tilted at an angle. Erosion and tectonics exposed layers at differing rates over millions of years, causing huge variations in both elevation and colour.

windows-spotlight-1562.jpg.title: Bartolomé Island Pinnacle Rock, Galápagos Islands, Ecuador
windows-spotlight-1562.jpg.headline: A not-quite-barren islet
windows-spotlight-1562.jpg.description: Life always seems to beat the odds here in the Galápagos Islands. Though it's one of the few green patches you'll find on tiny, barren Bartolomé Island, this narrow peninsula with its twin beaches teems with living organisms. More than 500 miles from any mainland, the local flora and fauna not only survive but thrive. When he explored the islands in the 1830s, a young Charles Darwin was inspired by such rich, resilient life: plants and animals much like those found on the mainland, but just a little different. Hypothesizing that even Earth's most far-flung organisms descended from a common ancestor, Darwin would advance these ideas more than 20 years later in his book 'On the Origin of Species,' becoming a pioneer in the field of evolutionary biology.

windows-spotlight-1564.jpg.title: Tunnel View, Yosemite National Park, California
windows-spotlight-1564.jpg.headline: Tunnel vision
windows-spotlight-1564.jpg.description: Nature carved these incredible features a million years ago, but what's maybe the best-known viewpoint in the US National Park System has only been easily reachable for less than a century. Yosemite's famous Tunnel View is named for the Wawona Tunnel, drilled in 1933, which opens behind us and leads through a mountain's base to the park's south entrance. Such easy access means you'll pretty much never be the only shutterbug clamoring for a snap here—but if ever a peak-packed panorama was worth queueing for, this is it.

windows-spotlight-1571.jpg.title: Karst Mountains Rice Paddies, Guilin, Guangxi, China
windows-spotlight-1571.jpg.headline: Of pillars and paddies
windows-spotlight-1571.jpg.description: Mountains pierce the mist like dragon's teeth in this enchanting location. Though it seems like the setting of a fantasy epic, the remarkable Guilin region is quite real, and one of the most popular natural attractions in China. The area is defined by limestone karst features, notably cone-like hills covered in lush greenery, but also craggy caves below the surface. The Li River flows through the jagged landscape, diverted in some places to irrigate rice paddies as seen here.

windows-spotlight-1573.jpg.title: Capo Testa granite formations, turquoise bay, sandy beach, Sardinia, Italy
windows-spotlight-1573.jpg.headline: A groovy getaway
windows-spotlight-1573.jpg.description: Perhaps the group of hippies that settled this Sardinian cove in the 1960s named it the Valle della Luna, or Valley of the Moon, as a nod to the then-raging Space Race. (Or could it have been inspired by some other out-of-this-world trip?) It sure wasn't referencing the bright blue waves or green shrubbery—though the dust-toned stones around here have a certain lunar character. In any case, the moon commune proved persistent, populating the cove's nooks and crannies well into the 2020s—and their spaced-out name for the place stuck.

windows-spotlight-1577.jpg.title: Paragliding, Green Mountains, Hiking Trail, Blue Sky
windows-spotlight-1577.jpg.headline: Soar spot
windows-spotlight-1577.jpg.description: These hills on the outskirts of Hong Kong SAR make the perfect place for this high-flying sport, but most any elevated point that abuts a wide-open expanse will do. Not to be confused with hang gliding, this is paragliding: Strapped to specially modified parachutes that vent air into the canopy to create forward motion, pilots take off by raising their chutes in the air like kites, then running to achieve flying speed until the winds carry them off. The craft is controlled by manipulating lines attached to the pilot's harness. While most paraglider flights last less than an hour and don't soar higher than a few hundred feet, skilled pilots can travel hundreds of miles and climb thousands of feet high.

windows-spotlight-1579.jpg.title: Sitting Meerkat
windows-spotlight-1579.jpg.headline: Little critter, big mouth
windows-spotlight-1579.jpg.description: What's this meerkat telling us with its gaze? We're not sure, but what we do know is that at least amongst themselves, these little mongooses are great communicators. Their squeaks, barks, clicks, and chitters may sound chaotic to the human ear, but a mob of meerkats (usually numbering a dozen or so, but sometimes up to 50) is actually a well-oiled social machine. Dominant meerkats, which tend to be female, use specific calls to coordinate group hunts for grubs and other tasty foods. Additional members act as sentinels to warn the mob against approaching predators, making precise sounds that identify the threat as near or far, bird or beast. Much like their fellow feliforms, meerkats may also hiss at meerkats from other mobs and purr in the company of family and friends.

windows-spotlight-1582.jpg.title: Scarlet Macaw
windows-spotlight-1582.jpg.headline: Marvelous macaws
windows-spotlight-1582.jpg.description: The scarlet macaw, pictured here in Belize, can be found from southern Mexico to Bolivia. While it's disappeared from some places because of habitat destruction or capture for the pet trade, in most of its range it remains widespread. And not hard to spot: Distinguishable from parrots by their white or light-colored facial patches, macaws grow to almost three feet long if you include their trademark tail feathers. They can even be seen in some more northerly locales like Florida, where they're among several escaped exotic pet species to have established wild populations.

windows-spotlight-1586.jpg.title: Snow-capped Matterhorn Reflection Riffelsee Sunset, Zermatt, Switzerland
windows-spotlight-1586.jpg.headline: Iconic and imposing
windows-spotlight-1586.jpg.description: Though it's not the tallest of the Alps or the most technical climb, this Swiss-Italian peak is one of the most famous mountains in the world. Between its jagged 14,692-foot summit and the Disneyland ride it inspired, the Matterhorn strikes fear and awe into people from all over the world, daring mountaineers and small children alike. Here we see the great stone pyramid from the Switzerland side, reflected in Stellisee—the first and largest lake encountered along the Five Lakes Trail in Zermatt.

windows-spotlight-1588.jpg.title: Margaret Bridge, Danube River, Sunset, Budapest, Hungary
windows-spotlight-1588.jpg.headline: Crossing the Danube
windows-spotlight-1588.jpg.description: We're seeing the sun set from the midpoint of the Margaret Bridge between Buda in the west and Pest in the east. Spanning the glassy Danube to link the two titular banks of Budapest, this second-oldest of the Hungarian capital's eight bridges (after the Széchenyi Chain Bridge) was built in 1876 from a design by Ernest Goüin. That name ring a bell? Probably not, but if it does, maybe you glanced it on another wrought-iron riverside landmark: He's one of the 72 French engineers and scientists whose names are etched in the Eiffel Tower.

windows-spotlight-159.jpg.title: Brown sloth hanging from mossy tree branch in tropical forest
windows-spotlight-159.jpg.headline: Let's hang
windows-spotlight-159.jpg.description: If you're moving slow today, that's just fine: You're outpacing our rainforest-dwelling photo subject, which spends 90% of its time scarcely moving a muscle. Sloths (this one's a three-toed sloth—count 'em) move very little to conserve the scant energy gained from their leaves-only diet. They live most of their lives hanging from their hooked claws in trees like this cecropia, whose leaves are a favorite sloth food. Sloths even sleep in a dangling position, and they often snooze away 20 hours of the day. Jealous?

windows-spotlight-1592.jpg.title: Cosmic Cliffs of NGC 3324
windows-spotlight-1592.jpg.headline: The star factory
windows-spotlight-1592.jpg.description: Today we're taking you 7,600 light years from Hollywood to show you where stars are really made. The NGC 3324 cluster is a stellar nursery where immense gravitational forces compress cosmic dust and gas into the extremely dense, high-energy objects we call stars. Of course, outside of 'Star Trek,' no human has boldly gone this far into outer space. So how are we seeing these 'Cosmic Cliffs' with such clarity? With the help of a really, really good zoom lens—in this case the James Webb Space Telescope. Able to spot young stars emitting infrared light through dense nebulae, NASA's newest imaging satellite captures these origin stories as never before told.

windows-spotlight-1593.jpg.title: Arid Islands Teal Ocean, Kimberley Coast, Western Australia
windows-spotlight-1593.jpg.headline: Land ho!
windows-spotlight-1593.jpg.description: This overview of Australia's Buccaneer Archipelago is one of countless finely detailed images available in the Microsoft Planetary Computer. This vast, cloud-powered database lets scientists see a whole timeline of crisp satellite captures and environmental data for any location in the world. By analyzing this data, scientists can explore better ways to manage resources and combat climate change. Here in northwest Australia, for example, a scientist might use data on coastal changes to help monitor the region's mangrove forests—essential for protecting coastlines from storm surges.

windows-spotlight-1594.jpg.title: Li River Karst Mountains Sunset, Guilin, China
windows-spotlight-1594.jpg.headline: A storybook scene
windows-spotlight-1594.jpg.description: The Li River flows through the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region in southern China, winding past rural villages and spiky, soaring karst mountains. These tall limestone peaks rise in especially dramatic fashion between the towns of Guilin and Yangshuo. The landscape of the Li River gorge is just as impressive below as it is above: Hundreds of caves honeycomb the area, with dozens stretching more than half a mile. Also nearby is Reed Flute Cave, with its 180 million-year-old rock formations illuminated by multicolored lights.

windows-spotlight-1600.jpg.title: White water river rapids, coniferous forest, large rocks
windows-spotlight-1600.jpg.headline: Thirsty?
windows-spotlight-1600.jpg.description: Consider this shot of rolling Alpine rapids your daily reminder to stay hydrated. We're seeing a river called the Gelgia as it tumbles from the Lai da Marmorera, a reservoir high in the Swiss canton of Grisons. Switzerland has been called 'Europe's water tower' for its enormous reserves of freshwater, accounting for 6% of the continent's drinking water supply. On top of that, two of Europe's most important urban rivers, the Rhine and Rhône, rise here in Switzerland as humble mountain streams not unlike the Gelgia.

windows-spotlight-1604.jpg.title: Humpback whale pod, icebergs, Greenland
windows-spotlight-1604.jpg.headline: A family vacation?
windows-spotlight-1604.jpg.description: Humpback whales are world travelers without peer, just as comfortable swimming the stormy open ocean as sheltering in a tropical cove. Or in this case, one that's the opposite of tropical, carved right out of a Greenlandic iceberg. Here to check out the krill situation and maybe chill a while, this humpback calf was probably welcomed into warm southern waters during the previous winter. After a long journey north with its mother and pod, the fresh-faced cetacean is getting acquainted with the group's summer feeding spots, where they'll all bulk up with blubber until winter sends them packing back to the tropics.

windows-spotlight-1607.jpg.title: Moss-covered Rocks, Fjord, Sunset, Milford Sound, New Zealand
windows-spotlight-1607.jpg.headline: A gem among gems
windows-spotlight-1607.jpg.description: The 10,000-square-mile World Heritage Site called Te Wāhipounamu encompasses four national parks defined by countless mountains, fjords, and glaciers. Perhaps the most precious gem in this swath of the South Island is known by two names: Piopiotahi in the native Māori language and Milford Sound in English. But many just call this 10-mile-long inlet the most beautiful place in New Zealand. A bold claim in this nation of natural wonders? Certainly, though the stunning sights around Piopiotahi's every bend sure make a strong case.

windows-spotlight-1612.jpg.title: Common Merganser
windows-spotlight-1612.jpg.headline: Well-traveled waterfowl
windows-spotlight-1612.jpg.description: Most ducks' quacks are worse than their bites, but a nip from this toothy beak could be a major ouch—just ask a fish. The common merganser is a diving duck found all over the Northern Hemisphere, snaring freshwater and saltwater swimmers alike in its sawtooth maw. To give an idea of the merganser's massive migratory range: The birds' breeding grounds extend well north of the Arctic Circle, while this specimen was spotted deep within the American Southwest in Flagstaff, Arizona.

windows-spotlight-1619.jpg.title: Krang Suri Waterfall, Meghalaya, India
windows-spotlight-1619.jpg.headline: A fall in the forest
windows-spotlight-1619.jpg.description: A few hours' country driving and a short-but-rugged hike will take you from Paraguay's capital, Asunción, to this jewel of the forest. The fall called Salto Cristal tumbles down a terraced stone face nearly 150 feet high, and during the rainy season, its thunderous flow makes approaching difficult. But throughout the sunny, dry period from May to September, the wispy waterfall flows into a calm pool that's perfect for a post-hike swim.

windows-spotlight-162.jpg.title: Monemvasia peninsular town, Peloponnese, Greece
windows-spotlight-162.jpg.headline: Peninsular paradise
windows-spotlight-162.jpg.description: The first thing to know about Monemvasia is right there in its name, which means 'one way in.' Like the Greek city's medieval walls, the description still holds up 15 centuries later: The western gate (at left—look for the cars!) still guards the only road to town, which approaches from a narrow causeway. If you're on foot, though, you can make a sneaky sidestep via a cliffside staircase (at center in our photo). It'll bring you to the upper city, uninhabited since the late 17th century but offering expansive views of the Aegean Sea and mainland Peloponnese.

windows-spotlight-1624.jpg.title: Helfštýn Castle sunset, Czech Republic
windows-spotlight-1624.jpg.headline: A resilient ruin
windows-spotlight-1624.jpg.description: Although called a ruin, from some vantage points it looks as if Helfštýn Castle is an impenetrable block of carved stone. Origins of a stronghold atop this Central Moravia hill date back to the late 13th century, and the castle grew massive during its Gothic-style renovation roughly a century later. The walls of Helfštýn stood strong against many ferocious attacks, even during the 17th century's cataclysmic Thirty Years' War. Things have since calmed down considerably, and now the castle—looking great after conservation begun in 1911—hosts visitors, and a world-renowned gathering of master blacksmiths known as Hefaiston.

windows-spotlight-1629.jpg.title: Moro Rock summit sunset view, Sequoia National Park, California
windows-spotlight-1629.jpg.headline: Moro or Morro?
windows-spotlight-1629.jpg.description: One letter can make a big difference. Moro Rock, the granite dome our photo was taken from, provides an unbeatable view of an inland paradise where gargantuan trees tower: Sequoia National Park. Slip an extra 'r' into your map directions and you'll find yourself kicking back with the surf crowd by the famous Morro Rock on the Central Coast. The good news is they're just about 190 miles apart by car, so if you fancy mountains and beach you can squeeze both into a weekend. California dreamin' yet?

windows-spotlight-1630.jpg.title: Snow-capped Cotopaxi Volcano, Ecuador
windows-spotlight-1630.jpg.headline: Fire on high
windows-spotlight-1630.jpg.description: One of the most elevated volcanoes in the world at 19,347 feet, Cotopaxi is one of the high points on a famous Ring of Fire (so much for down, down, down). Rising over rolling Andean foothills, this hotspot is the second-highest summit in Ecuador.Though Cotopaxi is active to this day, any magma headed up to its vent has a long trip in store. Situated in a country named for the equator, Cotopaxi's crater is among the farthest points on Earth from the planet's center thanks to the equatorial bulge. At 3,966 miles from the core, it's even farther out than Mount Everest. Pack your bags, lava!

windows-spotlight-1632.jpg.title: Icy St. Joseph North Pier Lighthouse, St. Joseph, Michigan
windows-spotlight-1632.jpg.headline: Who left the fridge open?
windows-spotlight-1632.jpg.description: Looks like Jack Frost nipped this Michigan port's nose extra hard this time. Sharing a roughly 1,000-foot pier with its sister light nearer to shore, the St. Joseph North Pier Outer Light is the first building in town to bear the brunt of Lake Michigan's bracing winds. Luckily, there's no unfortunate icebound lighthouse keeper trapped in there: The lights of 'St. Joe's' were decommissioned in 2005 (and, as the eventual thaw will reveal, beautifully restored in 2008).

windows-spotlight-1633.jpg.title: White Pocket wave rock formations, orange sand dune, Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, Arizona
windows-spotlight-1633.jpg.headline: Waves of stone
windows-spotlight-1633.jpg.description: Forming pillars and pockets that provide precious shade to a parched patch of our planet, this prehistoric chalk-white stone takes on a whole spectrum of shapes as it breaches the Sahara's sandy surface. Much of the limestone that defines White Desert National Park appears in low, rippled formations that resemble whitecapped ocean waves. Towering above the mineral mishmash, ghost-pale hoodoos rival Egypt's other great monuments. But these weren't sculpted by human hands, and seem to depict gawky heads on stalks instead of the usual gods-and-pharaohs fare. Ancient aliens at work? Nah—just eons of erosion by wind-whipped sand.

windows-spotlight-1638.jpg.title: White Barn Owl Snowdrop Field
windows-spotlight-1638.jpg.headline: A wide-ranging raptor
windows-spotlight-1638.jpg.description: This barn owl doesn't give a hoot, and we mean that literally. Instead of the gentle 'who-who' call of many owls, barn owls emit a hair-raising screech, leading some cultures to shun the birds as bad omens. That's no superstition if you happen to be a small mammal. Not only do barn owls have excellent hearing and sight that makes them ultra-precise night predators, they're also everywhere: These raptors range across all continents except Antarctica. Even still, well-lit sightings like this are uncommon—though some barn owl populations have even adapted to hunt during daytime. Geez, can a scurrying rodent catch a break?

windows-spotlight-164.jpg.title: Pine Tree, Mountain River Valley, Woraksan
windows-spotlight-164.jpg.headline: Wandering in Woraksan
windows-spotlight-164.jpg.description: Woraksan National Park protects more than 100 square miles of wilderness in central South Korea, centered on the park's namesake mountain. Pines and oaks add greenery to the stony landscape, including many small, knotty Korean red pines rooted among the rocks. While the hikes here reach high elevations, most aren't considered especially difficult, so photographers flock here during all seasons to capture soaring trailside views like this.

windows-spotlight-1640.jpg.title: Ksar Ait Benhaddou, Morocco
windows-spotlight-1640.jpg.headline: Star ksar
windows-spotlight-1640.jpg.description: Morocco's Aït Benhaddou is held up as the perfect example of a ksar, one of many fortified Amazigh villages found across North Africa. Often built beside desert oases and featuring adobe-like earthen clay construction, these largely enclosed villages provided protection from potential foes as well as the elements. In fame and physical elevation, the millennium-old Aït Benhaddou rises above the rest of the ksars. Set upon a creek in a hilly mountain pass, its position was highly strategic in ancient times, marking a major trade route connecting Marrakesh with Saharan communities beyond the Atlas Mountains.

windows-spotlight-1641.jpg.title: Snow-capped Mount Fuji, Ocean Waves, Tetrapods, Sunset, Japan
windows-spotlight-1641.jpg.headline: High and low
windows-spotlight-1641.jpg.description: From the shores of Japan's deepest bay, gorgeous blue-hued views of the nation's highest point abound. The 12,388-foot Mount Fuji rises just 15 miles or so from the edge of Suruga Bay, which measures 8,200 feet deep. In the mid-1800s, the traditional printmaker Hiroshige made deft use of Prussian blue pigment—then a fairly new sensation in Japan—to immortalize a similar view from Suruga Bay via woodblock prints. One thing you won't see in the old prints: distinctive barrel-shaped concrete breakwaters, which keep Suruga's rough waves at bay.

windows-spotlight-1642.jpg.title: Tre Cime di Lavaredo peaks, Rifugio Locatelli hut at sunset, Dolomites, Italy
windows-spotlight-1642.jpg.headline: A rugged refuge
windows-spotlight-1642.jpg.description: In the distance to our right, sunset bestows a bronze glow on the Three Peaks of Lavaredo, one of the most iconic mountain groups in the Dolomites. Also called the 'Pale Mountains,' the Dolomites are named for the extremely hard limestone that composes them. Hike these trails and you'll get one stunning view after another with each turn of the route. Tuckered out by all the scenery? Rifugios, or refuges—like the Locatelli hut, seen here framed by a shaded Monte Paterno—offer trailside beds for weary trekkers. At least those who booked ahead: Even here at 8,000 feet, tourist season draws sky-high numbers.

windows-spotlight-1649.jpg.title: Spotted Bobcat in Snow
windows-spotlight-1649.jpg.headline: Prowling among us?
windows-spotlight-1649.jpg.description: These wild cats are rare sights due to their stealth and crepuscular habits, but just because you can't see them doesn't mean they aren’t there. The bobcat's home range covers virtually all of the United States, plus most of Mexico and a chunk of Canada. So if you live in North America, there's a good chance that bobcats prowl your backyard—maybe even literally. Though most of them live deep in the wilderness, more and more bobcats make their homes in the woody outskirts of urban areas.

windows-spotlight-1654.jpg.title: Braided River Delta Reservoir
windows-spotlight-1654.jpg.headline: River meets reservoir
windows-spotlight-1654.jpg.description: For the Ōhau River, this spot marks the end of the line. Or more accurately, the end of multiple lines. The Ōhau is one of New Zealand's many braided rivers, in which several crisscrossing streams course over a wide, flat riverbed. Such twisting flows appear all over the Mackenzie Basin, a vast area in the middle of the South Island. Here, the Ōhau merges into a single flow as it reaches the artificial Lake Benmore, then makes one final split into a familiar delta shape, its silty sediment dissipating into the aquamarine deep.

windows-spotlight-166.jpg.title: Stone city stargazing
windows-spotlight-166.jpg.headline: Stone city stargazing
windows-spotlight-166.jpg.description: The ancient Nabataeans entered and exited their capital, Petra, through a narrow gorge near this spot, winding their way through these cliffs to a city carved right into the stone walls. The world was a very different place over a millennium ago—but as those travelers looked up at the sky, they gazed on the same stars we do, no doubt picking out shapes in the celestial canopy and swapping stories about what they saw.We're not sure if the Nabataeans had a name for the prominent constellation at our image's center: Orion the hunter, with his famous triple-starred belt. We borrow this stellar fellow's name and occupation from the Greeks, but various cultures have identified the shape with a shepherd, a giant, a dancer, and other mythic figures.

windows-spotlight-169.jpg.title: Yosemite Valley El Capitan Merced River Sunset, Yosemite National Park, California
windows-spotlight-169.jpg.headline: A famous valley view
windows-spotlight-169.jpg.description: The first humans to settle Yosemite wandered in as many as 10,000 years ago, following receding glaciers to discover a gash in the world guarded by stone giants. And after all these millennia, these mighty mounts still make many a mere human tremble. Nowadays this view up the Yosemite Valley is one of the most sought after in America's national parks, drawing more than 4 million visitors in a typical year.True to its name, El Capitan (The Captain, seen at left) leads the pack here in Yosemite as both a sight to see and a site to conquer. Keen-eyed photographers like Ansel Adams and daring climbers like Alex Honnold have made it one of the most famous chunks of rock on the planet. Not that it needed the help—where else can you see a 3,000-foot sheer cliff tumble straight into a pastoral ravine?

windows-spotlight-17.jpg.title: Illuminated Vaduz Castle, Winding Road Light Trails, Twilight, Vaduz, Liechtenstein
windows-spotlight-17.jpg.headline: Vaduz vista
windows-spotlight-17.jpg.description: Following this taillight trail, we've wended our way to a doubly landlocked land that's comparable to Brooklyn, New York, in land area and to Manhattan, Kansas, in population. Though little Liechtenstein is easily overlooked amid the modern world's enormity, this principality still manages to punch up, boasting a prosperous economy and 100% literacy rate. And as in all the alpine nations, history and nature merge at every twist and turn. Take Vaduz Castle for example, the medieval edifice that overlooks a same-named, valley-nestled town of 6,000 or so—the nation's capital.

windows-spotlight-171.jpg.title: Single tree, green hill, misty mountain, calm water reflection
windows-spotlight-171.jpg.headline: A well-seasoned city
windows-spotlight-171.jpg.description: Fog shrouds the mountains near Da Lat, Vietnam, the cultural and economic capital of the country's Central Highlands. Temperate rather than tropical, it stands in climatic contrast to other Vietnamese cities. Misty mornings like this often give way to sunny afternoons, crisp evenings, and chilly nights—leading some to say Da Lat sees all four seasons in a typical day.

windows-spotlight-172.jpg.title: Eroded badlands and mesa, purple pink sunset
windows-spotlight-172.jpg.headline: Good times on badlands
windows-spotlight-172.jpg.description: Inspired by rock domes that resemble the US Capitol, Capitol Reef National Park's name isn't the only architecturally themed one in these parts. About 14 miles east of the park border rises Factory Butte, named after a far less famous landmark: the large woolen mill in distant Provo. Now the mill is long gone, but these Utah badlands are still quite the fun factory: Rippling ridges and valleys make the Factory Butte Recreation Area a legendary destination for off-roaders.

windows-spotlight-175.jpg.title: Red Rock Ocean Reef, Kauai
windows-spotlight-175.jpg.headline: Kauai from on high
windows-spotlight-175.jpg.description: Though bounded by sandy saltwater scenes like this, Kauai's inland is green and fertile, giving rise to the nickname 'Garden Isle.' Centered on the extinct volcano Mount Wai'ale'ale—one of the rainiest places on the planet—Kauai is flush with rich volcanic soil that gets plenty of moisture even in the stereotypically sunny state of Hawaii. Kauaian farmers cultivate crops not often seen on the mainland, from guava to kava, and also supply staples like sugarcane and coffee.

windows-spotlight-177.jpg.title: Sunset Orange Lenticular Clouds
windows-spotlight-177.jpg.headline: Countess of the Winds
windows-spotlight-177.jpg.description: Against a Sicilian sunset, a strange cloud like a stacked pair of flying saucers looms motionless near Mount Etna's summit. Lenticular clouds form close to prominent mountains in special conditions where water vapor condenses over a summit, then is shaped and smoothed by waves of wind passing over the slopes. The lenticular cloud that forms over Etna appears often enough that locals gave it a nickname: Contessa dei Venti, or Countess of the Winds, perhaps after its billowy layers resembling a rotund noblewoman's dress.

windows-spotlight-180.jpg.title: Orange sand dunes, rock formations, sunrise, Wadi Rum, Jordan
windows-spotlight-180.jpg.headline: Star-studded sands
windows-spotlight-180.jpg.description: Whether you're a tourist, a film crewmember, or a Bedouin local, you'll find plenty of wandering room at Wadi Rum. Here, mountains like the backs of huge beasts bound 280 miles of windswept sand, a setting that captivated moviegoers in the classic film 'Lawrence of Arabia' and inspired many to visit Jordan. Wadi Rum continues to rack up film appearances, with recent sci-fi films like 'Star Wars,' 'The Martian,' and 'Dune' setting up shop on the spectacular spot. The visual arts are nothing new here, though: Petroglyphs etched by the ancient Nabataeans can be found on rock faces all over the wadi.

windows-spotlight-182.jpg.title: Golden Hour Cuernos del Paine Reflection Lake, Torres del Paine National Park, Chile
windows-spotlight-182.jpg.headline: Mirror, mirror…
windows-spotlight-182.jpg.description: Undisturbed by the tiniest ripple, these mountain waters are so mirror-smooth we're not sure which way's up. Luckily, in Patagonia, directions only matter so much: The views are amazing no matter which way you look in this land of majestic peaks, glaciers, valleys, and lakes. In our image, rays of sunlight glint off of the Cuernos del Paine, a group of granite mounts standing over 6,500 feet high. With their distinctive gnarled shape ('cuernos' means 'horns') and two-tone color scheme, they're a well-known symbol of the park and a landmark sight along the W Circuit, a popular multi-day trekking route here in Torres del Paine National Park.

windows-spotlight-184.jpg.title: Blue Orange Geothermal Basin, Yellowstone National Park
windows-spotlight-184.jpg.headline: A basin aboil
windows-spotlight-184.jpg.description: Easily explored on just a few miles of sturdy boardwalks, Norris Geyser Basin offers a concentrated dose of Yellowstone National Park's geothermal grandeur. Blue-water hot springs flush with bright bacterial mats match the intense tones of Grand Prismatic Spring, and most of the basin bubbles at 199 degrees Fahrenheit, the boiling point here at 7,500 feet. True to its name, the basin is pocked with geysers: Highlights include the acidic-as-vinegar Echinus Geyser and the tallest active geyser in the world, 300-foot Steamboat Geyser—twice as high as Old Faithful, but not half as famous due to its unpredictable schedule.

windows-spotlight-186.jpg.title: Green and golden patchwork rice fields
windows-spotlight-186.jpg.headline: Have a rice day
windows-spotlight-186.jpg.description: The flat, coastal Mekong Delta in Vietnam's southwestern corner powers one of the biggest rice-growing economies in the world. Of its 17 million people, 80% are involved in growing, harvesting, or threshing the grain-bearing grass. The Ta Pa rice fields shown here are renowned for their vibrant and varied tints: Farmers stagger their plantings, so greener grass is younger while the yellow crop is closer to chopping time.But aren't rice fields supposed to be full of water? Not always. Traditional paddies are kept under a few inches of water at all times, but as rising seas make more of the Mekong Delta salty, freshwater is less abundant. Some farmers have updated their methods with modern soil saturation monitors, only flooding their fields when moisture levels get low.

windows-spotlight-189.jpg.title: Breaching whale, ocean, snow-capped mountains, glaciers
windows-spotlight-189.jpg.headline: A scenic splash
windows-spotlight-189.jpg.description: From both coasts of the mainland United States, the breaches, spouts, and tail slaps of these colossal cetaceans can be seen for miles. But US-based whale lovers hoping to spot them may have the best luck venturing beyond the Lower 48. This humpback is attempting some acrobatics in one of these migratory whales' favorite summer feeding spots: Glacier Bay National Park in the massive 49th state. As the Alaskan autumn sets in, humpback pods will head to tropical spots to breed—making the 50th state of Hawaii one of the world's premier perches for wintertime whale-watching.

windows-spotlight-19.jpg.title: Cascades, Chapada
windows-spotlight-19.jpg.headline: Cascades of the chapada
windows-spotlight-19.jpg.description: Protected as a Brazilian national park in 1961 and made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001, this high plateau known as a chapada boasts a beauty that's far more ancient. It wouldn't  be too surprising to see a dinosaur stomping by as we behold the tall and thundering waterfalls of Chapada dos Veadeiros National Park. Indeed, giant creatures of prehistory may have been familiar with these cliffs and valleys. The forested chapada dates back about 1.8 billion years, and the Cerrado that encompasses it is one of the oldest tropical ecosystems on the planet.

windows-spotlight-191.jpg.title: Antelope Canyon Wavy Red Sandstone, Page, Arizona
windows-spotlight-191.jpg.headline: Waves of stone
windows-spotlight-191.jpg.description: The gentle ripples and swirls of Antelope Canyon seem to match the waters that formed it. Carved by erosion from red-tinged sandstone, the magnificent slot canyon in northern Arizona is still being shaped by the occasional water flow. In fact, care must be taken especially when exploring the canyon's lower level, since even a minor drizzle in this desert can herald a flash flood.A sacred space to the Navajo Nation that governs these lands, Antelope Canyon is accessed only by permit these days, generally on guided tours with tribal approval. But it doesn't take much exploration to see why this fragile formation carries spiritual significance to many, or why such care is taken to protect it.

windows-spotlight-193.jpg.title: Humpback whale, Hawaii
windows-spotlight-193.jpg.headline: A humpback hits Hawaii
windows-spotlight-193.jpg.description: The humpback whale's scientific name is Megaptera novaeangliae, or 'big wing of New England,' after its broad fins and once-frequent spotting by the whalers of old New Bedford and Nantucket. Ranging far beyond the shores of America's Northeast, these playful and talkative migratory mammals are now protected from hunting in nearly every part of the world. That means whether breaching in Buzzards Bay or (like our pal pictured here) taking a Hawaiian vacation, these cetaceans are safe to capture imaginations with their songs and spirited antics.

windows-spotlight-195.jpg.title: Sleeping sea lions
windows-spotlight-195.jpg.headline: The lions sleep today
windows-spotlight-195.jpg.description: Though it sounds more like seafarer jargon, 'hauling out' is the term biologists use for pinnipeds' practice of posting up outside the water. These female South American sea lions are probably just taking a (quite literal) breather between underwater foraging sessions, soaking up some sun in the process. Sometimes haul-outs are an extended affair, though, as it's also where the sea lions form social groups, mate, and give birth. Pinnipeds here in Peru tend to bask upon sea boulders like these on the Ballestas Islands, but in other parts of the world, hauled-out sea lions, seals, and walruses crowd beaches and ice floes as well.

windows-spotlight-197.jpg.title: Milky Way Galaxy, Blue Orange Night Sky, Ocean Coast
windows-spotlight-197.jpg.headline: Gazing into the past
windows-spotlight-197.jpg.description: On clear nights along this southern English shore, ancient meets even more ancient. Laden with fossils, the Jurassic Coast is aptly named (though remains from the Triassic and Cretaceous are also scattered here). To explore this place is to peek back in time—and the same applies to our skyward-tilted photo. The Milky Way's center is more than 25,000 light years away, meaning some of the starlight reaching our eyes today first emanated during the last ice age.

windows-spotlight-199.jpg.title: Tropical forest rocky seashore clear ocean
windows-spotlight-199.jpg.headline: Seashore lore
windows-spotlight-199.jpg.description: With its dense greenery and spiny mountains, Malaysia's Tioman Island is said in some folklore to be a dragon princess who came to rest here enroute to her wedding. Charmed by the clear blue seas, she chose to transform into an island on the spot (no doubt to the chagrin of her stood-up dragon groom). That's not the only tale of troubled romance featuring Tioman: For the 1958 movie musical 'South Pacific,' scenes of the mythic isle Bali Ha'i were shot on location here.

windows-spotlight-201.jpg.title: Kitesurfing yellow kite sunset beach
windows-spotlight-201.jpg.headline: One wild watersport
windows-spotlight-201.jpg.description: The long, skinny shape of Cat Island sits near the center of a 3,000-strong string of islands in the western Atlantic. During winter, this locale in the central Bahamas is tickled by trade winds, creating ideal conditions for kiteboarding. Also called kitesurfing, this rising sport combines techniques seen in waterskiing, surfing, and snowboarding. Strapped to a sleek board and sturdy line, kiters harness wind power to cut waves and catch air—sometimes soaring high above the sea for hang times of a minute or more.

windows-spotlight-203.jpg.title: Whitehaven Beach Hill Inlet, Whitsunday Islands, Australia
windows-spotlight-203.jpg.headline: World's best beach?
windows-spotlight-203.jpg.description: Maybe it's best that this shot was captured from afar and on high: The extremely fine, smooth sand of this Queensland beach is notorious for sifting its way inside cameras, phones, and other expensive electronics. As long as you keep your valuables stowed, though, a stroll on Whitehaven Beach is an experience you can brag about. Thanks to the snowy sands, sapphire waters, and scenic setting in the spectacular Whitsunday Islands, travel publications regularly name Whitehaven the world's best beach.

windows-spotlight-205.jpg.title: Red black striped hot air balloon, snow mountains, Bavaria
windows-spotlight-205.jpg.headline: Ballooning over Bavaria
windows-spotlight-205.jpg.description: If Germany's tallest mountain wasn't high enough for you, we can lift you to even greater heights. While visitors who summit the 9,700-foot Zugspitze may contend with snowdrift-whipping winds, passengers aboard this hot air balloon are carried by the gusts, enjoying a sense of stillness and silence no matter how stiff the breeze. Of course, that's no excuse to leave the hat and scarf at home: Sometimes cruising thousands of feet above solid ground, a balloon's basket can be a bracingly cold place, especially over alpine settings where the Earth is elevated to begin with.

windows-spotlight-207.jpg.title: Golden Island Mountains Road
windows-spotlight-207.jpg.headline: The golden island
windows-spotlight-207.jpg.description: Fuerteventura, the second-largest of the Canary Islands by area, is well known for its many beaches and strong coastal winds that make it a hub for watersports like windsurfing. The interior of the isle couldn't be more different, as arid plains and volcanic peaks stand in ochre-tinted contrast to the wide blue Atlantic. Stick around after this intense golden hour and you'll experience yet another light show: Known as the Sicasumbre observation point, this spot that's low on light pollution is a popular hangout for astronomy buffs.

windows-spotlight-209.jpg.title: Snow-capped Mount Salkantay, Peruvian Andes
windows-spotlight-209.jpg.headline: One prominent peak
windows-spotlight-209.jpg.description: The Andes so burst with skyscraping peaks that Salcantay is only the 38th-highest mountain in the range. But what a spectacle it provides: Reaching more than 20,000 feet in elevation, Salcantay is plenty tall, but it's the sheer vertical face of the mountain, and the deep valleys from which it rises, that provide the real wow factor. This region of southeastern Peru doesn't skimp on the sights—just north of Salcantay is the historic Inca citadel of Machu Picchu.

windows-spotlight-21.jpg.title: Burg Eltz castle, forested hill, morning mist, Wierschem, Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany
windows-spotlight-21.jpg.headline: Evolution of a castle
windows-spotlight-21.jpg.description: After centuries of glowups and makeovers, Braunfels Castle seems to have landed on its signature look. When it was built in the 1200s, it stood as a practical medieval fortress. A few centuries later, major expansions lent it a Gothic character, and in 1679, the castle was largely wrecked by fire and rebuilt with Baroque flair. Finally—amid a fad for medieval revivalism—its ruling prince ordered major additions in the 1840s, harmonizing the castle's varied historic components into a unified neo-Gothic style.

windows-spotlight-210.jpg.title: Milford Sound Piopiotahi, Fiordland National Park, New Zealand
windows-spotlight-210.jpg.headline: What's in two names?
windows-spotlight-210.jpg.description: We're visiting a landmark of the deep Southern Hemisphere that's a true stunner by any name, but as it happens, this magical 10-mile fjord has two. Milford Sound / Piopiotahi is among hundreds of locales throughout New Zealand that feature a dual official name, with ancient Māori names splitting the bill with more recent European ones. Another well-known example is Aoraki / Mount Cook, the highest peak here on the South Island and in all of New Zealand.

windows-spotlight-212.jpg.title: Mount Everest alpenglow, Nepal
windows-spotlight-212.jpg.headline: Height meets light
windows-spotlight-212.jpg.description: Called Sagarmāthā in Nepali and Chomolungma in Tibetan, this mountain's height would make it famous by any name. Of course, Mount Everest's fame has partly turned to notoriety in recent years, as climbers making successful summits have numbered over 800 a season, and images of long lines and garbage-strewn slopes have spread through social media. Though a ban on expeditions during the COVID-19 pandemic gave the mountain a break, many open questions remain about its future as a sustainable mountaineering destination.

windows-spotlight-215.jpg.title: Green Wave
windows-spotlight-215.jpg.headline: Blue waves, green isle
windows-spotlight-215.jpg.description: Ireland isn't the first place that comes to mind when folks think of prime spots for waveriding. But surfers find the breakers on County Clare's shores to be legendary. We're looking at Riley's Wave, a fierce barrel found somewhere between Kilkee and Doonbeg—not far south of the Wild Atlantic Way and the Cliffs of Moher, where wave-shy visitors can appreciate the surf's enormity from a high distance.

windows-spotlight-217.jpg.title: Matterhorn, Zmutt Glacier, Waterfall, Zermatt, Switzerland
windows-spotlight-217.jpg.headline: Sheer beauty
windows-spotlight-217.jpg.description: Peering past the Arbenbach waterfall outside of Zermatt, Switzerland, we're getting a straight-on view of the Matterhorn. This pyramidal peak's lofty vertex has long marked the Swiss border with Italy, where the massive, multinational mountain is known as Cervino. From this angle, we're seeing its north face—one of the six great north faces of the Alps. This nearly sheer stone wall is famed as one of the world's great mountaineering challenges.

windows-spotlight-219.jpg.title: Pamukkale Travertine Terraces, Turkey
windows-spotlight-219.jpg.headline: The 'cotton castle'
windows-spotlight-219.jpg.description: It's not hard to see where these travertine terraces in Türkiye got their name: Pamukkale, meaning 'cotton castle' in Turkish. In bright daylight, these huge stair-steps of puffy, porous limestone appear cloud-white, their multilevel pools a dazzling shade of sky blue. When the basins are full of hot spring-fed water, it's a fine place to relax after visiting neighboring Hierapolis for a dose of ancient history.

windows-spotlight-220.jpg.title: Melbourne Star Observation Wheel, Melbourne, Australia
windows-spotlight-220.jpg.headline: A star Down Under
windows-spotlight-220.jpg.description: Smaller, transportable versions of this rotating observation ride have been common at fairgrounds for a century or more, but the installation of really big, fixed wheels (sometimes deemed Giant Observation Wheels) didn't start in earnest until the 1990s. The London Eye opened in 2000 and really got the trend rolling, and now it seems every big city is giving this crowd-pleaser a whirl. Melbourne joined the revolution in 2008 with its Star wheel. It carries 21 enclosed cabins, each with a 20-guest capacity, and rises nearly 400 feet above the docklands area of the city.

windows-spotlight-222.jpg.title: Snow-capped mountain, blue high-altitude lake, golden grass, Altiplano, Bolivia
windows-spotlight-222.jpg.headline: Elevated aromas
windows-spotlight-222.jpg.description: Sights more than make up for smells here on the shores of this Bolivian saline lake. The sulfur-laden Laguna Hedionda (translating to 'stinking lake') lies above 13,500 feet on the Altiplano of the Andes, near the foot of the volcano Ollagüe. In contrast to its great elevation, Hedionda's depth is less than a foot on average, so even if you hold your nose, don't expect to do the backstroke on this backcountry water body. Time your visit right, though, and you'll see flocks of flamingos and other wallowing waterfowl.

windows-spotlight-224.jpg.title: Haystack Rock, The Needles, Seagulls, Sunset, Cannon Beach, Oregon
windows-spotlight-224.jpg.headline: Needles and a haystack
windows-spotlight-224.jpg.description: At low tide, seabird and human alike tread the soggy sands that sprawl in the shadow of Haystack Rock. Whether you're a beachcomber seeking seashells or a gull scavenging stranded crabs, this 235-foot Oregon Coast landmark (and the surrounding sea stacks, known as the 'needles') is a spectacular site. Even Hollywood agrees: Haystack Rock made for a memorable backdrop in the coming-of-age classic 'The Goonies.'

windows-spotlight-226.jpg.title: Boat floating, clear turquoise water, coral reef
windows-spotlight-226.jpg.headline: Flight or float
windows-spotlight-226.jpg.description: We're sailing the cerulean seas surrounding Crete, the largest island in Greece. Home to the ancient Minoans, it's well known as the supposed site of Icarus' ill-fated flight. In the popular version of the tragic tale, Icarus perishes after flying too close to the sun on waxen wings, which melt to send him plummeting to the water. In some tellings, though, he and his father Daedalus depart Crete by boat. (Of course, the ever-unfortunate Icarus still meets his doom by falling overboard. Wear your life jackets, folks!)

windows-spotlight-228.jpg.title: Milky Way night sky, mountain lake reflection
windows-spotlight-228.jpg.headline: No telescope required
windows-spotlight-228.jpg.description: All of the stars that you see in the night sky are part of the Milky Way galaxy, and some part of it is visible every night. But when people speak of seeing the Milky Way with the naked eye, they usually mean the cloud-like stretch of stars that can only be seen in especially clear skies. Unless you live way out in the sticks, a good glimpse of our cosmic neighborhood requires a little travel to less light-polluted locales like Yosemite National Park.

windows-spotlight-23.jpg.title: Three Peafowl in Green Rice Paddy
windows-spotlight-23.jpg.headline: Fowl party
windows-spotlight-23.jpg.description: Did you know there's no such thing as a female peacock? What we're seeing here is a trio of peahens—the term for ladies of the peafowl family. Lacking the fancy tail feathers boasted by males, peahens spend plenty of time on the prowl for peacocks' eye-popping posterior plumage, the males' main signal for attracting mates. Why so besotted with bodacious booty feathers? Some biologists say it's just an affinity for pretty colors, while others cite the handicap principle: the idea that toting long trails of feathers is so burdensome, only the fittest birds manage to survive with them. Either way, let's hope this peahen posse knows how to pick 'em.

windows-spotlight-230.jpg.title: Bear pair
windows-spotlight-230.jpg.headline: Bear pair
windows-spotlight-230.jpg.description: It'll be a while before this adorable cub is a fuzzy juggernaut like his mom, but until then, she'll stand guard. Female brown bears stick with their cubs for well over two years, taking on sole cub-rearing duties as males make an early exit. Mama bears are aggressive protectors of their litters—so as tempting as it is, don't try to play with this cute and curious-looking cub or you're sure to see some claws come out.

windows-spotlight-232.jpg.title: Orange Nebula
windows-spotlight-232.jpg.headline: A state in space
windows-spotlight-232.jpg.description: If humankind ever sends a spacefaring expedition to NGC 1499, call it Mission Burrito, because this cosmic cloud is better known as the California Nebula. Sadly, that mission is many years away if it's possible at all: The California Nebula is over a thousand light-years from Earth, meaning a visit would require a millennium of travel time even if you had a lightspeed vessel. So while the modern marvels of space photography allow us to see it zoomed out (where it recalls the shape of its namesake US state), NGC 1499 will have to wait a while for its close-up.

windows-spotlight-233.jpg.title: Dark Heron in Wetland Reeds at Sunrise
windows-spotlight-233.jpg.headline: One humungous heron
windows-spotlight-233.jpg.description: Ever since their cousin the Bennu heron went extinct, goliath herons stand tall as the largest wading birds in the world—when they're not hunkered down in the morning mists. Necks outstretched, these wetland waders can be up to 5 feet tall, with a wingspan well over 7 feet. Goliaths are native to sub-Saharan Africa, where they share ample wilderness—like the 7,500 protected square miles here at Kruger National Park—with zebras, elephants, rhinos, and other iconic species.

windows-spotlight-234.jpg.title: Fingal's Cave, Staffa, Scotland
windows-spotlight-234.jpg.headline: The singing sea cave
windows-spotlight-234.jpg.description: The columnar basalt bounding Fingal's Cave make this cavernous inlet on the isle of Staffa a sight to behold. The sea cave's other remarkable quality is one photos can't show you: its astounding acoustics. Thanks to the arched roof and irregularly shaped walls, visitors have long described the sound of the waves in Fingal's Cave as harmonious and hypnotic. That includes a few musical innovators who've drawn inspiration from the cave's melodies, from Felix Mendelssohn to Pink Floyd.

windows-spotlight-236.jpg.title: Striped Cliffs, Natural Arch, Sea Stack, Sunset, Étretat, Normandy, France
windows-spotlight-236.jpg.headline: Stripes on the seashore
windows-spotlight-236.jpg.description: With their zebra-like stripes and formations shaped like an elephant's trunk and a rhinoceros' horn, these cliffs might make you think you're on safari, even though we're thousands of miles from the African savanna. Instead you'll find this tableau along the Alabaster Coast of the English Channel—known here on its southern shore as La Manche ('the sleeve'). Streaks of flint between chalk layers form the dark pinstripes of this Normandy landmark, a surprising accent on this body of water better known for big, blank cliffs of pure chalk.

windows-spotlight-237.jpg.title: Pink Benthic Soft Coral
windows-spotlight-237.jpg.headline: A benthic 'blossom'
windows-spotlight-237.jpg.description: It's lucky this florid and seemingly fluorescent organism carries the nickname 'carnation coral,' because its more proper name is quite a mouthful. The deep sea-dwelling dendronephthya is a kind of soft coral, which is exactly what it sounds like, in contrast with its rigid, reef-forming cousins. Both soft and stony corals are colonies of tiny polyps—the 'blossoms' on the carnation coral. This reveals their kinship with jellyfish, which begin life in a polyp stage.

windows-spotlight-238.jpg.title: Morro Dois Irmãos, Fernando de Noronha, Brazil
windows-spotlight-238.jpg.headline: A distinctive duo
windows-spotlight-238.jpg.description: Dramatic volcanic features like these twin sea stacks, known as  Two Brothers Rock, make this archipelago easy to spot from afar—a lucky thing, given how out-of-the-way it is. Lying a couple hundred miles from the Brazilian mainland, the main island of the Fernando de Noronha group is the only inhabited one in the small chain. Despite its tiny size (well below 10 square miles), it's jam-packed with rugged terrain and relaxing beaches alike. Even more treasured is what surrounds the isle: In 2001, UNESCO declared Fernando de Noronha a World Heritage Site to protect the thriving undersea life that feeds here.

windows-spotlight-240.jpg.title: The Three Watchtowers Mountain Reflection, Dolomites, Italy
windows-spotlight-240.jpg.headline: The three watchtowers
windows-spotlight-240.jpg.description: The Three Peaks of Lavaredo offer a little something for everybody—spectacular views for the hikers (and, of course, photographers) who view them from afar, challenging routes for mountaineers who've been climbing these peaks for 150 years and plenty of history for military buffs. The three Dolomitic pinnacles acted as makeshift watchtowers during World War I, straddling Italy's border with its then-opponent Austria-Hungary. The high-altitude battles of the Italian Alps came to be called the White War due to their intense winter conditions. Remnants of the bitter skirmishes, including trenches and tunnels, are scattered in the shadows of this timeless mountain trio.

windows-spotlight-242.jpg.title: Mountaintop hiking trail above clouds at sunset, Madeira, Portugal
windows-spotlight-242.jpg.headline: A Madeiran mountaintop
windows-spotlight-242.jpg.description: If you're not a seasoned hiker but still seek the thrill of conquering a summit, this ascent is for you. Pico do Areeiro may be the third highest peak on Madeira, but a road leading up the slopes makes for easy access to its tippy-top, complete with ample parking. Looking to elevate the experience even further? A footpath follows the ridgeline to Pico Ruivo, the highest point on the Portuguese isle.

windows-spotlight-243.jpg.title: Meteora sandstone pillars, Kalambaka, Greece
windows-spotlight-243.jpg.headline: Monk's-eye view
windows-spotlight-243.jpg.description: The name and unique look of this place suggest celestial origins, but the stone formations of Meteora didn't fall from the sky. They're actually the compressed sediments of a prehistoric seabed, thrust upward about 60 million years ago by seismic events. Long after the elements weathered them to pillar-like shapes, Greek Orthodox monks began building precarious monasteries on the summits. Six of the original two dozen monasteries remain active communities today, hosting pilgrims and tourists from all over the world.

windows-spotlight-245.jpg.title: Cascading Waterfall, Tropical Forest, Rocky River
windows-spotlight-245.jpg.headline: Falls in the forest
windows-spotlight-245.jpg.description: These spectacular rainforest waterfalls are not far from the small village of Dominical. The Nauyaca waterfalls are said to be the most impressive in Puntarenas province and are a great reason to venture inland from Dominical's famed coastline. What's the buzz on the beach? Some of Costa Rica's best waves, and miles of sandy shores backed by a lush rainforest. The town's development from quiet fishing village to backpacker haven, and later to a place where folks strive for a balanced ecology, is an example of how Costa Rica has evolved over the decades.

windows-spotlight-247.jpg.title: Jagged Blue Glacial Ice
windows-spotlight-247.jpg.headline: Where icebergs are born
windows-spotlight-247.jpg.description: In this close-up, Chile's Grey Glacier is decidedly blue. That's because red light has a much longer wavelength than blue light, so reds and infrareds are easily absorbed by the crystalline structure of glacial ice while blues are easily reflected. Optical science aside, glaciers worldwide seem to be singing the blues. Nearly all of them are melting at alarmingly high rates. Grey Glacier has retreated more than a mile since the 1980s, and in 2017 an iceberg measuring 1.5 million square feet calved from the icy giant's face.

windows-spotlight-248.jpg.title: Múlafossur Waterfall, Gásadalur Village, Faroe Islands
windows-spotlight-248.jpg.headline: Faraway falls
windows-spotlight-248.jpg.description: The views here in the Faroe Islands village of Gásadalur are breathtaking, but getting around is difficult due to high cliffs and treacherous coastline. Back in 2004, the Gásadalstunnilin mountain tunnel was opened, and this isolated village with its hallmark 98-foot waterfall became much easier to witness in person. Even so, the Faroes are hardly a quick hop from most locales: The nearest mainland is 200 miles away in Scotland.

windows-spotlight-25.jpg.title: Red Squirrel eating nut on mossy stone wall
windows-spotlight-25.jpg.headline: Rodent on the rebound?
windows-spotlight-25.jpg.description: Known for their quirky behaviors and willingness to live near humans, red squirrels are popular with wildlife spotters across Europe. But in England, where our photo was captured, these quirky creatures have had a rough go recently. Constantly struggling to regain territory from rival grey squirrels (an invasive species introduced to Britain in the 19th century), in recent times they've also been hit with a nasty plague called squirrelpox, which gray squirrels carry but is only deadly to reds. Squirrel-loving Brits have banded together to make several areas of the UK into red squirrel havens, helping expand the rust-colored rodents' range.

windows-spotlight-250.jpg.title: Common Blue Butterfly Pollinator on Lavender
windows-spotlight-250.jpg.headline: A painted pollinator
windows-spotlight-250.jpg.description: You can thank this common blue butterfly's discerning palate for the delightful palette of our photo. Lavender is well loved by us humans as a delicious aromatic herb, and common blues agree, happily harvesting nectar from the tiny purple blossoms. Common blues' color patterns differ by sex, a perfect example of dimorphism. By the blue belly and grayish outer wings of this little guy, we can tell he's a male—if he were to spread his wings, we'd see where the 'blue' part of the name comes from.

windows-spotlight-253.jpg.title: Sulak Canyon River Mountains Sunset, Dagestan, Russia
windows-spotlight-253.jpg.headline: History flows here
windows-spotlight-253.jpg.description: This stunning sight has stopped generations of travelers in their tracks, whether journeying with a merchant caravan to East Asia or just road tripping in Türkiye. Long ago part of the Silk Road, and now a national park intercut with miles of trails, the Botan Valley was carved by (what else?) the Botan River—a tributary of the mighty Tigris. Ancient Baghdad-bound businessfolk have given way to watersports enthusiasts in these parts, so if you find a perch with a view, don't be surprised to spot a few windsurfers way down below.
windows-spotlight-253.jpg.copyright: © Abstract Aerial Art Digital Vision/Getty Images

windows-spotlight-256.jpg.title: Torres del Paine Turquoise Glacial Lake, Patagonia, Chile
windows-spotlight-256.jpg.headline: Of tarn and tower
windows-spotlight-256.jpg.description: On a nice summer day, the rewards for completing this difficult 11-mile hike are as clear as the blue sky. The steeple-like towers of the Cordillera Paine seem to rise straight up from this tiny, jade-tinted tarn, composing quite the tableau to take in while you rest those legs. Of course, it's still a long trek back, so you'll want to watch those gathering clouds: Weather changes fast here in Patagonia, and even the best views in Torres del Paine National Park can be fleeting.

windows-spotlight-257.jpg.title: Autumn Turquoise River Rapids Salmon Run
windows-spotlight-257.jpg.headline: Last stop for salmon
windows-spotlight-257.jpg.description: Before it joins the Strait of Georgia near Vancouver, the mighty Fraser River flows about 850 miles through the peaks and valleys of British Columbia. Carving gorgeous gorges, washing over waterfalls, and irrigating fertile, foggy farms, the Fraser is a huge factor in BC's rep as perhaps Canada's most photogenic province. Only 60-odd miles from the river's highland headwaters—and almost 800 miles from the ocean—the pictured Rearguard Falls is the farthest point up the Fraser you'll find spawning salmon that migrate from the Pacific. The rapids appear turquoise due to glacial runoff from adjacent mountains including Mount Robson, the Canadian Rockies' highest peak.

windows-spotlight-259.jpg.title: Green yellow harvest rice terraces
windows-spotlight-259.jpg.headline: Hues of the harvest
windows-spotlight-259.jpg.description: Young green grasses and mature yellow stalks form a multi-tinted tessellation on the terraces of Tư Lệ, a fertile farming region of northern Vietnam. We're up in the mountains far from the mighty Mekong River, which powers the massive rice-growing economy on the nation's southern floodplain. Here in the north, growers channel rain and runoff to irrigate their rice in a carefully engineered system. This high-elevation agriculture may require more planning, but here there's no need to fear saltwater intrusion that threatens crops in the Mekong Delta.

windows-spotlight-261.jpg.title: Keel-billed Toucan
windows-spotlight-261.jpg.headline: Big in the beak
windows-spotlight-261.jpg.description: It's also known fittingly as the rainbow-billed toucan, but this rainforest flyer's common name is the keel-billed toucan, probably because its big curving beak resembles the bladelike underside of a boat. They may look a little clumsy, but these toucans wield their bills with skill. Social birds that love to compete as well as cooperate, they use their bills to toss fruit to feathered friends in an acrobatic game of catch or to challenge the same compatriots in beak duels that resemble sword fighting. There's no fear of broken noses here, however, as toucans' bills are made up of keratin, the same sturdy protein found in horse hooves, rhino horns and your own fingernails.

windows-spotlight-263.jpg.title: King of Wings hoodoo sunset, Bisti De-Na-Zin Wilderness, New Mexico
windows-spotlight-263.jpg.headline: A seat for spacefolk?
windows-spotlight-263.jpg.description: With any luck, an extraterrestrial takeover of Earth is a problem for distant future generations to worry about. But should we ever welcome new alien overlords, expect their edicts to issue from this regal feature. The hoodoo dubbed the Alien Throne cuts an eerie figure against a Southwestern sunset, towering over remote New Mexican badlands crowded with other natural yet freakish formations. Though often associated with the nearby Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness, the Throne actually lies within another field of bizarre landforms: the Valley of Dreams.

windows-spotlight-265.jpg.title: Blue Glacier, Misty Fjord, Dark Mountains, Alaska
windows-spotlight-265.jpg.headline: The land of big
windows-spotlight-265.jpg.description: Remarkable as it looks on your desktop, Lamplugh Glacier is just a frosty face in the crowd back in its home neighborhood. Depending on how you count it, Alaska is home to between 27,000 and 100,000 glaciers. If that tally sounds unbelievable, get used to it: Here in the biggest US state by far, enormous numbers are the norm. Covering 571,000 square miles of land—more than Texas, California, and Montana combined—Alaska contains seven of the USA's top 10 largest national parks (including this one, Glacier Bay), 17 of its 20 tallest mountains, over 100 volcanoes, 12,000 rivers, 34,000 miles of coast, and 3 million lakes. The only figure that's small is its population density, well below two people per square mile.

windows-spotlight-267.jpg.title: Rolling green plains
windows-spotlight-267.jpg.headline: Passage to the plains
windows-spotlight-267.jpg.description: Meadows roll steeply to form foothills all across Moravia, a historical region of Central Europe. Part of the modern Czech Republic, its billowing topography is a hint to its strategic importance. Moravia is defined by a system of valleys that link the North European and Great Hungarian plains, so it's taken an outsized place in geopolitical history. To dig even deeper into the past, large mammals like mammoths once migrated through the Moravian gaps, and clever prehistoric humans settled along the bottleneck for many a successful hunt.

windows-spotlight-269.jpg.title: Red Sand Beach Turquoise Ocean Desert Cliffs, Paracas National Reserve, Peru
windows-spotlight-269.jpg.headline: Red vs. blue
windows-spotlight-269.jpg.description: A visit to this nature reserve in Peru should include a trip to the deep red sands of Playa Roja. Why is the sand here so rust-hued? A nearby massif, the Punta Santa Maria, contains the red, granite-like stone, which is pulverized and sloughed off by the waves of the mighty Pacific and washed onto this beach. Even if you know the mechanics of how the Playa Roja got this way, the deep jewel tones of the inland soil, the red sand, and the blue waters lose none of their mysterious allure. Paracas National Reserve protects this extraordinary coastline, along with inland desert areas, and archeological sites of the Paracas culture.

windows-spotlight-27.jpg.title: Pointe du Souffleur, Mauritius
windows-spotlight-27.jpg.headline: A coastal cruise
windows-spotlight-27.jpg.description: With steep green terrain rising on one side and deep turquoise seas stretching from the other, this road can be hard to keep your eyes on. The B9 coast road holds tight to the southwestern seashore of Mauritius, presenting a scenic challenge for drivers and cyclists alike. Here we see the hairpin-curve peninsula tipped by Macondé Rock, a hardened-lava promontory that's worth a pit stop for the view—as long as you don't mind taking a few stairs to the top.

windows-spotlight-271.jpg.title: Volcanic mountain range, Mokolii Island, Oahu, Hawaii
windows-spotlight-271.jpg.headline: A volcano's vestige
windows-spotlight-271.jpg.description: The mountain range that runs along Oahu's eastern edge is all that remains of a single, enormous shield volcano. Now known as the Ko'olau Range, this 34-mile stretch of steepled ridges was part of the massive rim encircling Ko'olau Volcano's crater, until an eruption sent most of it plummeting into the Pacific Ocean over 10,000 years ago. Small beach communities now dot the narrow windward shore between the peaks and the Pacific, giving it a rural feel in contrast to bustling Honolulu.

windows-spotlight-273.jpg.title: Sandstone arch, Milky Way night sky, Arches National Park, Utah
windows-spotlight-273.jpg.headline: A celestial window
windows-spotlight-273.jpg.description: One of the more than 2,000 formations that give Arches National Park its name, Skyline Arch becomes a window to the Milky Way on a clear Utah night. Arches' dark skies and otherworldly landscape make it a prime destination for stargazing and night photography. Come daylight, the park offers a variety of outdoor activities, including hiking, horseback riding, and rock climbing.

windows-spotlight-275.jpg.title: Chapel Bridge with Water Tower at blue hour, Lucerne, Switzerland
windows-spotlight-275.jpg.headline: Bridge at blue hour
windows-spotlight-275.jpg.description: The Kapellbrücke is the most enduring symbol of Lucerne, central Switzerland's biggest city. Spanning the river Reuss at the point where it flows from Lake Lucerne, it's Europe's oldest covered wooden bridge, dating back to 1395. It's also the world's oldest surviving example of a truss bridge, an efficient design stabilized by support beams arranged in sturdy triangular shapes—now seen worldwide on bridges of all sizes and materials. The Kapellbrücke's interior is also notable, its rafters lined with triangular paintings that depict local history. Unfortunately, most of the original 158 paintings burned in a 1993 fire, but around 30 were saved and restored.

windows-spotlight-277.jpg.title: Perching Atlantic Puffins
windows-spotlight-277.jpg.headline: Perching puffins
windows-spotlight-277.jpg.description: Good communication is important in relationships: Just ask these seabirds who are known to mate for life, often a span of two or three decades. While the call of the Atlantic puffin isn't the most romantic sound (think something between a hearty laugh and an armpit noise), that's just one way these highly social birds share their feelings. Males perform mating dances for females, and mating pairs often trade low grunts and chirps, sometimes rubbing their bills together affectionately.

windows-spotlight-279.jpg.title: American White Pelicans
windows-spotlight-279.jpg.headline: Felonious flyers?
windows-spotlight-279.jpg.description: Don't carry large bills around these long-billed pilferers. Well, actually, your money's safe. Just watch out if you're toting a tasty fish, because American white pelicans are among the deftest of kleptoparasites: Animals known for swiping other critters' food. Terns, herons, and other seabirds are frequent victims of such seafood snatchings. When pelicans stay on the straight and narrow, though, they're not bad at fishing—although they don't work as hard as some of their pelican cousins, preferring to trawl the water's surface and snap up prey rather than dive daringly from the air.

windows-spotlight-281.jpg.title: Pont Alexandre III golden statues twilight, Paris
windows-spotlight-281.jpg.headline: A bridge to history
windows-spotlight-281.jpg.description: Of the 37 bridges that cross the Seine in Paris, the Pont Alexandre III might be the most decadently designed. Elements of Beaux-Arts and Art Nouveau styles harmonize here into an intricate work of art, its sculptures speckled with delicate gilding. It was named for Tsar Alexander III of Russia, who forged a historic alliance with France, and whose ill-fated son Nicholas II laid the span's cornerstone in 1896. At right, the legacy of another doomed emperor looms: the dome of Les Invalides, which caps the atrium housing Napoleon Bonaparte's tomb.

windows-spotlight-284.jpg.title: Seealpsee mountain lake reflections, Appenzellerland, Switzerland
windows-spotlight-284.jpg.headline: Swiss bliss
windows-spotlight-284.jpg.description: Looking to get off the beaten path? That can be tricky here in Switzerland, where hardy mountain folk have beaten paths for millennia. But this quiet spot in the nation's northeast may be your best shot. Home to a little more than 16,000 people, Appenzell Innerrhoden is the least populous of Switzerland's 26 cantons. Sure, the name may be a seven-syllable mouthful—but that's just as well, because its beauty is sure to leave you speechless. (Or at least more inclined to yodel than speak.)

windows-spotlight-286.jpg.title: Paired Razorbills on rock
windows-spotlight-286.jpg.headline: Paired on a perch
windows-spotlight-286.jpg.description: Razorbills' passing resemblance to penguins is appropriate: They're the last living relatives of another large, land-bound bird. The great auk, once found all over the North Atlantic, was one of the first species to raise ecological concern around overhunting. By the mid-1500s, the bird was gone from European shores, and it went fully extinct by the 1850s. Today, the high-flying razorbill (sometimes called the lesser auk) faces threats of its own such as pollution and habitat destruction. But even as monogamous birds who mate for life, determined razorbill parents keep their species' numbers soaring. Up to 1.6 million razorbills—and counting—currently live in the wild.

windows-spotlight-287.jpg.title: Circular Laguna Garzon Bridge, Uruguay
windows-spotlight-287.jpg.headline: Circular logic
windows-spotlight-287.jpg.description: Rafael Viñoly, one of the most famous architects born here in Uruguay, designed the circular bridge in our image. Laguna Garzón Bridge consists of two semicircular one-way sections that form a kind of lagoon within a lagoon. Owing to the design, cars slow down on the stretch, and—bonus!—pedestrians get their own dedicated lanes running along both the inner and outer part of the circle, allowing for some fantastic sightseeing.

windows-spotlight-29.jpg.title: Green Amazon parrot pair
windows-spotlight-29.jpg.headline: Parrot pair
windows-spotlight-29.jpg.description: These near-identical parrots prove that birds of a feather flock together. But sometimes that feather is hard to put a name to, especially in the crowded world of amazon parrots. Most amazons share the genus' most visible trait—green plumage. Subtle differences in head, wing and beak colouration, however, result in a spread of about 30 species. That makes it tough to precisely identify amazons in the wild, although we're pretty sure our bird buddies here are yellow-crowned amazons. Would you like to do a little field research and see if you agree?

windows-spotlight-290.jpg.title: Snow-capped Mount Kilimanjaro, Tanzania
windows-spotlight-290.jpg.headline: Africa's rooftop
windows-spotlight-290.jpg.description: A staggering 19,341 feet tall, Mount Kilimanjaro is the highest point in all of Africa. In our twilit shot framed by acacia trees, its main cone known as Kibo dominates. That we're calling it a 'cone' might tip you off to another key fact about 'Kili': It's the world's tallest land volcano outside of South America. Its last eruption was 360,000 years ago, but this sleeping giant is merely dormant, not extinct, and could become active again someday.

windows-spotlight-292.jpg.title: Crashing Waves Turquoise Ocean Golden Beach
windows-spotlight-292.jpg.headline: Beware the waves
windows-spotlight-292.jpg.description: We're probably safer seeing these churning waves from high above: Swimming is forbidden on the much-Instagrammed Kelingking Beach due to the violence of the surf seen here. But this unique spot on Indonesia's Nusa Penida Island is well worth the visit, just for a glimpse at the surrounding rocky ridge (often noted for its resemblance to a T. rex). Experienced hikers can make their way to the top, earning a view to rival this spectacular drone's-eye shot.

windows-spotlight-295.jpg.title: Rakotzbrücke Devil's Bridge basalt arch, Kromlau Saxony Germany
windows-spotlight-295.jpg.headline: A cursed bridge?
windows-spotlight-295.jpg.description: Dozens of stone arch bridges across Europe are known as the "Devil's Bridge," often reputedly carrying a curse for those who cross. This one, the Rakotzbrücke in Gablenz, Germany, was built in the 19th century. While you may not be bewitched by demons for hoofing across, local police will likely hex you with a fine as the fragile bridge is legally off-limits.Even sceptics may be spurred to superstition by a stone span supported by seemingly nothing. How do they build these things anyway? It all begins with arched wooden falsework upon which stones are fitted in rows. Once the keystone at the centre has been snugly placed, the falsework is removed and the span's weight is transferred onto it, with the keystone holding the whole structure steady via gravity and friction. It's not black magic, just a clever use of physics!

windows-spotlight-297.jpg.title: Atlantic Puffin
windows-spotlight-297.jpg.headline: Portrait of a 'sea parrot'
windows-spotlight-297.jpg.description: The puffin is nicknamed the 'sea parrot,' but the brightly colored bill that lends it that title is only present for part of the year. A puffin's beak will become awash with reds and oranges just before breeding season, when puffins form nesting colonies of hundreds, thousands, or even millions of individuals. The beak's size and the depth of its hues signal whether a bird is a healthy mate. Once the year's young are raised, the beak's outer layer is shed to reveal duller colors. Each pair of new puffin parents then part ways—but these monogamous creatures usually return to each other season after season.

windows-spotlight-299.jpg.title: Aurora Borealis, Finland
windows-spotlight-299.jpg.headline: Fire in the Finnish sky
windows-spotlight-299.jpg.description: Rather than pull Santa Claus's sleigh (although Finnish folk legend says he does live in these parts), reindeer in Finland's Sápmi region are herded by the indigenous Sámi people, who've long made their home here above the Arctic Circle and beneath the aurora borealis. Though development and climate change have led to plunging reindeer populations, about 10% of Sámi people still carry on the traditional, sustainable herding practices of their ancestors. They live semi-nomadic lives following the migrating reindeer from pasture to pasture, making efficient use of reindeer milk, meat, and fur to beat hunger and cold in the bitter winter.

windows-spotlight-302.jpg.title: Green Aurora Borealis, City lights, Tromsø
windows-spotlight-302.jpg.headline: Tromsø aglow
windows-spotlight-302.jpg.description: Even when being upstaged by the aurora borealis, the streetlights of Tromsø see a lot of use each winter. One of the biggest cities above the Arctic Circle, the centuries-old Norwegian settlement is plunged into all-day darkness from November to January. Even still, the best time to see the aurora is at night—often multiple nights a week during this winter wonderland's peak viewing season.

windows-spotlight-305.jpg.title: Lake Matheson, temperate rainforest, snow-capped mountains reflection, West Coast, South Island, New Zealand
windows-spotlight-305.jpg.headline: A postage-stamp shot
windows-spotlight-305.jpg.description: Their glistening caps reflected in dark water, Aoraki and Mount Tasman complete one of the most famous sights in a country defined by incredible views. On a clear day, you can't beat the reflections seen in Lake Matheson for picture perfection. New Zealanders have celebrated the spectacle since at least the 1940s, when a postage stamp featuring this very scene first began circulating. Its renown has since spread far and wide, and a steady stream of tourists makes this 14,000-year-old lake the most photographed in New Zealand.

windows-spotlight-307.jpg.title: Bhumibol Bridge Night, Elevated Highway Interchange, Bangkok, Thailand
windows-spotlight-307.jpg.headline: Busy bridges
windows-spotlight-307.jpg.description: Beauty can sometimes be found in unexpected places , including here amid twisting concrete overpasses and glimmering streetlights. Despite its rather mundane name, the Industrial Ring Road is part of an impressive update to Bangkok's traffic system ordered by King Bhumibol Adulyadej in the early 2000s.
