The Thai capital's traffic jams are still infamous, but the Ring Road's tangled transitways offer some relief from the gridlock, flanked by towering twin bridges named Bhumibol 1 and Bhumibol 2 (the latter seen at left).

windows-spotlight-308.jpg.title: Kayakers, Great Falls, Potomac River
windows-spotlight-308.jpg.headline: Which way to DC?
windows-spotlight-308.jpg.description: The scraggly schists and gneisses that rise from this river rapid might deceive you to place this photo somewhere in the United States' mountainous west. But Great Falls Park is actually close to the East Coast, just a short drive (albeit a long paddle) from one of the nation's busiest cities. Keep on the Potomac another 14-ish miles southeast and you'll see familiar buildings like the Washington Monument and Lincoln Memorial break the horizon along its banks. As it flows past Washington, DC, the river opens into a gradually widening tidal passage, eventually emptying into the massive, multi-armed Chesapeake Bay.

windows-spotlight-31.jpg.title: Loch Etive with autumn island, Scotland
windows-spotlight-31.jpg.headline: A tale of two lochs
windows-spotlight-31.jpg.description: The Gaelic word 'loch' is pretty loose in its use, as the case of Loch Leven illustrates. Or is that Loch Levens, plural? This saltwater inlet in the Scottish Highlands, reflecting the rugged Pap of Glencoe, shares the name Loch Leven with a lowland freshwater lake near the town of Kinross. Hey, sometimes language is less about precision and more about the vibe—and a look at each loch will communicate Scotland's diverse beauty better than words ever can.

windows-spotlight-310.jpg.title: Old Man of Storr rock pinnacles, mountain loch, sunset, Isle of Skye, Scotland
windows-spotlight-310.jpg.headline: Primeval isle
windows-spotlight-310.jpg.description: The rugged terrain seen here is the result of lava tubes cooling and eroding over millions of years—evidence of the extinct volcanic complex that gradually formed the Isle of Skye. This largest island of the Inner Hebrides is defined by its knurled coastline of peninsulas and inlets, its irregular shape on a map often compared to a contorted wing or claw. Angular obstacles are scattered all over its surface, too, such as the fingerlike Old Man of Storr shown in our picture.

windows-spotlight-312.jpg.title: Snow-capped Volcanic Mountains, Green Valley Stream, Iceland
windows-spotlight-312.jpg.headline: Tuff and stuff
windows-spotlight-312.jpg.description: Just over the mountains from the Eastfjords' snaggled coastline lies a valley that's so sunny and green in the summer, it's easy to forget this nation has 'ice' right in its name. Iceland's Stórurð ('giant boulders') valley is named for the many large masses of tuff—that is, compressed volcanic ash—strewn amid the meadows long ago by retreating glaciers. Standing far taller are the peaks of Dyrfjöll, a sharp, steep range made of the same tuff.

windows-spotlight-314.jpg.title: Cloughoughter Castle Ruin at Sunset, Lough Oughter, County Cavan, Ireland
windows-spotlight-314.jpg.headline: An Irish isle ruin
windows-spotlight-314.jpg.description: All you need for a river is two banks and a steady flow of water, but that only describes part of this Irish river's 80-mile course. Here at Lough Oughter, the River Erne widens into a broad basin—part of a series of loughs that stretches northward almost to the Atlantic, dotted with islands large and small. This one holding Cloughoughter Castle seems so tiny the ruined fortress might flip it right over. Its battle scars from a 1649 siege still visible, Cloughoughter has been a fave of painters (and, of course, photographers) for centuries.

windows-spotlight-317.jpg.title: Jan Pálffy Mausoleum, Bojnice, Slovakia
windows-spotlight-317.jpg.headline: The tyrant's haunt
windows-spotlight-317.jpg.description: Designed by noted Bohemian architect Jan Santini Aichel, this skull-shaped cemetery comes complete with a scary story. Legend has it this town near the Czech Republic's center, Žďár nad Sázavou, was once governed by a tyrant named Ulrich. When he died, a wave of relief washed over the townsfolk—but even after they buried Ulrich here, his ghost continued to torment them. Only when Ulrich's grave was opened and filled with quicklime and poppy seeds did the hauntings end. It's said, though, that once as many years pass as there are seeds in Ulrich's coffin, his vengeful spirit will return.

windows-spotlight-319.jpg.title: Daereungwon Tomb Complex, illuminated white blossom tree, sunset, Gyeongju, South Korea
windows-spotlight-319.jpg.headline: A 'museum without walls'
windows-spotlight-319.jpg.description: The Korean city of Gyeongju is renowned for the well-preserved history that permeates it. These rolling landforms are all exhibits in themselves—they're not natural hills but built-up burial mounds called tumuli. Each tumulus hosts the remains of royalty from the ancient Silla kingdom that ruled much of the Korean peninsula for about a millennium, from 57 BCE to 935 CE. Almost two dozen of these tombs make up the Daereungwon complex nestled within modern Gyeongju.

windows-spotlight-320.jpg.title: Two moose wading in lake with snow-capped mountains, Denali National Park, Alaska
windows-spotlight-320.jpg.headline: Weighty waders
windows-spotlight-320.jpg.description: Though they're mainly crepuscular creatures, moose can sometimes be spotted in the daytime. Especially here in Alaska, which has the biggest population of moose of any state, estimated at up to 200,000. Even in broad daylight, though, bull moose have few predators to fear given their sheer size, sometimes more than 1,500 pounds and with antler spans over 6 feet. These two comrades can't throw caution completely to the north wind, though—they share the lands around Denali (pictured in the background) with a healthy cohort of brown bears.

windows-spotlight-322.jpg.title: Male lion lying in grass
windows-spotlight-322.jpg.headline: A lion's lie-down
windows-spotlight-322.jpg.description: Ever wonder why lions star in ancient stories and myths from all over the world, yet are only found in scattered pockets of sub-Saharan Africa? It's because these proud predators once had a much wider swath to stalk. Long ago, lions were found not only throughout Africa, but across South and Central Asia, the Middle East, and Southern Europe—possibly as far north as France. Though the passing of millennia has seen lions' numbers dwindle, their regal image still captivates people everywhere—even though these powerful cats are only active four hours a day, spending the rest of it resting like this king.

windows-spotlight-324.jpg.title: Wooden pier, two rowboats, autumn forest, water reflection, Lago di Braies, Dolomites, Italy
windows-spotlight-324.jpg.headline: Stunning in any tongue
windows-spotlight-324.jpg.description: Ever wanted to row your boat where life is but a dream? Well, hop in and grab the oars. When you're afloat on these peaceful waters, you'll find the alpine vistas in all directions are so beautiful it's surreal.But back to reality for a second: What do you call this lovely lake? To local Italian speakers it's Lago di Braies—but they're less than a quarter of the population in this part of Italy. Most people here in South Tyrol province refer to the lake in their native German as Pragser Wildsee. Of course, like  the Dolomites (or le Dolomiti, or die Dolomiten…) that surround it, this body of water is a gem by any name.

windows-spotlight-326.jpg.title: Not so desolate after all
windows-spotlight-326.jpg.headline: Not so desolate after all
windows-spotlight-326.jpg.description: Camdeboo National Park's name comes from a word that's tricky for non-Khoekhoe speakers to say (though it's fun to try). !Xamdeboo, with '!' pronounced as a click consonant, means 'green valley.' In sharp contrast, the park's signature feature—this 400-foot-tall mass of pillarlike diabase—is named the Valley of Desolation. A paved road leads park visitors to this stark stone sight, also a great place for surveying the Karoo scrubland where kudu, eland, and even the occasional Cape mountain zebra roam.

windows-spotlight-328.jpg.title: Red-capped Downy Woodpecker
windows-spotlight-328.jpg.headline: Of pecks and pest control
windows-spotlight-328.jpg.description: Though it may seem like woodpeckers have it out for trees with their namesake hole-boring behavior, these birds are actually crucial to the survival of forests. Many woodpeckers drill into dead, decaying trees as they search for grubs and small insects within. And those that peck at living trees are actually helping to prevent pest infestations that might otherwise destroy a tree. The tree can survive the holes drilled by the woodpecker's beak, and the birds gobble up termites and other insects that are a bane to the tree's health. This hard-working species, the hairy woodpecker, offers its forestry services all over North America, where it's a common sight from coast to coast.

windows-spotlight-33.jpg.title: Red-brown Tsingy rock formations, Madagascar
windows-spotlight-33.jpg.headline: A tsingy of beauty
windows-spotlight-33.jpg.description: The Malagasy word 'tsingy,' used to describe irregular, eroded blades of stone like these, translates to 'where you can't walk barefoot.' Ever since humans first settled here sometime over a millennium ago, the unfriendly karst terrain has served to keep most of us out of the Tsingy Rouge region—allowing Madagascar's unique array of wildlife to flourish in its countless nooks and crannies. Here on the world's fourth-largest island, 90% of the fauna is found nowhere else on Earth, so this is heaven to any naturalist with a good pair of boots.

windows-spotlight-332.jpg.title: Alnes Lighthouse, rocky breakwater, sailboat, fjord mountains, Godøya, Norway
windows-spotlight-332.jpg.headline: Anybody home?
windows-spotlight-332.jpg.description: It's been more than a century since Høgsteinen Lighthouse had a keeper, but here on the majestic expanse of Norway's coast, somehow it doesn't seem all that lonely. Built in the 1850s on a reef reinforced by an artificial jetty, it's been fully automated since 1905, dutifully guiding vessels to the western port of Ålesund. It's a busy job, but during sunny downtimes like this, the lighthouse gladly welcomes visitors to relax on its stone base and bask in the mountainous maritime panorama.

windows-spotlight-335.jpg.title: Dark Mountain Range, Ocean Waves, Coastal Rock, Small Isles
windows-spotlight-335.jpg.headline: Small Isles, big views
windows-spotlight-335.jpg.description: We're both seeing and standing on the Small Isles—so known even though they make many of the Hebrides' rocky islets and outcrops look even tinier. Standing on the long, flat tidelands of the isle of Eigg, we're seeing the distant sawtooth hills of its big sister Rùm. These two, plus a handful of smaller islands, form an archipelago that's home to about 150 people. A remote region indeed, but it's hardly Robinson Crusoe for these scrappy Scots: The Small Isles lie near Great Britain's westernmost tip, so ferries from the mainland make regular trips.

windows-spotlight-337.jpg.title: Desert Sand Dunes Rock Formations Sunset
windows-spotlight-337.jpg.headline: Deep, deep desert
windows-spotlight-337.jpg.description: As the largest nation by area in Africa, Algeria covers almost a million square miles in the north of the continent. But as with most North African nations, its population mainly sticks to a narrow strip along the Mediterranean—far from Saharan sights like Tin Akachaker, this stone field near the Hoggar Mountains. Getting here from Algiers is a multi-day affair, requiring 24-hours' drive from the capital to the desert outpost of Tamanrasset, then another 50-mile offroad haul to the rock-dotted dunes.

windows-spotlight-338.jpg.title: Rainbow Mountains, Zhangye Danxia National Geological Park, China
windows-spotlight-338.jpg.headline: Cataclysmic colors
windows-spotlight-338.jpg.description: If you need proof that beauty can come from chaos, look no further than the Rainbow Mountains of Zhangye, China. When Insular India collided with the Eurasian tectonic plate 55 million years ago, the punishing force crumpled Earth's crust so drastically it formed not only the mighty Himalayas, but this watercolor landscape some 600 miles to the northeast. As tremendous tremors reconfigured vast swaths of flatland, once-smooth layer cakes of hardened silt and sand were thrust off kilter, creating the angular stripes we see today.

windows-spotlight-340.jpg.title: Lion Cub
windows-spotlight-340.jpg.headline: King-size kitten
windows-spotlight-340.jpg.description: Spot one cute, speckly lion cub like this one, and chances are there are more to be found. Lionesses usually have two to four cubs at a time, often banding together with other moms to form even larger groups called crèches. The crèche structure not only helps socialize cubs of the same age (they start at six weeks old and 'graduate' after about two years) but keeps them all in a safe place under watchful adult eyes. Think of it as day care for little lions.

windows-spotlight-341.jpg.title: Three-toed sloth clinging tree
windows-spotlight-341.jpg.headline: Born a tree hugger
windows-spotlight-341.jpg.description: If your ideal day involves snoozing and munching snacks, three-toed sloths can relate. They spend 15 to 20 hours a day sleeping, and even while awake they're the slowest mammal on dry land (well, sort of dry—this is a rainforest, after all). As for eating, sloths stick to a fairly bland diet of leaves, but thanks to their tough digestive systems and efficient use of energy, a low-nutrient diet is enough to do the job. Even so, a quick bite is rarely out of their long limbs' reach, since they spend most of their time up in the trees.

windows-spotlight-342.jpg.title: Indian Spot-billed Duck flapping
windows-spotlight-342.jpg.headline: Happy flapping
windows-spotlight-342.jpg.description: Though they're genetically similar to the mallards familiar all across the Northern Hemisphere, Indian spot-billed ducks stick to a smaller range. Still, these dabbling ducks are found throughout the entire Indian subcontinent, preferring to populate reedy wetlands instead of open water. Spot-bills lack the dimorphism of their mallard cousins, with both males and females marked by blue-green wing accents and (surprise, surprise) spot-tipped bills.

windows-spotlight-347.jpg.title: Tsingy Rouge, Madagascar
windows-spotlight-347.jpg.headline: It's a tsingy thing
windows-spotlight-347.jpg.description: The karst formations known by the Malagasy term 'tsingy' are found in multiple locations in Madagascar. But nowhere except here, near the island's northern tip, will you find them in these Mars-like colors. The Tsingy Rouge, or Red Tsingy, is formed from compressed, clay-rich earth that's been slowly eroded to form strange, shroudlike figures. Remarkable as it is, relatively few tourists visit the Tsingy Rouge—seeing it in person takes a four-wheel-drive vehicle and a penchant for hiking in dry, dusty heat.

windows-spotlight-349.jpg.title: Sumidero Canyon Green Cliffs, Chiapas, Mexico
windows-spotlight-349.jpg.headline: Less grand, more green
windows-spotlight-349.jpg.description: In geological terms, you can think of Sumidero Canyon as the Grand Canyon's fraternal twin: Though much different in size and appearance, it came into the world at nearly the same time. About 35 million years ago, while the Colorado River was carving grand gashes through the American Southwest, the Grijalva River was hard at work here in Chiapas, Mexico. The result is substantially shallower than the Grand Canyon at around 3,200 feet deep, but Sumidero Canyon makes up for that shortcoming with its friendlier climate (no hundred-degree desert slogs here!) and abundant greenery.

windows-spotlight-35.jpg.title: Irabu Ohashi Bridge, Miyakojima, Okinawa, Japan
windows-spotlight-35.jpg.headline: Bridge to paradise
windows-spotlight-35.jpg.description: The long bridges that connect one green gem to the next in this string of islands have made getting around easier, but travel writers note there is no crush of crowds in the Miyako Islands. That's good news for residents and visitors on the six major isles located in Japan's far southern Okinawa prefecture. The coastal waters here are remarkably transparent, and when the sun is shining (which is most of the time) it's hard to say which is brighter—the sea, the bright white sand, or the super-blue sky. These islands boast uncommon culinary treasures along with their natural splendor. One delicacy is 'umibudō' (sea grapes), a type of seaweed so delicately shaped and vividly colored that it’s been nicknamed 'green caviar.'

windows-spotlight-351.jpg.title: Growing Blue Ice Glacier, Water
windows-spotlight-351.jpg.headline: The growing glacier
windows-spotlight-351.jpg.description: It's hard to grasp the scale of this shot at first glance, but as the creeping clouds probably tipped you off, we're seeing something much larger than a half-frozen pond. To give you just an idea, the edges of that ice sheet rise 240 feet above the surface of Argentino Lake. Sail along the whole length of the sheer ice cliff and you'll have traveled more than 3 miles. And this is just the tip of the iceberg—er, glacier. Beyond this narrow end that feeds the 1,640-foot-deep lake, Perito Moreno Glacier covers almost 100 square miles. Even bigger news: Unlike most of Earth's glaciers, this ice giant is actually growing.
windows-spotlight-351.jpg.copyright: © Joseph Sohm; Visions of America/Corbis Documentary/Getty Images

windows-spotlight-355.jpg.title: Green Algae Volcanic Rock Formations, Laomei Green Reef, Taiwan
windows-spotlight-355.jpg.headline: Green today, gone tomorrow
windows-spotlight-355.jpg.description: As the tide drops and the fog rises, these ruffled ridges of hardened lava take on an unearthly look. But the effect is as ephemeral as the mists that slither through the stones: The algae that grows here each spring, putting the green in Laomei Green Reef, dies off in early summer. So if you want to catch this unique spectacle on Taiwan's northern tip, plan your visit between March and May, and keep an eye on the tidal charts.

windows-spotlight-359.jpg.title: Red, white, purple eroded sandstone cliffs, ocean, Morro Branco, Ceará, Brazil
windows-spotlight-359.jpg.headline: An imperiled paradise
windows-spotlight-359.jpg.description: The cliffs of reddish, sandy clay that rise above Morro Branco beach are beautiful, but not invincible. The parade of waves we see in the distance washes endlessly against the lower layers of the Beberibe Cliffs, while wind and rain batter the upper reaches. So whether through slow erosion or sudden landslips, this Brazilian natural monument is continually crumbling away. Add heavy foot traffic to the mix and it spells danger to humans and the landscape alike—so only guided tours are allowed to explore here.

windows-spotlight-361.jpg.title: Green forested mountain valley, snow-capped peaks, river, Hjelledalen, Norway
windows-spotlight-361.jpg.headline: Hill, dale, and Hjelledalen
windows-spotlight-361.jpg.description: This deep valley named Hjelledalen is just one example of the extreme topography you'll find in the county of Vestland. Centered around Norway's second city, Bergen, the county is carved with undulating fjords and winding valleys like this, bounded by steep and spectacular mountains. Hjelledalen lies just inland from the inner reaches of Nordfjorden: a 66-mile channel that nearly transects the whole county, ending not far from the Innlandet border.

windows-spotlight-363.jpg.title: Adélie penguins diving from iceberg, Antarctica
windows-spotlight-363.jpg.headline: Roly-poly divers
windows-spotlight-363.jpg.description: A small diving team of Adélie penguins is but a tiny fraction of Paulet Island's penguin population. This mass of land and ice off the Antarctic Peninsula is home to hundreds of thousands of the charming, curious creatures. Though small in stature (about 30 inches tall), Adélies are nonetheless known for their fearlessness. Visitors from early Antarctic explorers to modern cruise passengers have been delighted as flocks of the plucky penguins rush to greet them up close. During the fraught Scott expedition, the English chronicler Apsley Cherry-Garrard became an Adélie admirer, later writing fondly of the bird as 'an almost human friend.'

windows-spotlight-365.jpg.title: Two African Penguins, Rocky Coast, Sunset, Boulders Beach, Simon's Town, South Africa
windows-spotlight-365.jpg.headline: Hey there, neighbors
windows-spotlight-365.jpg.description: The hours between sunset and sunup are prime dining time for 3,000 of this residential area's denizens. So if you're lucky enough to live by this unique beach southeast of Cape Town, step out at twilight and see the neighbors. But you probably won't want to join them for a bite, unless whole raw fish is your fancy. That's right, African penguins and people practically live next door to each other here on the famed Boulders Beach. The arrangement is an exception made by these increasingly rare birds, most of which shun the mainland to breed on tiny islets along the South African and Namibian coasts. But the Boulders bunch seem content sticking around to delight tourists and locals alike.

windows-spotlight-368.jpg.title: Iridescent Green Hummingbird Nectar Feeding Pink Foxglove
windows-spotlight-368.jpg.headline: Humming along
windows-spotlight-368.jpg.description: The fiery-throated hummingbird is one of roughly 360 species of hummingbird worldwide, all of which are crucial to healthy ecosystems. Many flowers, like this hot pink foxglove, have evolved funnel-shaped blooms specifically to attract these fast flappers. While large insects like bumblebees can't always squeeze into the tubular blossoms, hummingbirds can plunge their long, narrow bills inside to feed on nectar that accumulates deep at the base. They spread pollen from flower to flower this way, enabling the plants to propagate, resulting in more tasty nectar. Now that's sustainable cuisine!

windows-spotlight-37.jpg.title: Three pelicans flying ocean waves golden hour
windows-spotlight-37.jpg.headline: Featherweight? Hardly.
windows-spotlight-37.jpg.description: As they flitter in a Florida sunrise, these seabirds seem lighter than air. But get them standing on a scale and it'll likely tip past 10 pounds, placing them well into the heavyweight category among avians. And they aren't afraid to throw that girth around: By plunging their big bird bodies into the surf, pelicans can stun fish that they swiftly scoop into their ample gullets. Once full, the birds can rest by floating on the waves, buoyed by air pockets in their bones that help keep all that weight above water.

windows-spotlight-370.jpg.title: Colorful lakeside village sunset, Varenna, Lake Como, Italy
windows-spotlight-370.jpg.headline: A vivid village
windows-spotlight-370.jpg.description: Put extra gas in your time machine if you want to get ahead of this lakeshore's tourism boom: The mild microclimate created by Lake Como has drawn posh throngs since ancient times. Imperial Roman bigwigs and Hollywood stars alike have relished the lake's pleasant ambience that reminds of the Mediterranean, even though we're roughly 100 miles from that great sea's ample warm air. Here at the edge of the Alps, warm weather is much more scarce, so properties set along northern Italy's humid subtropical lakes have always been hot items—like these dazzling buildings on the Varenna waterfront.

windows-spotlight-372.jpg.title: Beech forest sunset
windows-spotlight-372.jpg.headline: Meet the beech
windows-spotlight-372.jpg.description: Often growing up to 100 feet tall, beech trees have plenty of surface area for the sun to set alight. That's not the only way they can take on a fiery glow: Here in Germany, beech is considered one of the best sources of firewood. Smoke from its long-burning, gentle flames is the secret that flavors many German smoked beers, meats, and cheeses. So if you enjoy the local charcuterie's toasty notes, why not also visit a beech forest like this for a quick thanks?
windows-spotlight-372.jpg.copyright: © Design Pics/Radius Images/ Alamy Stock Photo

windows-spotlight-375.jpg.title: Le Morne Brabant Underwater Waterfall illusion, Mauritius
windows-spotlight-375.jpg.headline: This way to freedom
windows-spotlight-375.jpg.description: The Mauritian monolith known as Le Morne isn't just any tropical escape: There was a time in history when most who approached these shores were on the run from enslavement. In the 18th century, Le Morne was home to a refugee society of people who'd escaped the Dutch slave trade—one of many similar communities on Mauritius and islands all over the world. As a prominent symbol of the long struggle for freedom, Le Morne was named a Cultural Landscape by UNESCO in 2008.

windows-spotlight-377.jpg.title: Shaggy Valais Blacknose sheep, Matterhorn, Switzerland
windows-spotlight-377.jpg.headline: Shaggy sheep story
windows-spotlight-377.jpg.description: While the looming Matterhorn hides its nose in the clouds, snouts are about all we get to see of these sheep's faces. An all-covering coat of wool is essential when you call the windy Swiss foothills home, and the Valais Blacknose is well equipped to brave these slopes for a snack of alpine grass. A perseverant breed with six centuries of history here in southwestern Switzerland, the Blacknose has only recently been introduced abroad—to the United Kingdom in 2014 and North America in 2018. Between cuckoo clocks and these cuddly critters, could Switzerland be cornering the export market on cuteness?

windows-spotlight-379.jpg.title: Sunrise Fannette Island, Emerald Bay, Lake Tahoe
windows-spotlight-379.jpg.headline: The lonely island
windows-spotlight-379.jpg.description: You're looking at the only island on the whole surface of a lake that sits on the border of two US states and covers almost 520 square kilometres. Protected within California's Emerald Bay State Park, Fannette Island is the only bit of land that manages to breach the waters of Lake Tahoe. Most of the lake's topography is submerged in a basin that reaches down more than 500 metres. The exceptional depth means that Tahoe Tessie, a legendary lake monster supposedly seen in these parts, has 150 cubic kilometres of water to explore here in the USA's most voluminous lake barring the Great Lakes.

windows-spotlight-380.jpg.title: Giant's Causeway basalt columns sunset, Northern Ireland
windows-spotlight-380.jpg.headline: Polygon patch
windows-spotlight-380.jpg.description: If you're a geometry buff looking for a break outdoors, we've found the place for you. Here at the Giant's Causeway, you'll find not only a great abundance of hexagons, but squares, octagons, pentagons and even a handful of heptagons. Numbering around 40,000 and arranged in tumbling terraces, the Causeway's polygonal shapes showcase the signature columnar jointing of some types of igneous rock—in this case basalt. As lava flows cooled to form this rocky coast 60 million years ago, stress fractures followed the shortest distance between two points to create tight, uniform shapes. It's a pattern found all over the world, but this Northern Ireland landmark is probably the best-known example, drawing about a million visitors a year.

windows-spotlight-382.jpg.title: Humpback Whale breaching
windows-spotlight-382.jpg.headline: Busting a big move
windows-spotlight-382.jpg.description: Disko Bay isn't just for Saturday night fever: Humpback whales are ready to boogie any day of the week. These iceberg-dotted waters off western Greenland are a popular pit stop for humpbacks, which migrate thousands of miles a year between chill zones like this and hotspots in the tropics. The best time to see these big mammals hit the Disko dance floor? That'd be just after the sea ice melts in late spring, bringing tasty plankton and tiny fish to the warming surface for the whales to gobble en masse.

windows-spotlight-384.jpg.title: Valle de las Animas, La Paz, Bolivia
windows-spotlight-384.jpg.headline: Backyard badlands
windows-spotlight-384.jpg.description: One does not simply walk into Mordor, but luckily, this similarly spiky landscape is a pretty easy amble from one of South America's great cities. The Valle de las Animas, or Valley of the Souls, towers just outside the eastern neighborhoods of La Paz, Bolivia, beckoning outdoorsy urbanites to explore its deep gorges and lofty overlooks. The valley's ethereal name comes from either the ghostly wailing sound that wind through the rocks makes, or from the shape of the formations, said to resemble crowds of lost spirits wandering the wilderness.

windows-spotlight-385.jpg.title: Night urban highway interchange light trails
windows-spotlight-385.jpg.headline: Transit tangle
windows-spotlight-385.jpg.description: Reliant on roads cut well before cars were commonplace, Bangkok was infamous in the mid-20th century for its colossal traffic jams. An ever-expanding road system has succeeded in speeding the flow over decades, with twisting and turning freeways adding to the Thai capital's increasingly futuristic look. Of course, this Southeast Asian hub hasn't fully conquered its congestion conundrum. With more than 10 million motor vehicles in Bangkok today—eight times more than the roads are rated for—jam-ups are still a fact of life here.

windows-spotlight-387.jpg.title: Golden Autumn Arctic Mountains Conifer Forest
windows-spotlight-387.jpg.headline: An arctic expanse
windows-spotlight-387.jpg.description: The mighty Brooks Range marks a 700-mile-long continental drainage divide in North America's far northern reaches. Here, rivers running north empty into the Arctic Ocean, while those running south flow into the Yukon River. This remote massif is estimated to be 126 million years old and contains a rich fossil record of the ancient seabed it once was. Found among the tundra and stands of spruce trees are fossilized corals from the Cambrian period. The mountains also teem with living wildlife, with a portion of the range lying within the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.

windows-spotlight-389.jpg.title: Sea Stacks, Ocean Waves, Dusk Sky, Uradome Coast, Tottori, Japan
windows-spotlight-389.jpg.headline: A staggering sea scene
windows-spotlight-389.jpg.description: The sharp-edged sea stacks of Pegadung speak to an intense tectonic history here on Sumatra, the largest island within Indonesia and one of Earth's most volcanic places. Its mountainous spine still includes nearly 70 active volcanoes, stretching more than a thousand miles from the Strait of Malacca in the north to these craggy shores in the south. Rivaling the massive isle's wild geology is its biology: Sumatra boasts unique types of elephant, rhinoceros, tiger, and orangutan.

windows-spotlight-39.jpg.title: Crags Vineyard Blooming Trees Golden Hour
windows-spotlight-39.jpg.headline: Crags meet agriculture
windows-spotlight-39.jpg.description: The limestone that lines Catalonia's coast is even more abundant inland, forming bold shapes such as the Roques de Benet. These castle-like formations are considered icons of this autonomous community of Spain—as are the two crops arrayed before us. Neat vineyard rows, still foliage-free as spring unfolds, point the way to a grove of blossoming almond trees. Tinted to a marzipan tone by the setting sun, the bloom will soon give way to a multitude of snack-size fruits—likely the coveted Marcona variety, which originated right here in Catalonia.

windows-spotlight-391.jpg.title: Okavango River Wetland Sunset, Botswana
windows-spotlight-391.jpg.headline: Okavango flow
windows-spotlight-391.jpg.description: From the Nile to the Mississippi to the Mekong, most famous river deltas empty into an ocean. The Okavango Delta, though its splitting streams still take a familiar triangle shape, is instead ultimately swallowed by the deep, dry Kalahari desert. But before reaching their endorheic endpoints, the Okavango's streams hydrate vast blankets of greenspace. During the rainy season, wetlands and waterways laze over 5,800 square miles of Botswana flatland, creating habitat for a host of endangered species.

windows-spotlight-393.jpg.title: Wooden pier, cloud reflections, Lake Prespa
windows-spotlight-393.jpg.headline: One lake, three nations
windows-spotlight-393.jpg.description: The tripoint of North Macedonia, Albania, and Greece lies on the surface of Great Prespa Lake, the larger of two lofty, interconnected lakes that are among the biggest, highest, and oldest in the Balkans. While shared by three nations, Great and Little Prespa Lake have a wildlife profile all their own, hosting no fewer than nine endemic fish species. Other creatures thrive in this rich, remote environment as well, including a unique freshwater sponge and several varieties of migratory marine birds.

windows-spotlight-394.jpg.title: Climbing tawny lion cub on log
windows-spotlight-394.jpg.headline: Climber cub
windows-spotlight-394.jpg.description: The most famous tree-climbing lions live in Uganda, but it seems this intrepid cub is looking to bring the pastime to Zambia. Though as adults they'll be fearsome hunters, lion cubs are prime targets for other predators like hyenas and leopards. So when it comes to finding safe hiding spots, whether up on a tree limb or burrowed in the bushes, the craftier the cub the better. After all, though their mothers (and other lionesses in the pride) care for them until about age 2, young cubs are often left unattended for a full day at a time as their parental figures go out on the prowl.

windows-spotlight-395.jpg.title: Mirrored Massif, Autumn Forest Lake, Pink Sky
windows-spotlight-395.jpg.headline: A mirrored massif
windows-spotlight-395.jpg.description: Any season is a fine time to visit the Italian Alps, but autumn might just be the best. This time of year, peaks are beautifully dusted in snow, while lower elevations have yet to fully settle into winter's chill. That means alpine lakes like Lower Lake Fusine, shown here, can still offer mirrorlike reflections of the rocky ranges. Our backdrop is a massif that includes the high point known as Mangart, which marks the border with Slovenia and is that nation's third-highest summit.

windows-spotlight-396.jpg.title: Golden Jixian Pavilion Sunset, West Lake, Hangzhou
windows-spotlight-396.jpg.headline: Perfect harmony
windows-spotlight-396.jpg.description: With seemingly numberless gardens, ornaments, artificial islands, and pagoda-style pavilions like this one, West Lake (also called Xi Lake) is hailed as one of the most beautiful sights in China. A symbol of the city of Hangzhou, just southwest of Shanghai, the lake formed from a gulf that was cut off from the sea as sediment washed down from the adjacent mountains. Then, over thousands of years and more than a dozen dynasties, engineers further altered the lake's layout by adding dams, wells, and causeways. Innovative garden designs helped harmonize the artificial changes with nature, and techniques developed here centuries ago influenced horticulture across Asia, earning West Lake a spot on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

windows-spotlight-397.jpg.title: Cuernos del Paine two-tone rocky peaks, golden light, Torres del Paine National Park, Patagonia, Chile
windows-spotlight-397.jpg.headline: Rocking the two-tone look
windows-spotlight-397.jpg.description: Here in Chilean Patagonia, mountains like the Cuernos del Paine are often shrouded in mist. But the clouds cleared and the sun hit just right for the fortunate photographer who snapped this shot, offering us a peek at these peaks' unique geology.Ancient glaciers stripped much of this mountain chain to its granite bones. You can see this granite exposed in the broad, light-colored stripe across the base of the Cuernos ('horns'). But the glaciers spared the peaks' caps, leaving dark patches of sedimentary rock. Geologists call this feature a 'roof pendant'—we call it the crown on a majestic massif.

windows-spotlight-399.jpg.title: Lupine Meadow, Snow-capped Mountains, Alpenglow, San Juan Mountains, Colorado
windows-spotlight-399.jpg.headline: Hinterland hues
windows-spotlight-399.jpg.description: Dolly Parton sang that 'wildflowers don't care where they grow,' but we think these purple lupines would opine that Colorado beats out other potential potting locales.  During July and August, visitors here will find rocky cliffs, streams, unique rock formations, and some spectacular blossoms. And not only the purple lupine that dominates this shot outside Silverthorne, but also Rocky Mountain columbine (Colorado's state flower), elephant's head, Parry's primrose, and marsh marigold. Bring us back a bouquet, OK?

windows-spotlight-400.jpg.title: Illuminated log cabin, snow-covered mountains, winter forest, Lake Louise
windows-spotlight-400.jpg.headline: Lovely Lake Louise
windows-spotlight-400.jpg.description: It takes a special something to achieve fame as a Canadian lake: the Great White North has more than 800,000 of them. Lake Louise, with its crystal waters that mirror Banff National Park's majestic mountains, manages to rise above the crowd. Photographers flock here during all seasons to snap this stunner. And when the weather warms up, the boathouse ahead will open for business renting canoes—so you can paddle out for an even better angle.

windows-spotlight-402.jpg.title: Puducherry Promenade Pier, Sunset Long Exposure Ocean, Puducherry, India
windows-spotlight-402.jpg.headline: A 'bridge' to the sea
windows-spotlight-402.jpg.description: Ponte dos Ingleses, or the Bridge of the English, is named for the British architects who designed it. This landmark of Fortaleza, Brazil, is really a pier, not a bridge—inspired by Brighton Pier back on the designers' native isle. Atlantic waves have battered it for more than a century, sometimes leaving it in disrepair for lengthy stretches of time. But in its long history it's been put to several uses, including as a lookout during World War II.

windows-spotlight-405.jpg.title: Spotted Whale Shark
windows-spotlight-405.jpg.headline: Whale or shark?
windows-spotlight-405.jpg.description: The idea of a 15-ton, 40-foot fish might be a bit freaky, especially when that fish is a shark. But humans have nothing to fear from the biggest non-mammalian swimmer in the ocean. It's one of just a few shark species that, rather than chomping large prey with fierce fangs, use their gaping mouths to filter plankton and small sea life into their gullets. It's this gentle nature, and of course gargantuan size, that lends this not-so-monstrous sea monster its name: the whale shark.

windows-spotlight-407.jpg.title: Yellow canola field with farm buildings and blue sky
windows-spotlight-407.jpg.headline: Holy canola
windows-spotlight-407.jpg.description: Sweden's color palette tends to be dominated by green in the summer and white in the winter. So where's all the yellow coming from? This canary-colored field is full of canola, a common crop here in the country's south whose buttery blossoms pop open every May. When the plains turn to gold, you know it's not long until summer, when the sun will brighten this countryside well into the night.

windows-spotlight-409.jpg.title: Rocce Rosse sunset, Arbatax
windows-spotlight-409.jpg.headline: Ancient Arbatax
windows-spotlight-409.jpg.description: Sardinia's fewer than 10,000 square miles are outlined by over a thousand miles of towering sea cliffs and tide pools teeming with life. The Italian island's coasts, though largely rocky rather than beachy, still draw a sizeable faction of tourists awed by impossibly ancient landmarks like the Red Rocks of Arbatax. These spectacular porphyry pillars are just one product of Sardinia's once-violent geology that dates back 500 million years. But it seems the sunny isle got all that moving and shaking out of its system: Today, it's one of the few regions of Italy not susceptible to earthquakes.

windows-spotlight-41.jpg.title: Boreal Forest River
windows-spotlight-41.jpg.headline: Boreal beauty
windows-spotlight-41.jpg.description: A back-and-forth rivalry may linger between Quebec and its Old World cousin France, but if size is the game, there's no contest. Wild and woody Quebec is about three times the area of Metropolitan France—or to put it in American terms, triple the size of Texas. Within its nearly 600,000 square miles, you'll find more than half a million lakes and thousands of rivers, accounting for 3% of Earth's fresh water. When not caked in snow, most of the province's upper reaches resemble this scene, being part of Canada's vast, evergreen boreal forest.

windows-spotlight-413.jpg.title: Fitz Roy massif red peaks Laguna de los Tres sunrise, Patagonia, Argentina
windows-spotlight-413.jpg.headline: An icon illuminated
windows-spotlight-413.jpg.description: Hot pink and deep blue complete a complex palette for one of Patagonia's foremost peaks. As a sizzling sunrise lights up Monte Fitz Roy, Laguna de los Tres appears like a frosted mirror, awaiting the sun's rays. Looking west toward this Argentine national icon, we'll see its multiple summits reflected perfectly on the frigid water once midday light washes the landscape.

windows-spotlight-415.jpg.title: Stout seal on sandy beach
windows-spotlight-415.jpg.headline: A stout seal
windows-spotlight-415.jpg.description: From the Wash in the west to the Winterton Dunes out east, the Norfolk Coast stretches about 90 miles along the top of East Anglia. The gently curving coast plays host to beachgoers from all over Britain and beyond each summer, but here we see a more permanent resident. Less common but larger than their harbor seal cousins, gray seals like this well-fed juvenile are a frequent sight upon the cold seas of Northern Europe. A gray seal colony on Blakeney Point, a shingle spit right here in Norfolk where over 3,000 pups are born per year, is the biggest single-site pinniped population in England.

windows-spotlight-417.jpg.title: Golden Gate Bridge Beach Sunset, San Francisco
windows-spotlight-417.jpg.headline: State of nature
windows-spotlight-417.jpg.description: We're strolling north on San Francisco's Baker Beach for a quintessential California view. Here in the northwest of town, Pacific waves wash the sands with vigor, in contrast to the calmer waters of San Francisco Bay. If the bay side's more your speed, it's about a mile's walk straight ahead to the Golden Gate Bridge, which separates open ocean from sheltered haven. Fair warning, though: North Baker Beach is clothing-optional, so you might see more of the locals than expected as you pass by.

windows-spotlight-418.jpg.title: Three wooly sheep, mossy ground, foggy cliffs, Iceland
windows-spotlight-418.jpg.headline: A wooly welcoming committee
windows-spotlight-418.jpg.description: Overlaid with a thick fleece of moss and sporting stone outcrops that look like horns, the landscape here matches its inhabitants. Double-coated for warmth (and exceptional shagginess), Icelandic sheep are well equipped to thrive on the cold, windswept island they've called home ever since Vikings brought them here a millennium ago. During summer, Icelandic sheep are traditionally left out to wander and graze freely in rugged settings like this. The sheep are then gathered each September in an event called a rettir. In this festive effort by farming families, sheep are tracked far and wide on horseback, sorted with the help of sheepdogs, and returned safely to their homesteads.

windows-spotlight-420.jpg.title: Coastal Rocks, Foaming Ocean Waves, Sunset, Galicia, Spain
windows-spotlight-420.jpg.headline: Glorious Galicia
windows-spotlight-420.jpg.description: Misty and mild in contrast to the semi-arid interior, this section of Spain has a similar climate to Britain, New Zealand, or the Pacific Northwest. Though that means sunbathing isn't often on the bingo card in Galicia, the beach offers beautiful views of the jagged granite coastline and open Atlantic beyond. Indeed, watching the seas is something of an industry here: Galicia's coast boasts 44 lighthouses across its many inlets and islets.

windows-spotlight-421.jpg.title: Dry Desert Sand Dune, Rock Formations, Atacama Desert, Chile
windows-spotlight-421.jpg.headline: Dry, dry desert
windows-spotlight-421.jpg.description: Though it boasts more than 600 miles of coastline upon a vast, misty ocean, Chile's Atacama Desert is the driest place on Earth (besides certain snowless spots in Antarctica). Here in the Valle de la Luna (Valley of the Moon), wind-whipped dunes loom large along the shore, and the inland flats are dotted with dry salt lakes. But despite the desolation, it's a place of understated beauty. The lack of light pollution offers some of the world's best stargazing, and the landscape is dotted by petroglyphs—from small to gargantuan—that prove ancient peoples also learned to love this unique patch of land.
windows-spotlight-421.jpg.copyright: © David Rius 和 Núria Tuca/Moment/Getty Images

windows-spotlight-423.jpg.title: Curled hedgehog, green foliage, yellow flowers
windows-spotlight-423.jpg.headline: Hogging the spotlight
windows-spotlight-423.jpg.description: It'd be awfully tempting to cuddle this cute little critter, spines and all, but we'd better let this wild hog be. If you're lucky enough to live in the parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe where hedgehogs roam natively, finding one in your flowerbed can be a great sign. Hedgehogs snuffle through underbrush to feed on insects and other tiny pests, helping to keep plants healthy. Startle one while it's scavenging and you'll see it roll into a defensive ball like this—though since hedgehogs also sleep curled up, it's just as likely we woke this one from a nap.

windows-spotlight-424.jpg.title: Stone Sentry Granite Formation, Golden Hour, La Maddalena Archipelago, Sardinia, Italy
windows-spotlight-424.jpg.headline: A stone sentry
windows-spotlight-424.jpg.description: Overlooking the sea from more than 350 feet up, this pocked rock formation is named for the fierce creature it's said to resemble. Sailors since at least the days of Homer have valued Roccia dell'Orso (Bear Rock) as a navigation aid in rounding Sardinia's northern tip. From a distance, the 'bear' appears as a watchful guardian over the sea. Up close, its heavily eroded form proves that just like passing ships, this stone sentry is at the winds' and waters' mercy.

windows-spotlight-425.jpg.title: Blue Black-naped Monarch
windows-spotlight-425.jpg.headline: Birdie of blue
windows-spotlight-425.jpg.description: When it comes to flying creatures, the title of 'monarch' conjures the image of a butterfly, but that iconic insect isn't the only king on the wing. Instead of the monarch butterfly's blazing orange, the male black-naped monarch boasts brilliant baby blue feathers—the better to gain the lady birds' attention. Therein lies another big difference between bug and bird: While both sexes of monarch butterfly display similar color schemes, black-naped monarchs are dimorphic, with females featuring gray-blue heads and brownish wings.

windows-spotlight-427.jpg.title: Paved road to Fitz Roy Massif sunset, Patagonia
windows-spotlight-427.jpg.headline: A dramatic drive
windows-spotlight-427.jpg.description: In these parts, the scenic route is the only route. Follow it to its end and you'll find yourself in El Chaltén, a former frontier town in the highlands of Patagonia. This tiny Argentinian community is much like those found in foothills all over the world, with plenty of hippie vibes and passion for the outdoors to go around. Most folks here come and go, drawn by seasonal work and world-class hiking and climbing in Los Glaciares National Park. But about 1,600 stalwart souls hold down the fort year-round, kept under watch by Cerro Torre (the finger-like crag at left) and Monte Fitz Roy (the mighty mountain on the right).

windows-spotlight-43.jpg.title: Blue-footed Booby, Galápagos Islands, Ecuador
windows-spotlight-43.jpg.headline: Fishies beware
windows-spotlight-43.jpg.description: Its name and appearance may come off a bit silly, but when it comes to angling, this stocky seabird means serious business. When a soaring blue-footed booby spots a school of tasty fish from as high as 300 feet, it swoops into a plummeting nosedive before slamming the water's surface at 60 miles an hour. Even deep swimmers aren't safe: Boobies are able to dive around 80 feet to scoop their squirming prey, whose nutrients help pigment the birds' bright blue dancing shoes.

windows-spotlight-431.jpg.title: The case of the lost stones
windows-spotlight-431.jpg.headline: The case of the lost stones
windows-spotlight-431.jpg.description: This monument is known as Nine Stones Close, so why are there only four stones here? Six of the original nine are accounted for: the four seen here upon a bright British dawn, a fifth serving unceremoniously as a fencepost close by, and another found lying flat in an adjacent field. As for what became of the last three (or possibly even more), that's a mystery lost to history.Nine Stones Close is one of many small stone circles found around Derbyshire, England. Like its partial disappearance, its purpose remains mysterious. We have some clues: The stones are etched with markings seen on other Bronze Age artifacts, and their placement seems to trace the setting moon to the nearby Robin Hood's Stride. But the stones' true significance to a prehistoric society—ritual, astronomical, or otherwise—may never be known.

windows-spotlight-433.jpg.title: Grizzly Bear Fishing River Mountains
windows-spotlight-433.jpg.headline: Gone fishing
windows-spotlight-433.jpg.description: There are more than 2,000 grizzlies living in this wilderness on the Alaska Peninsula and each adult can swell to more than 450 kilograms. That's a lot of weight for Katmai National Park to bear, especially when you add the nearly 40,000 humans who visited the Brooks River each year as it swells with countless salmon. Bears can be spotted fishing for their fill along the river in the summer and autumn, gorging on sockeye to fatten up for hibernation. Good news, you don't have to trek all the way to Alaska to observe them—you can get a great view of the feeding frenzy via webcam.

windows-spotlight-434.jpg.title: Island with autumn trees, clear turquoise lake, Eibsee, Bavaria, Germany
windows-spotlight-434.jpg.headline: Busy lake, silent island
windows-spotlight-434.jpg.description: Nestled in the Alps near Germany's highest peak, the elevated lake called the Eibsee is often abustle with visitors. Hikers and beachgoers flock to enjoy the natural splendor, while one of the world's longest tramways draws crowds looking to head higher up the slopes. See the Eibsee from the right angle, though, and the lake's potential for serenity becomes as clear as its emerald waters. Undeveloped islets like this one, Ludwig Island, dot the water's surface near the northern shore—beckoning paddlers and adventurous swimmers for a break from the busy mainland.

windows-spotlight-435.jpg.title: Red dunes, blue lagoons, Shark Bay, Western Australia, Australia
windows-spotlight-435.jpg.headline: Red dunes, blue lagoons
windows-spotlight-435.jpg.description: Next to the open waters of Shark Bay, green streams and blue lagoons ripple amid deep red dunes in Francois Peron National Park, one of several protected areas upon the bay. In the tinted bedrock below the dunes, cut-out cave shelters offer proof of Aboriginal peoples' long history fishing and shellfishing the rich bay (known in the Malgana tongue as Gutharraguda, or 'two waters'). Just offshore, something even older sways in the waves: The bay's seagrass fields are one huge clonal plant, sprouted millennia ago from a single seed and now considered the largest organism on Earth.

windows-spotlight-436.jpg.title: Ama Dablam snow peak, Nepal
windows-spotlight-436.jpg.headline: 22,349 feet high and rising
windows-spotlight-436.jpg.description: With its steep, sharp summit, Ama Dablam has been called the 'Matterhorn of the Himalayas.' But in terms of height, the Alpine icon hardly rivals it: Ama Dablam is more than 7,000 feet higher. Here in the world's tallest mountain range, though, it's barely a contender at 22,349 feet—more than 100 of its neighbors rise well past the 23,000 mark. And they're not even fully grown yet: Due to gradual activity in the faults that formed them, the Himalayas rise in elevation almost an inch a year.

windows-spotlight-437.jpg.title: Moai statues, grassy hillside, Easter Island, Chile
windows-spotlight-437.jpg.headline: Face facts
windows-spotlight-437.jpg.description: Roam the tiny, remote Rapa Nui (aka Easter Island) and you'll find almost a thousand of the stern stone faces called moai. Exactly how the statues were made and why are still open questions—but it's known that the many visages represent the ancestors of the Rapa Nui people, some of whose descendants still live on this isle more than 1,200 miles from any other settlement. The moai may seem older than these grassy hills and maybe even a little alien, but they were actually sculpted between 500 and 800 years ago from compacted volcanic ash that's as terrestrial as it comes.

windows-spotlight-438.jpg.title: Tropical beach sunset with palm trees, ocean waves, Angola
windows-spotlight-438.jpg.headline: Angola goals
windows-spotlight-438.jpg.description: The capital of Angola and home to a third of the country's people, Luanda is rapidly growing and modernizing. But some parts of this African metro area remain relatively undeveloped. Situated on a long sand spit not far from the city, Mussolo is a getaway enjoyed by locals and visitors alike. While the rough and windy Atlantic side of the spit is less visited, sheltered beaches on the bay side are popular for seaside dining, swimming, and nature viewing.
windows-spotlight-438.jpg.copyright: © Kostadin Luchansky - Angola Image Bank/Moment/Getty Images

windows-spotlight-440.jpg.title: Houseboats, Historic Buildings, Canal, Bare Trees, Dusk, Oud-West, Amsterdam
windows-spotlight-440.jpg.headline: A wander in Oud-West
windows-spotlight-440.jpg.description: Dense with dens of vice and fine dining alike, Amsterdam's canal-woven city center offers more than plenty. But if you ask us, any visit to the Dutch capital should venture beyond the Singelgracht: A whole patchwork of diverse neighborhoods awaits. In nearby sectors like Oud-West, where waterways are spaced wider and city blocks surround gardens and green strips, tourists can mingle with locals at a lower-key pace. Venture further west and you'll discover large greenspaces like Vondelpark and Rembrandtpark, bounded by planned cityscapes inspired by the garden city movement.

windows-spotlight-441.jpg.title: Village Weaver on acacia branch
windows-spotlight-441.jpg.headline: An avian artisan
windows-spotlight-441.jpg.description: Native to sub-Saharan Africa (our friend here is pictured in Uganda), the village weaver has been introduced to places as far-flung as Puerto Rico, Portugal, and Mauritius, to name a few. This male specimen is distinguished by his black head and wings: females' crowns are yellow and their wing markings less pronounced. The bird gets its name from its delicately woven, teardrop-shaped nests that are suspended from tree branches, with 'villages' of numerous nests often clustered in a single tree.
windows-spotlight-441.jpg.copyright: © Queen Elizabeth National Park, Uganda/Adobe Stock

windows-spotlight-443.jpg.title: Three Snow Monkeys Snuggling
windows-spotlight-443.jpg.headline: Simian snuggles
windows-spotlight-443.jpg.description: This snuggling trio of young Japanese macaques—aka snow monkeys—may have a touch of frost in their fur, but this spot has just the cure for winter chills. When the weather outside is frightful, snow monkeys of all ages descend from the forest and soak in the hot springs, known as onsen, found here at Jigokudani Monkey Park. It's said that in the 1960s, someone tossed an apple to a monkey who then chased it into an onsen. Rather than bound back out, the monkey stayed put for a steamy soak, and since its fellows followed suit, generations of these simians have been hooked on spa days.

windows-spotlight-444.jpg.title: Orange Red Sunset Beach Reflection
windows-spotlight-444.jpg.headline: Sunset-scorched shores
windows-spotlight-444.jpg.description: The Iberian Peninsula's northern coast is widely known as Green Spain, its rainy climate and lush woods more reminiscent of Britain than Barcelona. But sometimes you'll find its beaches awash in decidedly hotter tones. The sunset isn't all you'll find sizzling here in the Basque Country: In this unique autonomous community, coal-fire grills glow late into the night, adding delicious char to traditional dishes of seared meat and fish.

windows-spotlight-445.jpg.title: Two Baby Grey Squirrels in Tree Hollow
windows-spotlight-445.jpg.headline: Home in a hollow
windows-spotlight-445.jpg.description: An adorable pair of baby gray squirrels squeeze from their hidey-hole high in a tree to say hi to the camera. Squirrel pups live a high-rise lifestyle from the start, usually nesting about 20 feet above the forest floor. While many squirrels build large, raggedy stick nests, others save the assembly step by simply finding a hollowed-out spot in a tree—whether bored by a woodpecker or naturally formed like this one.

windows-spotlight-447.jpg.title: Green Sea Turtle underwater
windows-spotlight-447.jpg.headline: Turtle time
windows-spotlight-447.jpg.description: The green sea turtle is among the largest of the seven sea turtle species, with some reaching 5 feet in length and weighing 700 pounds. They live throughout the world's subtropical waters, and like other sea turtles, they migrate long distances for food—but will return to hatch their own eggs on the same select nesting beaches where they were born. This turtle was spotted swimming in its Great Barrier Reef habitat near Lady Elliot Island, a coral cay that's a key nesting site for both green sea turtles and less bulky loggerheads.

windows-spotlight-449.jpg.title: Santorini caldera islands, Greece
windows-spotlight-449.jpg.headline: Remains of Atlantis?
windows-spotlight-449.jpg.description: This Pegasus'-eye view of Santorini, Greece, is one of countless finely detailed images available in the Microsoft Planetary Computer. This vast, cloud-powered database lets scientists see a whole timeline of crisp satellite captures and environmental data for any location in the world. By analyzing this data, scientists can explore better ways to manage land and water resources, combat climate change, and prepare for natural disasters. All hot topics here in Santorini, whose distinct arc shape resulted from a volcanic eruption some 3,600 years ago—a disaster for the Minoan culture that possibly gave us the Atlantis legend.

windows-spotlight-45.jpg.title: Lindos Acropolis Sunset, Rhodes
windows-spotlight-45.jpg.headline: Rhodes to ruins
windows-spotlight-45.jpg.description: The acropolis of Lindos may be only the second-most famous ancient Greek marvel to grace the isle of Rhodes, but it has the advantage of still existing. Unlike the Colossus of Rhodes—a Wonder of the Ancient World raised here in 280 BCE, only for an earthquake to topple it in just half a century—much of the ruined acropolis remains standing. That includes structures predating the Colossus, like the columns of the Temple of Athena Lindia seen here.

windows-spotlight-450.jpg.title: Sea cow underwater
windows-spotlight-450.jpg.headline: A sea cow's close-up
windows-spotlight-450.jpg.description: Enter a staring match with a curious manatee if you want, but don't challenge these "sea cows" in a bulkiness contest. Despite their balloonish appearance as they float through shallow seawater, Florida manatees can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms and reach almost 4 metres long.Manatees were a rarity in Florida as recently as 50 years ago after boat collisions and habitat destruction nearly drove them to extinction. Since being listed for protection under the Endangered Species Act, the seagoing mammals have managed to rebound, being upgraded to "threatened" in 2017, (still not a great title, but it's an improvement).

windows-spotlight-452.jpg.title: Illuminated Old Town harbor, Rovinj, Croatia
windows-spotlight-452.jpg.headline: An Old Town aglow
windows-spotlight-452.jpg.description: Streetlights brighten the byways and plazas of this pleasant peninsula-on-a-peninsula-on-a-peninsula. Rovinj, Croatia, is encircled by the mild Adriatic Sea on the west coast of Istria, a large peninsula jutting off the much larger Balkan Peninsula. Perusing the Old Town's many streets and alleys, you'll hear chitchat in Croatian, a bit of Italian, and maybe even a smidge of Istriot—a now-rare Romance language once widely spoken in this diverse region of Europe.
windows-spotlight-452.jpg.copyright: © Vicki Jauron, Babylon and Beyond Photography/Moment/Getty Images

windows-spotlight-454.jpg.title: Pink Flamingos, Pink Lake, Desert Mountains
windows-spotlight-454.jpg.headline: Party in pink
windows-spotlight-454.jpg.description: The flamingo is a balanced bird—literally and figuratively. Not only does it sleep standing on one leg, it strikes that perfect mix of elegance and goofiness that makes it one of our most beloved avians.Flamingos come in six different species found all around the world. Most if not all the flamingos in this flamboyance (yes, that's what they call a group of flamingos) are Andean flamingos. They'll trawl the shallow lakes here in Bolivia and other high Andes countries throughout the summer, making snacks of small fish and microorganisms like diatoms. Each winter, these lakes evaporate into desiccated salt flats, leaving the birds high and dry—but no worries: Andean flamingos are migratory, able to travel hundreds of miles a day in search of a feast.

windows-spotlight-456.jpg.title: Hawksbill sea turtle with school of fish over coral reef
windows-spotlight-456.jpg.headline: A hawksbill says hi
windows-spotlight-456.jpg.description: Hawksbill sea turtles might be the most photogenic of the world's many shell-dwellers. Even if you can't get a nice sunny shot like this, hawksbills are the only reptiles known to biofluoresce, showing off their elegant shape and ornate, pearly shells even in benthic darkness. That's where you'll often find them, raking the seafloor for sponges (a hawksbill staple that's toxic to most other creatures), using the sharp beaks they get their name from. Though habitat destruction and the tortoiseshell trade has left them endangered, today these unique turtles are the subject of recovery plans by conservation and wildlife management agencies worldwide. So watch your six, Mr. SquarePants, because these sponge-munchers could be due for a comeback.

windows-spotlight-457.jpg.title: Pink Chrysanthemum
windows-spotlight-457.jpg.headline: Petals of pink
windows-spotlight-457.jpg.description: If you visit this quirky outpost in the Pacific Northwest, you'll be stunned by the flora. Though not native to the area, pink dahlias like this one join the countless flower species accenting Portland's eternal greenery. As you revel in the vast assortment of blossoms, don't forget to stop and smell the local favourite. Portland is known as the City of Roses (among other quirky nicknames), with its misty winters and dry, sunny summers creating the ideal rose-growing climate. As well as the Portland Rose Festival, it's home to the International Rose Test Garden, a centre of rose research where 600 varieties bloom each June on a staggering 10,000 bushes. Trust us, it's worth the thorns!

windows-spotlight-460.jpg.title: Blue Crested Black Palm Cockatoo
windows-spotlight-460.jpg.headline: How do you do, cockatoo?
windows-spotlight-460.jpg.description: Icons of the bush and protected by federal law, red-tailed black cockatoos are beloved across their native Australia, but perhaps most of all in the state of Western Australia. Annually since 2009, hundreds of Aussies from the region have volunteered for the Great Cocky Count—a wonderful example of citizen science during which volunteers observe and tally cockatoos at sunset on a selected day. This single-serving census gives researchers a large pool of data gathered from hundreds of distinct roost sites, which they can put together to help track populations year after year.

windows-spotlight-463.jpg.title: Ama Dablam snow-capped peak, Glacial lake, Nepal
windows-spotlight-463.jpg.headline: 'Mother's necklace'
windows-spotlight-463.jpg.description: Only about 7 miles from the summit of Everest, the spire seen here is a common sight for those climbing the world's highest mountain. Ama Dablam's name means 'mother's necklace' in Nepali, referring to traditional pendants worn by local Sherpa women—though the mountain's swooping shape is also said to resemble a mother cradling a child. Easily identified by its picture-perfect pyramidal peak, Ama Dablam is one of the great landmarks of Sagarmatha National Park (but topped, of course, by the park's namesake).

windows-spotlight-466.jpg.title: Red Panda
windows-spotlight-466.jpg.headline: A panda apart
windows-spotlight-466.jpg.description: This critter feels most at home up in the trees, but its precise place on the mammal family tree is still debated by biologists. The red panda shares a name (and bamboo diet) with the giant panda, but gene studies have suggested a tighter evolutionary link with mustelids like weasels and skunks. In any case, the red panda remains alone in the Ailuridae family—but that could change. Some researchers think the Himalayan highlands' red pandas are distinct enough from those in southwest China (like our bushy-bodied buddy here) to be another species. Hey, why not? Cute deserves company.

windows-spotlight-467.jpg.title: Benagil Cave Skylight, Algarve, Portugal
windows-spotlight-467.jpg.headline: A skylit sanctum
windows-spotlight-467.jpg.description: Had your fill of all that sunshine on the Algarve coast? From the beach at Benagil you can hire a boat, pilot your own kayak, or—if you're really adventurous—swim out to the fantastic sea caves carved into the rocks just offshore. The Atlantic Ocean has been working on the architecture here for a very long time indeed. Visitors to this exquisitely rugged part of the Portuguese coastline are treated to surreally textured rock stacks, weathered pinnacles, and cavernous limestone 'rooms' carpeted by soft sand and surrounded by turquoise waters.

windows-spotlight-468.jpg.title: Fort Canning Park Tree Tunnel, Singapore
windows-spotlight-468.jpg.headline: Tunnel to the trees
windows-spotlight-468.jpg.description: Things are looking up for Singapore. Powered by one of the world's most important ports, the nation often places near the top in rankings of economic and human development. Singaporeans have managed to balance their high population density—second among nation states only to Monaco—with their region's natural beauty. This tree-canopied spiral staircase is part of a pedestrian 'Tree Tunnel' through Fort Canning Park, one of many carefully planned green spaces within the bustling city-state.

windows-spotlight-47.jpg.title: Henry Mountains Desert Badlands Sunset, Utah
windows-spotlight-47.jpg.headline: Fly me to…
windows-spotlight-47.jpg.description: The moon lacks an atmosphere to scatter light, so there are no sunsets there, but Utah's Moonscape Overlook gives a good idea of what one might look like. And if you're in a really meta mood, you can see this lunar landscape under moonlight as well: Since it's overseen by the Bureau of Land Management, backcountry camping here is open and free (though limited to 2 weeks). Just bring plenty of food and water, because you'll find about as many foraging opportunities here as on the actual moon.

windows-spotlight-470.jpg.title: Rubjerg Knude Lighthouse, sand dunes, Hjørring Denmark
windows-spotlight-470.jpg.headline: Nothing lasts forever
windows-spotlight-470.jpg.description: Built upon swirling dunes next to the North Sea, this lighthouse is destined to be swallowed by the serene landscape that surrounds it at some point in the future. First lit in 1900, Rubjerg Knude Lighthouse served the shipping lanes for almost 68 years, but wind-piled sands and rapid coastal erosion forced its retirement. The tower was expected to be totally buried by 2023, but a bout of clever engineering placed it on rails and moved it 75 metres inland, hopefully buying it several more decades. But as many a lighthouse-watching sailor can tell you, the sea can claim its due without warning, so see this unique Denmark landmark while it still stands amid the sands.

windows-spotlight-472.jpg.title: Kallur Lighthouse, green cliffs, ocean, Faroes
windows-spotlight-472.jpg.headline: The far-flung Faroes
windows-spotlight-472.jpg.description: Connected to the remote island of Mykines by a short footbridge, this landmass less than a mile long is home to a century-old beacon. Built in 1909, Hólmur Lighthouse stands surrounded by sea cliffs and seabirds on the westernmost tip of the Faroe Islands. If you were to sail due west from this North Atlantic archipelago administered by Denmark, you'd cover more than 1,000 miles of chilly seas before spotting the fjord-laced coast of Greenland—where, should you manage to alight on the icy shore, you'd still be on Danish soil.

windows-spotlight-474.jpg.title: Rocky coastline turquoise sea caves
windows-spotlight-474.jpg.headline: Which Portland is this?
windows-spotlight-474.jpg.description: Like the Isle of Portland is tied to the mainland via a skinny strip of shingle beach, this whole stretch of southern English shore is tied to the distant past—and not just in name. The fossils and formations found along the 95-mile Jurassic Coast present a geologic record that covers not just the Jurassic period, but the whole Mesozoic era and beyond. It's a story spanning hundreds of millions of years, still being written through continual coastal erosion. As winds and waves crumble this World Heritage Site's chalky cliffs bit by bit, new fossils and sediment layers are constantly being uncovered.

windows-spotlight-476.jpg.title: Dawn Winding Mountain Road, Quiraing, Isle of Skye, Scotland
windows-spotlight-476.jpg.headline: Dawn on a rugged road
windows-spotlight-476.jpg.description: Take a good look at this winding road, because it might not appear quite the same next season. Known as the Quiraing, this cluster of cliffs and crags on Scotland's Isle of Skye formed from an ancient landslide—and the ground is still moving. Sure, it's only an inch or two a year, but that's enough to make road repairs necessary on a regular basis.While the collapse that created these crags was indeed massive, it was nothing compared to the colossal rumblings that built the isle's bedrock. The basalt backbone of the Trotternish peninsula formed from lava flows that belched from a once extremely active volcano—one of several that formed the Isle of Skye's distinctive rock formations and coastal cliffs, but have long lain extinct.

windows-spotlight-477.jpg.title: Urquhart Castle ruins, autumn foliage, sunset, Loch Ness, Scotland
windows-spotlight-477.jpg.headline: See any serpents?
windows-spotlight-477.jpg.description: As a mythic spectacle, maybe only a legendary local lurker can top this lochside ruin. Steps from the shores of Loch Ness, the now-headless fortress must once have been a great perch to search for a slippery back breaching the water's surface. Folks from the Bronze Age might even have watched for Nessie's great-great-great-great-grandserpents here—evidence shows this promontory's been occupied by humans for 4,000 years. The structure we see now was built much later, in the 13th century, and was the site of many a Scottish clan's skirmish. That is, until the jolly English blew it up in 1692. Since then it's stood guard in peace, with only an elusive lake monster to keep it company (well, that and literal boatloads of tourists).

windows-spotlight-478.jpg.title: Tantallon Castle Bass Rock sunset, Seacliff Beach Scotland
windows-spotlight-478.jpg.headline: Of drills and decoys
windows-spotlight-478.jpg.description: There's a lot going on in this shot, from the ruin of Tantallon Castle at left to the solitary Bass Rock at right—and a beach bathed in sunset in between. During World War II, this spot would have been witness to yet more action, as the Royal Air Force used this part of the outer Firth of Forth for training. It's not the most famous beach in WWII history, but there's a connection to the war's best-known battle: The RAF developed a technique here to confuse German radar by dropping decoy aluminum strips into the sea, which they did during the D-Day landings to distract the enemy from the beaches of Normandy.

windows-spotlight-480.jpg.title: Human-made Tiered Cascade Sunset Mountains
windows-spotlight-480.jpg.headline: A human-made cascade
windows-spotlight-480.jpg.description: From this perspective, these falls look a bit like a palatial staircase. From high above, they look more like dragon scales, and their human-made origin is evident. Our low angle obscures the bridges and buildings of Huyuan township, one of several scenic villages this brook bisects as it's corralled by water management features like this one. Huyuan is among a great many townships dividing up the vast Chinese municipality of Hangzhou, home to almost 12 million people across 6,500 largely rural square miles.

windows-spotlight-481.jpg.title: Green trees, blue seas, rocky coast
windows-spotlight-481.jpg.headline: Green trees, blue seas
windows-spotlight-481.jpg.description: Look at a map of Croatia and the first thing you'll probably notice is its long, tangled coastline of peninsulas, inlets, islands and waterways. Zoom in and you'll find a variety of seaside landscapes, from rugged rock outcrops like this one to calm (but often crowded) beaches. Add it all together and there's more than 5,700 kilometres of beautiful Adriatic Sea shoreline to explore within this bustling Balkan nation.

windows-spotlight-483.jpg.title: Red sandstone cliffs, blue ocean, Prince Edward Island, Canada
windows-spotlight-483.jpg.headline: A princely province
windows-spotlight-483.jpg.description: This province may be Canada's smallest, but it sure stands out against the clear blue Gulf of St. Lawrence. The soil and sandstone of Prince Edward Island has an earthy red color because it's full of iron oxide, better known as rust. That might not sound appetizing, but the island's top-grade spuds, sold all over Canada, speak for themselves. The red landscape also recalls the ginger hair of a local literary heroine: Anne of Green Gables, whose creator Lucy Maud Montgomery grew up here in Cavendish.

windows-spotlight-484.jpg.title: Snow-capped peaks, high altitude lake, golden grasslands
windows-spotlight-484.jpg.headline: A well-earned view
windows-spotlight-484.jpg.description: You've truly reached the heights of backcountry trekking if you find yourself circling the Peruvian peak called Ausangate. Hikers here will contend with elevations ranging from 12,000 to nearly 17,000 feet, making this 43-mile trek one of the most elevated on the South American map. The big upside: You'll find far fewer folks here than at other attractions in the vicinity of Cusco, like Vinicunca and the ever-crowded Machu Picchu.

windows-spotlight-487.jpg.title: Bugling Bull Elk Pine Forest
windows-spotlight-487.jpg.headline: A beast on the bugle
windows-spotlight-487.jpg.description: The distinctive call of the bull elk—known as a bugle—is a familiar sound each fall here in Colorado's Rocky Mountain National Park. Human visitors often describe the vocalizations as eerie and haunting, but if you're a cow elk, they're downright dreamy. Bugling is a key element of elk mating rituals, and every bull does it differently, weaving high-pitched whistles with throaty grunts to create compositions all their own. Bugles are complex and able to convey a variety of messages—but usually the gist is, 'Hey ladies, look at me!'

windows-spotlight-488.jpg.title: Orange Red Yellow Magenta Sunset Clouds Ocean
windows-spotlight-488.jpg.headline: Painting or photo?
windows-spotlight-488.jpg.description: Although this sunset snapshot may remind you of an abstract expressionist painting, Mother Nature creates these colors not by adding together pigments but by cutting light apart. At sunset or sunrise, white light from the sun must travel farther to reach your eye, striking more tiny atmospheric particles along the way, than at high noon. The particles scatter light like a prism, preventing portions of the color spectrum from entering your retinas—especially cool, low-wavelength blues and greens. Your optic nerves supply your brain with what remains: a wash of warm brushstrokes in orange and violet.

windows-spotlight-490.jpg.title: Benagil Cave skylit beach, Algarve, Portugal
windows-spotlight-490.jpg.headline: Skylit shore
windows-spotlight-490.jpg.description: Even amidst the many spectacular cliffs and sea caves that line southern Portugal's Algarve coast, Benagil Cave is an eye-catcher. The cave was formed about 20 million years ago from the pounding waves that sweep in from the Atlantic. Rainfall has caused softer segments of limestone to erode, creating a giant hole in the cave's roof, which is what we're looking down through in our photo. The eye-shaped opening allows sunlight to stream into the cave, illuminating the golden beach and azure waters within its walls.

windows-spotlight-493.jpg.title: Rainbow rooftops coastal village, Punta Brava, Tenerife
windows-spotlight-493.jpg.headline: A rainbow of rooftops
windows-spotlight-493.jpg.description: In this section of Spain, coastal settlements form a big ring around the nation's highest mountain, Mount Teide, as cold Atlantic waters crash against cliff-lined outcrops like Punta Brava. From this spot on the bustling isle of Tenerife, Morocco lies much closer across the waters than mainland Spain, as does Madeira, a territory of Portugal. The centre of culture here in the Canary Islands, Tenerife is the most populous place in Macaronesia, made even livelier by droves of tourists seeking the sultry south from across Europe when it's cold on the continent.

windows-spotlight-496.jpg.title: Meerkat family huddle
windows-spotlight-496.jpg.headline: Not the mama?
windows-spotlight-496.jpg.description: We're not sure if this adult meerkat is these pups' mama or their babysitter. Both roles are important in rearing meerkat young, as most pups are born to older, dominant females and then cared for by the mob's younger adults. This adorable family-portrait pose is actually a defensive posture: By covering the pups with its body, the adult is helping hide the pups from birds of prey, one of many dangers for meerkats as they scavenge wide-open plains for insects to eat.

windows-spotlight-499.jpg.title: Twisting Red Sandstone Slot Canyon, Antelope Canyon, Page, Arizona
windows-spotlight-499.jpg.headline: Twisting twin canyons
windows-spotlight-499.jpg.description: This probably isn't your first time seeing Antelope Canyon—this red-sandstone marvel is the most photographed slot canyon in the United States. But did you know it's not just one canyon, but two?
